standard_paragraphs.label: RADON
standard_paragraphs.text: Radon is a radioactive gas that naturally forms from the decay of uranium in soil, rock, and water, and can accumulate in buildings, potentially posing health risks. Data provided by the UK Health Security Agency (previously Public Health England) shows that the property is situated in an area with elevated radon potential within a 1km radius, with a maximum potential of 3-5%. Radon levels of 3-5% can pose health risks, such as an increased risk of lung cancer, with increased danger for smokers and long-term exposure. It is not possible to determine whether radon gas is present at the property since the gas is colourless and odourless. Every building contains some level of radon, but the likelihood of higher radon levels in your home depends on the levels in the ground below, with radon typically entering through the floors. It is uncertain as to whether basic radon protection measures have been installed at the property. You may wish to enquire with the vendor as to whether they have installed any protective measures or whether they are aware of any measures having been installed in the past. You may consider the benefits of home radon testing. To our knowledge, you can order a Home Measurement Pack from https://www.ukradon.org/ for a small fee which is measured by the UK Health Security Agency upon return of the device. We are not specialists in this field and the exact impact of this on health and the saleability of the property cannot be confirmed as the matter falls outside the scope of a home survey. Should you have concerns, it is advisable to seek advice from the UK Health Security Agency and a radon specialist.

standard_paragraphs.label: Tenanted
standard_paragraphs.text: The property is currently tenanted. It is crucial to ask your legal adviser to confirm whether the property will be sold with full vacant possession and to explain the implications of this. If the property is sold with tenants in place, you will inherit their existing tenancy agreements, which may impact your plans for the property. This means you would need to comply with the terms of the lease, and any attempts to regain possession would have to follow legal procedures, potentially delaying your use or renovation plans. In contrast, purchasing with full vacant possession means that the property will be empty at the time of sale, allowing you to take immediate control and make decisions about the property without dealing with existing tenants. Your legal adviser should also clarify any potential issues related to tenant eviction, rental income, and the tenant's rights. Ensure that these details are fully understood and agreed upon to avoid complications after the purchase.

standard_paragraphs.label: Cladded at upper levels 5&6 storeys NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: The upper floor level of the building and the areas surrounding the balconies are metal-clad. We could not ascertain if these panels are ACM, MCM, or HPL panels as we are not specialists in this area, and this also falls outside the scope of a Home Survey. It should be appreciated that visual inspections and assessments based on as-built information have limitations. In some cases, an intrusive inspection may be necessary to fully identify the cladding system and essential fire safety components. The RICS Guidance Note advises that for buildings of 5-6 storeys, and where there are ACM, MCM, or HPL panels on the building, an EWS1 form will be required. RICS guidance was drafted with reference to government guidance in force at the time, which has now been withdrawn. However, the RICS guidance note remains valid at this time. The EWS1 form is not a safety certificate, and the fact that an EWS1 form is not required for a particular building does not mean that the building may not require some form of remediation in the future. There may be costs of remediation at some point in the future depending upon a full fire risk assessment of the building, which includes a fire risk appraisal and assessment of the external wall construction. Many high street lenders still do not lend on a property where there are ACM, MCM, or HPL panels installed, irrespective of the height of the building and irrespective of where the panels are in relation to the subject property. Therefore, the building management should confirm if the cladding may be ACM, MCM, or HPL panels. If a legally binding meaningful confirmation cannot be obtained, then your solicitor should request an EWS1 form as this may well affect the future saleability of the property. Only one assessment will be needed for each building, and this will be valid for five years (see Section H1). Note: The process to obtain an EWS1 will require a fire safety assessment to be conducted by a suitably qualified and competent professional to inspect the cladding applied to the property and provide a report on its combustibility. The EWS1 form must be completed by a fully qualified member of a relevant professional body within the construction industry. Qualified professionals, such as chartered members of the Institution of Fire Engineers (IFE) and the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), are expected to have the expertise to identify relevant materials within the external wall cladding and attachments, including the correct installation of fire-resisting cavity barriers and fire stopping. These professionals should possess the necessary self-assessed competence and professional indemnity insurance to carry out this work. However, there are very few people in the UK with the qualifications and experience required to sign an EWS1 certificate. Although the building was constructed in 2019/2020, an EWS1 form may still be required for a new build from 2019 in certain situations. EWS1 (External Wall Fire Review) forms have become more commonly requested following concerns over fire safety in buildings with cladding or other external wall systems that may pose a fire risk. Even though a new build from 2019 should theoretically comply with current building regulations, some mortgage lenders and insurers may still require an EWS1 form as part of their due diligence process. This is especially true if the building has any external wall materials or systems that could potentially pose a fire risk, such as certain types of cladding. You are advised not to proceed to purchase until all recommended further investigations have been undertaken and you have been made fully aware of your immediate and longer-term liabilities.

Building Regulations approvals are required for any structural alterations and are a very important part of any building works. If no certificates are available, the matter must be discussed with the Local Authority Building Control Body (BCB), and depending on the date of the works, the Local Authority may advise that a “Regularisation Certificate” be sought. A Regularisation Certificate is a retrospective application relating to previously unauthorised works, i.e., works carried out without Building Regulations approval starting on or after the 11th of November 1985. Only work carried out after this date can be approved in this way. It is our understanding that if the building works were carried out before November 1985, they would not require Building Regulations approval. If a certificate has been lost, a copy can be obtained from the local authority, although a fee may be payable. standard_paragraphs.label: Poor Condition £2000 Assumption NEW LONG PARA AMEND
standard_paragraphs.text: As per the Terms of Engagement dated 9th September 2024, we have undertaken a Market Valuation of the property. The valuation is provided on a “Market Value” basis, which is defined by the RICS Valuation –

standard_paragraphs.label: Global Standards 2022 (the Red Book) as follows
standard_paragraphs.text: “Market Value” is the estimated amount for which a property should exchange on the date of the valuation between a willing buyer and a willing seller, in an arm’s length transaction after the property was properly marketed wherein the parties had each acted knowledgeably, prudently and without compulsion. We measured the property utilising a calibrated laser distometer. The total floor area of the property, based on IPMS 3B of the RICS Property Measurement Professional Standards, is 140 sq.m (1507 sq.ft). This measurement is exclusive of the lean-to, as explained later. We have disregarded the presence of the lean-to due to its very poor state and substandard quality. As per our Terms of Engagement, given the property’s poor state of repair, the valuation figure provided in the report is based on a “Special Assumption” that the remediation costs to carry out necessary repairs would not exceed £2,000 to bring the property to an ‘average’ condition. A Special Assumption is made to assist a valuation scenario and is a supposition accepted as fact, even though it may not be true. A valuation of this property in its current state of repair is not possible, as it would make the valuation highly subjective. Therefore, the only viable way to value the property is by way of a “Special Assumption.” The necessary repairs highlighted in this report primarily involve Condition 3 ratings, which will require immediate attention. The valuation is based on special assumptions that: A) Any major defects listed as Condition Rating 3 in this report have been resolved by competent contractors; for example, leaks to the roof and damp, along with other necessary repairs detailed later in the report, have been addressed, bringing the property to an average standard acceptable to lenders and prospective purchasers. This is not an exhaustive list. The assumption is that by completing essential repair works and resolving the Condition Rating 3 defects identified in this report, the property will achieve a minimum average condition. B) The presence of the lean-to at the rear has been disregarded due to its deteriorated state. It has been excluded from the valuation, as additional expenditure will be required for its demolition. C) In accordance with our terms of engagement, we have assumed that all necessary local authority consents, including Building Regulations and Planning Consent, have been obtained for any structural alterations or modifications made to the property. The valuation provided is based on the special assumption that all regulatory requirements have been satisfied and that there are no breaches of Building Regulations or Planning Consent. We have considered, as much as possible, the overall poor state of the property and fittings when using the comparative method of valuation. However, valuation is not a scientific mathematical approach to calculate the exact costs of repairs and deduct them from the value. Valuation is a mixture of art and science, and a level of subjectivity is involved. It is anticipated that the remedial costs will exceed £2,000. To clarify, the £2,000 figure is a conservative estimate intended to reflect a hypothetical scenario for repair costs on a property of this age and in average condition, where some necessary repairs are typically expected and are unlikely to significantly impact the property’s value. However, this figure is not binding and bears no specific relevance to this property other than as a guide to facilitate valuation purposes. In this case, it is highly likely that the actual cost of repairs will significantly exceed £2,000. It is important to note that cost does not always equal value. For instance, spending £10,000 on repairs, redecoration, or refurbishment may not increase the property’s value by £10,000. It is important to note that before making any commitment to purchase, you should obtain reports and quotations from a range of specialists and competent contractors, and conduct full investigations into all defects as highlighted in the report. These should provide detailed cost estimates for necessary repairs and further advice. We must caution that should you proceed to exchange contracts without securing this information, you accept the risk that unforeseen adverse issues may arise in the future. Additionally, any cost estimates you obtain may serve as a potential negotiating tool for the purchase price, depending on your bargaining position as the buyer. However, please be aware that our valuation and such quotations are not typically binding on the vendor, and we are unable to provide further comment on this matter. Please note, in accordance with our Terms of Engagement, we do not provide cost estimates for repairs. A limitation in our valuation is the uncertainty surrounding the current economic climate, influenced by factors such as inflation and mortgage rates. Elevated inflation, high mortgage lending rates, and the rising cost of living are undermining consumer confidence and directly impacting the housing market. High mortgage interest rates are causing many potential buyers to reconsider their purchasing decisions due to affordability concerns. The current Bank of England base rate is 5% as of 19th September 2024, with the next review scheduled for 7th November 2024. According to Moneyfacts, the average two-year fixed rate has decreased from 5.64% last month to 5.47%. Rates tend to be lower for new buyers, especially those with large deposits, as lenders are focused on attracting new business, whilst remortgaging rates remain higher. However, these rates remain high compared to historical levels. Nationwide reports that many first-time buyers are hesitating to enter the market due to high house prices and borrowing costs. Approximately half of those considering their first home purchase within the next five years have postponed their plans over the past year. Prospective buyers are struggling to save for deposits, while the benchmark lending rate is at its highest level in 16 years. Despite predictions of a significant downturn last year, the UK housing market’s recent recovery has been lacklustre. Reports from Nationwide suggest that market momentum is unlikely to rebound quickly due to weak consumer confidence and the strain on household budgets caused by high inflation and rising interest rates. Although we are mindful of the above, our valuation is based on the date of inspection and the data available at that time, without consideration of future price predictions. Our valuation is reported on the basis of “material uncertainty” as per VPS 3 and VPGA 10 of the RICS Red Book Global 2022. As a result, less certainty—and a higher degree of caution—should be attached to our valuation than would normally be the case. We recommend that you keep the valuation of this property under regular review. The Market Value of the property, based on the above assumptions and caveats, as well as the uncertainty involved, as of the date of inspection, is £540,000 (Five Hundred Forty Thousand Pounds). It is important to distinguish between price and value. The price a seller may wish to market the property for is not necessarily the same as its market value. For instance, if a seller consults a local estate agent to market their property, they are likely to suggest a higher price, reflecting the amount they believe could be achieved, depending on the number of potential buyers and their influence in the market. Please note that any valuation provided by an estate agent is considered an "appraisal," not a formal RICS Red Book valuation, unless the agent is a registered valuer. Our valuation is not binding, and the final decision regarding the sale price ultimately rests with the property owner.

standard_paragraphs.label: Cavity Wall Insulation
standard_paragraphs.text: The existing EPC report recommends cavity wall insulation as a measure to improve energy efficiency. However, as noted in section D4, we could not determine whether the main walls currently have any retrospective cavity wall insulation. Without detailed and potentially invasive investigations, it is not possible to confirm the presence of cavity insulation. If cavity wall insulation is present, it may contain urea formaldehyde (foam fill). Your solicitor should investigate further, and if this is the case, you should review any guarantees associated with the insulation work to ensure the benefit is transferred upon completion of the sale (see section I3). Cavity wall insulation (CWI) can effectively improve a home's energy efficiency, but it comes with potential risks that must be carefully considered. Incorrect or inappropriate installation can lead to moisture penetration, especially if the insulation material becomes saturated with water, which can then bridge the cavity and seep into the interior walls. This moisture can cause mould growth, structural damage, and deterioration of internal finishes. Cavity foam can adhere to mortar droppings on wall ties, creating a bridge across the cavity and leading to localised damp spots on internal walls. Therefore, the quality of installation is crucial. Poor installation can result in gaps or uneven distribution of insulation material, reducing effectiveness and creating cold spots or thermal bridging. Different insulation materials have varying properties, such as water absorption rates, thermal performance, and resistance to settling over time. Some materials, like certain foams, can break down or shrink, compromising the insulation’s effectiveness. Using inappropriate materials for your property type or climate can lead to reduced performance and potential structural issues. Additionally, cavity wall insulation reduces the natural ventilation through walls. If not properly managed, this can trap moisture inside the structure, exacerbating dampness, reducing indoor air quality, and causing condensation problems. If you decide to install cavity wall insulation, it is essential to hire experienced and certified installers who will use appropriate materials suited to your property. You should also inquire whether they offer meaningful guarantees backed by independent bodies or insurance companies, ensuring that these guarantees can be transferred to future buyers. This will help ensure that the work is of high quality and that you are covered for any potential structural problems, such as internal dampness or other complications, that might arise after installation.

standard_paragraphs.label: Wall insulation Flats and conservation NEW (Amend)
standard_paragraphs.text: In the section “Steps you could take to save energy” of the EPC certificate, there are references to both internal and external wall insulation. Most solid walls were originally built to be ‘vapour-open’, allowing moisture to pass through. Insulating walls with ‘vapour-closed’ materials, such as foil-faced insulation foam, risks trapping moisture inside the wall, which could lead to damp, mould, and structural damage. Installing internal or external wall insulation carries several risks that should be carefully considered. Internally, wall insulation can reduce room space and, if not properly installed, may cause moisture build-up, leading to mould growth and poor indoor air quality. Whilst external wall insulation preserves internal space, it can alter the building’s appearance and often requires Building Regulations approval. Additionally, planning permission may be necessary depending on the extent of the work, particularly as this property is in a conservation area. In any case, applying insulation only to the walls of the subject flat will not be practical, and there are implications such as the need for consent from neighbouring properties or the building management. Therefore, overall, this advice cannot be easily followed. Poor installation can result in thermal bridging, where gaps in the insulation allow heat to escape, reducing its effectiveness. Both types of insulation can be costly and may require significant investment in high-quality materials and professional installation to ensure long-term benefits and avoid structural damage. A thorough assessment and installation by qualified professionals are essential to mitigate these risks and achieve optimal energy efficiency and comfort.

standard_paragraphs.label: Suspended timber insulation, internal damp noted VERY NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: In the section "Steps you could take to save energy" of the current EPC certificate dated xxx, which is the latest EPC record available from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, reference is made to insulation in suspended timber floors. It is essential to maintain adequate ventilation beneath timber ground floors to prevent moisture conditions that could lead to underfloor rot. As noted in Section E3 of the report, we recorded high damp readings at ground floor level in various locations. Suspended timber floors require adequate subfloor ventilation, which allows moisture ingress to evaporate gradually as part of the natural vapour permeability and breathing cycle of a traditional building. The introduction of insulation to suspended timber floors can interrupt this cycle, potentially exacerbating moisture retention and leading to further damp-related complications. Adding insulation to suspended timber floors may increase the risk of interstitial condensation affecting the subfloor timbers. Accordingly, we advise against implementing such measures.

standard_paragraphs.label: Internal wall insulation
standard_paragraphs.text: In the section 'Steps you could take to save energy' of the EPC certificate, references are made to internal wall insulation. It is important to note that most solid walls were originally constructed to be 'vapour-open,' allowing moisture to pass through naturally. Insulating such walls with 'vapour-closed' materials, such as foil-faced insulation foam, carries the risk of trapping moisture within the wall structure, potentially leading to damp, mould growth, and even structural damage. Both internal and external wall insulation carry inherent risks that require careful consideration. Internally, insulation can reduce room space and, if not correctly installed, may lead to moisture accumulation, causing mould growth and compromised indoor air quality. Whilst external insulation preserves internal space, it can alter the building's external appearance and may require Building Regulations approval. In some cases, planning permission might also be necessary, depending on the scope and location of the works. Poor installation of either system can create thermal bridging, where gaps in insulation allow heat to escape, reducing the overall effectiveness. Furthermore, both methods represent a significant financial investment, requiring high-quality materials and professional expertise to ensure durability, energy efficiency, and the prevention of long-term damage. A thorough assessment by suitably qualified professionals is therefore essential, both to identify the most appropriate solution for the property and to ensure correct installation, thereby minimising risks and maximising energy efficiency and comfort.

standard_paragraphs.label: Minimum requirement by 2028
standard_paragraphs.text: As of now, the minimum energy efficiency standard for private rented properties in England and Wales remains an EPC rating of Band E, under the Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES), legally required since April 2020 . However, the government is now advancing plans to raise these standards. A consultation launched in late 2024 and closed in February 2025 revisited proposals to upgrade MEES to Band C, taking account of evolving EPC metrics, including fabric performance, heating-system efficiency, and smart-readiness, due to planned EPC reforms in 2026. Under proposed new timelines, which remain subject to final legislation, all new tenancies will be legally required to meet a minimum EPC rating of Band C from 2028. This requirement will then extend to all existing tenancies by 2030, in line with the government’s revised timetable and anticipated reforms to the EPC framework.

standard_paragraphs.label: Tree roots explanation
standard_paragraphs.text: Tree roots extract moisture, causing shrinkage in the subsoil on which the foundations are bearing, particularly during drought conditions when shrinkage of the subsoil can cause subsidence of the foundations. Conversely, when trees are removed swelling of the subsoil can occur causing 'heave' resulting in upward movement of foundations.

standard_paragraphs.label: Seek specialist tree advice
standard_paragraphs.text: When trees are removed the roots no longer extract moisture and this can result, over a period of years, in gradual expansion of the clay subsoil to its natural volume, which carries a risk of possible structural damage. Advice from an Arboriculturist would be prudent before contemplating major tree surgery.

standard_paragraphs.label: NEW-sandy clays, silty clays
standard_paragraphs.text: According to British Geological Survey online records, the geology of the Harwich Formation is characterised by a mix of sandy clays, silty clays, and fine to medium-grained sands, often with a glauconitic (green mineral) component. This formation, deposited in shallow marine to estuarine and deltaic environments during the early Eocene epoch (approximately 56 to 47.8 million years ago), may also contain calcareous materials. The presence of clay within the formation, often mixed with sand and silt, suggests variable soil properties, including potential low permeability and shrink-swell behaviour. Found predominantly in southeastern England, particularly around the Thames Estuary and parts of Essex and Suffolk, the Harwich Formation's composition and depositional history make it a notable feature of the region's subsurface geology. Bomb Damage

standard_paragraphs.label: Minor Blast Damage (AMEND)
standard_paragraphs.text: According to our research into the London County Council Bomb Damage Maps from 1939–1945, the subject property and adjacent buildings sustained bombing during World War II, with the map indicating “minor blast damage.” Bombing was widespread across London during this period, and such damage is not uncommon. Properties in affected areas may have undergone partial reconstruction or refurbishment, and there is a possibility of lingering structural issues or concealed damage resulting from those historical events. However, this does not necessarily indicate severe structural concerns, provided adequate repairs and reinforcements were made. Bomb damage maps are general in nature and do not offer precise information about the type or extent of damage to individual buildings. Therefore, each property should be assessed on its own merits, with an emphasis on current structural performance rather than historical classifications alone. The actual impact on the subject property is largely unknown and may have been concealed by refurbishments over time. For example, as noted in Section D4 of the report, some brickwork to the rear appears to have been replaced in the past. Nonetheless, a visual inspection of both internal and external elements of the flat did not reveal any significant defects or signs of structural instability. That said, the first-floor level and roof structure were not inspected internally, therefore no conclusions can be drawn regarding those areas. In summary, whilst the precise extent of historical bomb damage remains uncertain, current visual observations do not indicate cause for concern.

standard_paragraphs.label: Bomb Damage (General Blast)
standard_paragraphs.text: According to our research into the London County Council Bomb Damage Maps from 1939–1945, the subject property and adjacent buildings were damaged by bombing during World War II. The rating provided on the map indicates "general blast damage." When considering the purchase of a property in an area with a history of bomb damage, it is important to acknowledge that properties in such locations may have undergone substantial or partial reconstruction or refurbishment due to past incidents. As a result, there could be lingering structural issues or concealed damage that may affect the property's construction. Whilst this does not necessarily indicate severe structural issues with the building, as long as adequate repairs and reinforcements have been carried out, purchasing a property previously affected by bomb damage should not inherently pose a concern. During wartime, many London houses were impacted, making this a common occurrence. However, this factor alone should not dictate your decision-making process. Instead, the overall structural performance of the building should be assessed, as the extent of damage is typically unknown. Bomb damage maps are generic in nature and may not provide precise details regarding the specific type of damage sustained by individual properties. standard_paragraphs.label: Medium risk from surface water increased to high (NEW)
standard_paragraphs.text: According to the Environment Agency (the government body responsible for flood management), the property is located in an area identified as being at medium risk of flooding from surface water. Medium risk indicates an annual probability of flooding of between 1% and 3.3%, whilst high risk indicates a probability greater than 3.3%. It is projected that this area will have a higher likelihood of surface water flooding between 2040 and 2060. Climate change is increasing the risk of flooding, with climate models forecasting warmer, wetter winters and more frequent extreme weather events. These models use projected rainfall, sea level rise and river flows to estimate flood risk for different periods: 2040 to 2060 for surface water and 2036 to 2069 for rivers and the sea. However, they cannot predict exactly when an increase in risk will occur within these periods. You should refer this matter to your legal adviser and contact your insurance provider to confirm that they will offer cover for a property in this location. If insurance is unavailable or prohibitively expensive, it may affect the property’s future saleability (see Section H3 of this report).

Whilst the subject unit is less likely to be directly affected by potential defects to the chimney stacks, these could form part of a shared management commitment. We have not studied the lease. In any event, rights and responsibilities for maintenance should be investigated by your legal adviser. From ground level, we observed two chimney stacks serving the building and the property. As previously mentioned, the roof is of a butterfly structure, and due to the lack of an accessible vantage point, these could not be fully inspected. It is likely that some deterioration has occurred, and minor works can be expected. Repairs should be anticipated, and the chimney pots may also require rebedding. The chimney stacks are of brick construction, topped with clay chimney pots set in cement flaunchings. Chimney stacks are particularly exposed to the weather, so regular maintenance must be carried out to ensure their stability and weather-tightness. Chimney repairs tend to be expensive due to the associated scaffolding costs. Modern chimney stack designs incorporate barriers intended to reduce dampness below roof level. Such precautions are unlikely to have been included in a building of this age, so some measure of damp penetration must be expected. There are TV aerials attached to the chimney stacks. From a limited view, the aerials and fixings currently appear satisfactory. However, they should be inspected every six months for signs of deterioration.

standard_paragraphs.label: Strong Mortar
standard_paragraphs.text: Missing pointing will result in water penetration and further deterioration to the mortar bedding. The existing mortar appears to contain a high cement ratio which is not good building practice for a property of this age, and over time can cause problems such as spalling of the bricks. A common misconception is that mortar requires a large proportion of cement in the mix, but too rich a cement content can cause serious problems. Unfortunately, this damage has already been done to the bricks and removing the existing pointing may cause even further damage to the bricks, therefore at this stage, it is advisable to just undertake localised repointing including the replacement of all damaged bricks. The chimney stack then should be monitored on a regular basis and in the case of any future spalling noted, the existing mortar should be raked out and replaced with lime mortar. Some bricks may have to be replaced as this work can be destructive to an old building. In this case, it will be essential for the joints to be raked out sufficiently, usually to a depth of not less than 15-20 mm so the new mortar is given sufficient key. Failure to do this can result in the new pointing simply cracking and falling out over a relatively short timescale. Any work will have to be entrusted to an experienced bricklayer to provide further advice and a cost estimate for remediation should be obtained before a commitment to a purchase is made. standard_paragraphs.label: unfelt not lapped inside of the gutter
standard_paragraphs.text: Where partially visible, we observed that the underfelt at the edges of the roof on the two-storey rear addition is not correctly lapped into the gutter. The primary function of roofing underfelt is to provide an additional layer of protection against water penetration. Properly lapping the felt into the rainwater gutter ensures that any water that gets beneath the roof tiles is directed into the gutter, preventing it from running down the fascia or into the building structure. If the roofing felt is not properly lapped into the gutter, water could potentially seep behind the gutter or into the wall structure, leading to dampness, rot, or other moisture-related issues. The underfelt should extend beyond the edge of the roof and into the gutter to ensure that water flows directly into the gutter. Care must be taken to avoid sagging of the felt, as this can cause water to pool and potentially overflow into unintended areas. If the underfelt is not properly supported and installed, it can "sag," causing rainwater to collect and allowing the leading edge of the felt to fall behind the gutter. Further investigation by a competent roofing contractor is recommended to carry out the necessary repairs and ensure the roof coverings are fully watertight. Additionally, the condition of the roof timbers at the edges of the roof should be checked to ensure there is no rot. Whist this work is not urgent; since no visible signs of water ingress were noted during our inspection, hidden defects may exist. It is advisable that when the roof is eventually replaced in the future, a complete overhaul of this area be carried out by a competent roofing contractor to ensure proper detailing and compliance with Building Regulations. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.text: Whilst the subject unit is less likely to be directly affected by potential defects to the main roof, these could form part of a shared management commitment. We have not studied the lease. In any event, rights and responsibilities for maintenance should be investigated by your legal adviser. The main roof is a butterfly structure. The roof coverings could not be inspected as there was no available vantage point. This type of roof structure utilises horizontal valley gutters to aid rainwater runoff. These are usually concealed from view by parapet walls or the building’s façade. Valleys are always potential problem areas and should be regularly inspected and repaired as necessary. However, we could not inspect this section due to the lack of an available vantage point. Condition Rating: NI. Where visible from the rear communal garden, the mortar bedding in the roof verges showed signs of deterioration, with some areas of mortar missing, creating holes. Although this is less likely to affect the subject flat, over the long term, any potential water ingress could affect the roof structure or surrounding areas. Condition Rating: 2. The horizontal valley gutter between the pitched slopes could not be inspected due to the lack of an accessible vantage point. Access would require a long builder’s ladder, which falls outside the scope of this survey. Valley gutters are notoriously prone to leakage and should be fully inspected prior to any legal commitment to purchase. Even if in good condition, they can become blocked by leaves, snow, or ice, causing water to overflow and seep into the building’s structure. Condensation on the underside of the lead lining can also lead to dampness and decay in roof timbers. Maintenance and repairs for valley gutters can be costly, making regular inspection and cleaning essential. Condition Rating NI. When carrying out repairs to the verges of the roof, it is advisable to closely inspect the condition of the roof coverings, including the separating walls, the parapet wall at the front, and all roof elements, such as the horizontal valley gutter. This will help to ensure that any other potential defects are identified and addressed simultaneously.

Moss and lichen can inhibit the roof’s efficiency by trapping moisture, which can lead to the deterioration of roof materials over time. Additionally, the build-up of moss can cause blockages in gutters and rainwater goods, impeding the proper drainage of rainwater and increasing the risk of water ingress into the property. We also recommend that when moss removal is undertaken, the pointing and bedding of the ridge tiles are thoroughly inspected. Over time, moss can dislodge or conceal cracks and weaknesses in the mortar, which may compromise the roof’s structural integrity and weatherproofing. Regular maintenance will help preserve the roof’s condition and prevent costly repairs in the future. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Cement mortar flashing GENERAL NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: Cement mortar flashing is a type of waterproofing material commonly used in construction to seal joints and transitions in building structures, particularly in areas where water might penetrate, such as roof abutments, chimneys, and parapet walls. It typically consists of a mixture of cement, sand, and water, which is applied in layers to create a durable barrier against moisture. However, over time, cement mortar flashing can be prone to cracking and deterioration, especially when exposed to harsh weather conditions. This deterioration can compromise its effectiveness in preventing water ingress, leading to potential leaks and damage to the building.

standard_paragraphs.label: Lead CARBONATION causing staining on glazing NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: The abutments of the pitched skylight with the rear elevation have been dressed with lead flashing. We noted white staining on the glazing panels of the rear pitched skylight, a common issue caused by lead carbonation. The lead flashing showed signs of discolouration, which also appeared to have caused staining on the glazing of the skylight. Lead carbonation is a chemical reaction where lead reacts with carbon dioxide in the air to form lead carbonate, a white or light-coloured compound. This process affects the structural integrity and appearance of lead-containing materials. In the early stages after construction, lead carbonate can form and run onto the surrounding areas below. If cleaned promptly, this does not cause a problem, but if left untreated, the lead carbonate can dry on the surrounding surfaces, leaving a stain that resembles limescale on a shower screen. Once dried, the staining can be difficult to remove and often requires an abrasive cleaner. The staining appeared to be of some age and appeared to have caused permanent discolouration on the glazing. These stains reduce the skylight's visual appeal and clarity. They are not merely a cosmetic concern; they also indicate ongoing chemical processes that may compromise the material's integrity. Repairs will be required to mitigate lead carbonation, which is essential to maintain the skylight's appearance and durability. Effective cleaning prevents further reactions, maintaining the skylight's clarity and beauty. The lead flashing should be checked closely by a competent contractor and cleaned/restored if possible. In some cases, lead flashings may deteriorate and need to be replaced. Lead is recyclable and has a life expectancy in excess of 100 years if installed correctly and kept in good condition. The stains on the glazing may be difficult or impossible to remove completely, therefore a competent glazier should provide further advice. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Discolouration to lead flashings
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted signs of discolouration on the lead flashings. Lead can become discoloured over time due to exposure to the elements. This discolouration is typically caused by oxidation, which occurs when lead reacts with oxygen, carbon dioxide, and other environmental pollutants. Acid rain and air pollution can accelerate this process, leading to uneven colouring and potential streaking. Regular cleaning and maintenance can help manage discolouration, but it is generally considered a natural and expected characteristic of aging lead. In some cases, specialised treatments can be applied to restore or preserve the appearance of the lead surface. However, in cases where lead deteriorates, there may be no option but to replace it. Lead is recyclable and has a life expectancy in excess of 100 years if installed correctly and kept in good condition. The lead flashings should be checked closely by a competent contractor when repairs to other areas are undertaken and cleaned/restored if possible. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Butterfly roof description
standard_paragraphs.text: Butterfly roofs are also commonly known as inverted pitch roofs, or London roofs. They consist of two V shaped roof slopes which meet at the base of the V in a central valley gutter, running from front to rear of the property, which usually drains through a gap in the rear parapet wall into a hopper gutter and downpipe. There is a horizontal valley gutter at the junction of the butterfly roofs and this is lined with lead. Valleys are always potential problem areas and should be regularly inspected and repaired as necessary. Valley gutters are notoriously prone to leakage problems and a full inspection is recommended prior to legal commitment to purchase. Even valley gutters which are in sound condition can become blocked by leaves, snow and ice, causing water levels to rise above the edges of the lead and seep into the fabric of the building. Condensation on the underside of the lead lining to the valley gutters can also cause dampness, with an associated risk of decay to the roof timbers. It should be noted maintenance and repair costs, when needed, tend to be expensive. It is important the valley gutters should be regularly inspected and cleaned. Where partially visible, no significant defects were noted. Hidden defects may exist in unseen areas. Condition Rating 1.

standard_paragraphs.label: Spalled concrete tiles and slipped(AMEND) NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: Where visible, some of the roof tiles had slipped, some tiles had spalled, and some tiles had lifted, creating gaps that could allow for water ingress internally. Concrete roof tiles can experience spalling, which is the flaking or breaking off of layers, often due to prolonged exposure to moisture and freeze-thaw cycles. This deterioration can compromise the integrity of the tiles, leading to leaks and potential structural damage. Spalling is typically identified by the presence of chipped or delaminated surfaces on the tiles. The rough, uneven surface created by spalling can also accumulate debris and moisture, exacerbating the deterioration process. Repairs often involve replacing the damaged tiles to ensure the roof remains watertight and functional. Ignoring spalling can lead to more extensive and costly repairs in the future. The slipped and spalled tiles should be replaced, and all lifted tiles should be laid flat to prevent wind-driven rain from entering the roof space. Further investigation by a competent roofing contractor is required, and you should obtain a cost estimate for the repairs. Regular inspection and maintenance are essential to identify and repair spalled concrete roof tiles promptly, ensuring the longevity and functionality of the roofing system. Condition Rating 2. This is required because a roof is considered a 'thermal element'. The requirement applies even if you are replacing the tiles with the same material. You must submit an application to Building Control and ensure that the roof is insulated to current standards.

standard_paragraphs.label: Original Butterfly roof has been built over, AMEND NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: You should note that roof repairs tend to be expensive due to the associated scaffolding costs. The butterfly roof, prevalent in many London properties, is characterised by its V-shaped design, resembling a butterfly's wings. Based on experience and knowledge of older buildings, we believe the original roof of the main building would have been a London roof, also known as a butterfly roof. Therefore, the flat at the top floor level should be an addition built over the original traditional butterfly roof. The new roof is now in the shape of a Mansard roof, with a flat roof that cannot be seen from ground level, typically covered with bituminised felt, and mono-pitched roofs at the front and rear. We had a view of only the front section from the street, which is covered with imitation slate tiles. In the 1970s and 1980s, many London properties with butterfly roofs were converted and built over to create an additional storey, primarily to add an extra flat to the building. This is apparent in the case of this property as several neighbouring buildings have undergone the same alterations. This trend was driven by several factors. Firstly, the demand for housing in London was growing rapidly, and property owners sought ways to maximise their available space. Converting the butterfly roof into an additional storey allowed them to increase the building's living area without expanding its footprint, making it an efficient solution in the city's densely populated neighbourhoods. Secondly, the architectural design of the butterfly roof, with its inward-sloping sides, provided a convenient framework for such conversions. By filling in the central valley and extending the roof upwards, developers could create a new level with minimal structural alterations. This approach was often more cost-effective than other forms of extension or new construction. Lastly, the economic climate of the time encouraged property owners to enhance the value of their investments. Adding an additional flat not only increased rental income potential but also significantly boosted the property's overall market value. The combination of these practical and economic incentives made the conversion of butterfly roofs into additional storeys a popular strategy for property owners and developers in London during this period. The central valley of a butterfly roof would have provided for the runoff of rainwater to the rear hopper head and downpipe. However, when these roofs are built over, this arrangement is disturbed as the front section, in particular, will then require a drainage provision to be installed. Therefore, additional provisions will have to be in place to allow for the runoff of water from the structure, particularly from the front section of the roof, in the gap between the front section of the Mansard-shaped roof and the front parapet wall. On the side of the neighbouring buildings, several properties have hopper-heads and downpipes installed as a way of drainage. However, this arrangement was not noted on the side of the subject building. It is important to ensure that the front gap between the pitched section of the Mansard roof and the front parapet wall is adequately fitted with a horizontal valley gutter draining the water away from the structure. We can only hope that this arrangement is in place, directing the rainwater to the hopper head of the neighbouring building to the left. However, this could not be confirmed as there was no available vantage point. This area is prone to water accumulation, making effective drainage systems essential to prevent leaks and water damage. It is important to ensure this arrangement is in place and adequate drainage is provided. Also, regular inspections of this area and maintenance are crucial to ensure any potential debris accumulation is regularly removed to avoid potential blockages, ensuring the longevity and performance of this area of the roof. We observed signs of deterioration on the front parapet wall, including water staining, plant growth, spalled brickwork, and missing mortar joints. Whilst these defects may not directly affect the subject flat, they could worsen the condition of the parapet wall, which may be part of our shared maintenance responsibility. Once the plants are removed, further deterioration of the brickwork may become more visible, potentially necessitating repointing or partial reconstruction. Therefore, a closer inspection by a competent contractor is required to carry out the necessary repairs and to check if adequate drainage provisions are in place. This work will require the use of scaffolding, which can be costly. Condition Rating 2. The roof tiles to the front section of the mansard roof appeared to be of some age and brittle. Factory made roof tiles have a limited life expectancy, normally in the region of 20-40 years depending on the quality of the slate and the quality of the installation. Future maintenance should be anticipated. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: FRONT DORMERS
standard_paragraphs.text: There are dormers at the front of the roof that are clad with lead on the side walls. The flat roof of the dormers could not be inspected. The walls to the dormers appeared to be of timber framed construction. This is essentially a lightweight structure and will be more prone internally to mould, condensation and heat loss. Some upgrading including insulation may prove necessary and regular maintenance is recommended. The structural design of timber frame structures relies upon sound workmanship and thorough supervision during the construction process. The structural strength and stability largely depends upon the way in which the inner and outer skins are connected, fixings are hidden and cannot be examined. The weatherproofing similarly relies upon the waterproof membranes being complete and these cannot be seen from an inspection of the surface. Where areas of the external walls are clad, you should be aware that this is generally regarded as an inferior type of construction and that increased maintenance and repairs are likely. These areas are also more likely to suffer internally from condensation, mould and heat loss. We noted signs of discolouration to the lead coverings to the dormers. Lead can become discoloured over time due to exposure to the elements. This discolouration is typically caused by oxidation which occurs when lead reacts with oxygen, carbon dioxide, and other environmental pollutants. Acid rain and air pollution can accelerate this process, leading to uneven colouring and potential streaking. Regular cleaning and maintenance can help manage discolouration, but it is generally considered a natural and expected characteristic of aging lead. In some cases, specialised treatments can be applied to restore or preserve the appearance of the lead surface. In some cases, lead may deteriorate and there will be no option but to replace them. Lead is recyclable and has a life expectancy in excess of 100 years if installed correctly and kept in a good condition. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: REAR DORMER
standard_paragraphs.text: The roof to the rear top floor dormer is of flat construction. The roof coverings appeared to be of Glass Reinforced Polymer (GRP). Such roof coverings should be professionally fitted and your legal adviser should therefore make enquiries into whether the covering was installed by a suitably qualified company and that an insurance backed guarantee is available. It is not possible to confirm the precise construction of the flat roof. Without opening up the structure we cannot determine whether a vapour barrier or adequate insulation or ventilation is provided. We noted signs of water ponding in some areas of the dormer roof. Ponding is common on flat roofs, where water accumulates on the surface in puddles, and is caused by an inadequate fall of the roof itself, which can only be corrected by relaying the roof boards and inserting a firring piece to create an improved gradient, thereby facilitating rain water run-off and reducing the risk of leaking. Ponding can be responsible for decreasing the life span of the roof coverings and can bring a range of potential problems. This includes creating a permanently damp environment which is perfect for moss growth. Also, water can freeze in the winter and ice can make the roof heavier and put additional weight and unnecessary stress on the roof structure leading to sagging and consequently more ponding. However, we did not note any visible signs of internal damp penetration to the ceilings, indicating the flat roof covering is functional. Therefore, there is no immediate need for repairs. Future maintenance however should be anticipated. Condition Rating 2. Flat roof

Regulation

standard_paragraphs.label: Replacing more than 25%
standard_paragraphs.text: You will need to submit a Building Regulations application to carry out repairs on or re-cover an existing pitched or flat roof if more than 25 percent of the total 'building envelope' (walls, floor, roof, windows, doors, roof windows, and roof-lights) is affected, and more than 50 percent of the roof is affected. This is required because a roof is considered a 'thermal element'. The requirement applies even if you are replacing the tiles with the same material. You must submit an application to Building Control and ensure that the roof is insulated to current standards.

standard_paragraphs.label: Two storey rear addition replaced (1/3) AMEND
standard_paragraphs.text: The roof on the two-storey rear addition has been replaced. According to guidelines from the Planning Portal, Building Regulations approval would likely be required for this roof replacement on the two-story rear addition. A Building Regulations application must be submitted when repairing or re-covering an existing pitched roof if more than 25 percent of the total 'building envelope' (which includes walls, floors, roofs, windows, doors, roof windows, and roof lights) is affected, or if more than 50 percent of the roof is impacted. This requirement is necessary because a roof is considered a 'thermal element.' The rule applies even if you are replacing the tiles with the same material. An application to Building Control must be submitted, and the roof must be insulated to meet current standards. In this case, the roof replacement on the two-story rear addition accounts for approximately one-third of the entire roof coverings of the building. Whilst the main pitched roof does not appear to have been changed recently, the replacement of the roof on the two-story rear addition represents a significant portion of the total roof area. As such, Building Regulations approval would likely have been required, as the replacement impacts a considerable portion of the "thermal envelope" of the building. It is, therefore, our understanding that Building Regulations approval was likely necessary. This ensures that the new roof is insulated according to current standards and that the work complies with structural and thermal performance regulations. Your solicitor should make further enquiries to determine whether Building Regulations approval was obtained and provide additional advice and insights on this matter. If Building Regulations approval has not been obtained, your solicitor may request that the current vendor obtain a regularisation certificate, which is a retrospective approval. However, it is important to note that this process may take time and could delay the sale. Your solicitor can advise on alternative approaches that may be available to you (see Section H1).

standard_paragraphs.text: Where visible, some of the roof tiles had slipped, and some tiles have spalled. Some areas are worse than others, with gaps that could allow for water ingress internally. Slate roof tiles can experience spalling, which is the flaking or breaking off of layers, often due to prolonged exposure to moisture and freeze-thaw cycles. This deterioration can compromise the integrity of the tiles, leading to leaks and potential structural damage. Spalling is typically identified by the presence of chipped or delaminated surfaces on the tiles. Repairs often involve replacing the damaged tiles to ensure the roof remains watertight and functional. Ignoring spalling can lead to more extensive and costly repairs in the future. These tiles should be replaced to prevent wind-driven rain from entering the roof space. Additionally, lead tingles have been used to refix some of the slates at the front, as it is not possible to renail slates in position when the fixing nails have failed. Slate roofs require regular maintenance, and ongoing repairs must be expected until such time as the roof is stripped and re-covered. Further investigation by a competent roofing contractor is required, and you should obtain a cost estimate for the repairs. standard_paragraphs.label: Slate nail sickness (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: The slate coverings are showing signs of ageing and decay and a number of metal clips (tingles) are visible where slates have been refixed following slippage. This indicates the fixing nails are rusting away, termed nail sickness, and further slippage is inevitable. Nail sickness occurs when metal nails, which secure the slates in position,corrode to such an extent the weight of the slate breaks through the corrosion thus allowing the slate to slip. In the short to medium-term,patch repairs can be made on an ‘as and when’ basis. This can be done by resecuring the slipped slates with metal tingles (tingles are“S'' shaped sections of metal, usually lead, where the top part is hooked over the timber roofing batten). In the short to medium term,the incidence of slipping slates will increase, as more nails rust through and a decision will have to be made as to whether it would be more cost?effective to take up the slates and re?lay them using new fixings or continue repairing. standard_paragraphs.label: NEW-Boarded inside the loft (Sloping and a horizontal Valley AMEND)
standard_paragraphs.text: There are sloping valley gutters at the junction of the roofs at the front. Additionally, there appeared to be a hidden horizontal valley gutter between the subject property and the neighboring property to the right. From ground level, the sloping valley gutters appeared to be lined with lead. However, we had a limited view of the valley gutters from ground level and there were blind spots, and the horizontal valley gutter was not visible as there was no available vantage point. Internally, inside the loft space, the undersides of the valley gutters are concealed from view due to the presence of boardings attached to the undersides of the roof ceilings, which means hidden defects may exist. Valley gutters are notoriously prone to leakage problems. Even valley gutters which are in sound condition can become blocked by leaves, snow and ice, causing water levels to rise above the edges of the lead and seep into the fabric of the building. Condensation on the underside of the lead lining to the valley gutters can also cause dampness, with an associated risk of decay to the roof timbers. It should be noted maintenance and repair costs, when needed, tend to be expensive. It is important the valley gutters should be regularly inspected and cleaned. It is advised that the condition of valley gutters be checked closely by a competent roofing contractor, when repairs to other areas of the roof is undertaken to ensure they are fully watertight.

We noted signs of discolouration to the lead valley gutters. Lead can become discoloured over time due to exposure to the elements. This discolouration is typically caused by oxidation which occurs when lead reacts with oxygen, carbon dioxide, and other environmental pollutants. Acid rain and air pollution can accelerate this process, leading to uneven colouring and potential streaking. Regular cleaning and maintenance can help manage discolouration, but it is generally considered a natural and expected characteristic of aging lead. In some cases, specialised treatments can be applied to restore or preserve the appearance of the lead surface. In some cases, lead may deteriorate and there will be no option but to replace them. Lead is recyclable and has a life expectancy in excess of 100 years if installed correctly and kept in a good condition. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Finlock (concrete) construction

If this critical part of the system was not properly carried out by the builder, the weight is transferred to the window frames and often the problem only becomes apparent when the windows are replaced with weaker plastic framed double glazing. The connection of surface water drainage into the sewage system is generally not allowed by local authorities, and the general solution is therefore to pipe surface water to garden soakaways, which should ideally be at least 4.5 metres from the building, and the same distance from a public highway. Therefore, if this proves impossible you should be aware that the current drainage configuration will inevitably lead to some degree of wet or icy conditions on the front paved yard area, and the possibility of damp ingress through the front wall of the house. standard_paragraphs.label: History of underpinning

It should be noted that different lenders may have different policies and approaches towards properties with history of underpinning. For example, some high street lenders state that properties that have been subject to underpinning must have the residue of a 10 (some 20) year guarantee, evidence of full Building Regulations approval and be given a supportive valuation to be acceptable security to the Bank. Some state that in some cases it may be prudent only to accept underpinned terraced or semi-detached dwellings if the abutting ones have been similarly treated, or where it is proved that the proposed security is unaffected by a local or inherent individual problem. Also, some lenders do not accept properties which have been underpinned within the last 3 years. This is generally not welcomed by some lenders and therefore may affect the future saleability of the property. However, I did not note any visible signs of structural movement which indicates that any works have been functional so far. standard_paragraphs.label: RAAC 2
standard_paragraphs.text: could not ascertain whether the building contains Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (RAAC). RAAC is a lightweight form of precast concrete, frequently used in public sector buildings in the UK from the 1950s to the 1990s and can be found mostly in flat roofing, but can also be found in flooring and cladding, and this is not an exhaustive list. It is less durable than traditional concrete. Research has shown that this material has a far lower structural loading capacity than other generic reinforced concrete products. Its condition deteriorates further if water is present, due to leaks from roofs etc, which can compromise the reinforcement bars contained within RAAC planks. Over time, if not properly maintained, these materials can deteriorate, potentially leading to structural issues. As the building is of public sector origin and has a concrete frame with concrete elements in various locations, there is a possibility that this material may be present. We are not specialists and have not undertaken any intrusive investigations or specialist tests. We are not sure if the material is or is not present however as your surveyor, it is our duty to highlight any potential risks associated with the property and you should be aware of the worst-case scenario. Your solicitor should make further enquiries with the building management as to whether any RAAC has been detected or if there is any information they may hold in their records, including any action plans, in regard to this matter. If RAAC has been or is identified, this is likely to have a large impact on the future saleability of the property and more importantly, on the health and safety of the occupiers of the building. As RAAC is a new subject, we cannot rule out the possibility that in the future, some high street lenders may decide not to lend on properties containing this material. Whilst this is a worst-case scenario, these are the risks you should be aware of prior to purchase. You should ask your legal adviser about this and also check with the building management to confirm if adequate and valid building insurance is in place to include any future defects arising as a result of the potential presence of this material.

standard_paragraphs.label: Weep holes General
standard_paragraphs.text: Weep holes are openings placed in mortar joints at the level of flashing, typically found above windows, doors, or other penetrations. They allow for the drainage of moisture from the cavity between the inner and outer wall layers, which may reach the back of a wall or the inside leaf of a cavity wall through penetration, capillary action, condensation, or flooding. Weep holes also provide ventilation to prevent mildew and dampness, which can otherwise reduce the lifespan of building materials such as cavity insulation and wall ties. Weep vent caps are often used to prevent the entry of vermin. It is crucial to keep weep holes unobstructed; they should never be blocked, covered, filled, or sealed during construction or renovations, as this can trap moisture and cause long-term damage. Regular inspection and maintenance are essential to ensure weep holes remain effective in preventing water buildup, dampness, mold growth, and structural damage.

standard_paragraphs.label: Borescope NEW (AMEND)
standard_paragraphs.text: We recommend that the identified cracks are repaired and monitored. If further cracking is observed, or as a precautionary measure, we advise arranging an investigation to assess the adequacy and condition of the wall ties. This investigation should be undertaken by a qualified professional using a borescope to inspect the ties. They should provide a detailed report and a quotation for any necessary remedial works. Remedial actions may include isolating or removing corroded ties (if not wire type) and installing stainless steel replacement ties mechanically or chemically bonded to the masonry layers. Additionally, it was not possible to determine whether cavity wall insulation is present in the property. If insulation exists, it may impede a borescope inspection. Moreover, if the walls are found to be of solid construction, such an inspection would not be applicable. Condition Rating 2. NOTE: We were unable to confirm the presence of any retrofitted cavity wall insulation in the main walls. To determine whether cavity wall insulation is present, several methods can be employed. Firstly, enquiries should be made to the vendor to see if they are aware of its installation. A more definitive method involves using a borescope. This requires drilling a small hole into the wall, or inserting the borescope through air bricks or cavity vents, if present. The camera allows for a direct visual confirmation of whether insulation material is present within the cavity. Additionally, a thermal imaging survey can be useful. This method detects heat loss through the walls; areas with greater heat loss may suggest the absence of insulation, whereas uniform heat distribution typically indicates the presence of insulation. In some cases, more detailed and potentially intrusive investigations are required to determine the presence of cavity fill insulation. However, these investigations fall outside the scope of a standard home survey. By employing a combination of the above methods, it can be determined whether a property has cavity wall insulation. It is also important to note that some cavity wall insulation may contain urea formaldehyde (foam fill). This type of insulation can adhere to mortar droppings on wall ties, creating a bridge across the cavity that could lead to localised damp spots on internal walls. Your solicitor should make further enquiries to confirm the type of insulation used, if any, and obtain any guarantees related to the installation. It should also be ensured that the benefit of the guarantee is transferred upon completion (see Section I3). Not ascertained NEW: We were unable to confirm the presence of any retrofitted cavity wall insulation in the main walls. standard_paragraphs.label: Weep holes blocked/ No vent caps
standard_paragraphs.text: There are weep holes on top of the window lintels. Weep holes are openings placed in mortar joints at the level of flashing. They provide an opening that allows for the drainage of any moisture that may reach the back of a wall or the inside leaf of a cavity wall from the outside through penetration, capillary action, condensation, or flooding. They also provide ventilation for the back of the wall to prevent mildew, and damp, which might otherwise reduce the life of building materials such as cavity insulation and cavity wall-ties. Weep holes are typically found above flashing, windows, doors or other penetrations. At the time of our inspection, some of the weep holes were blocked by mortar. Also, there were no weep vent caps for the weep holes. Weep holes should be kept unobstructed. They would also require weep vent caps to prevent entry of vermin. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Spalled (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: Some deterioration has occurred to the wall surfaces, including spalled brickwork and mortar joints. Spalling occurs when brickwork becomes wet due to rain. If freezing conditions occur before the bricks dry out, the entrapped moisture expands and forces off the hard face of the brick, thus exposing the softer inner core. Repairs including repointing by a competent contractor will be required to avoid the risk of water ingress internally. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Cavity wall tie corrosion (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: There was evidence of horizontal cracking to the walls, indicating that cavity wall tie corrosion may be a current problem. It is recommended you arrange for further investigation to ascertain the adequacy and condition of the wall ties. It is also recommended you arrange for a registered wall tie replacement company to inspect the cavities and provide a report, together with a quotation for any necessary remedial work. Replacement work may involve the isolation or removal of the original ties if they are anything other than a wiretype, followed by the insertion of remedial stainless steel ties which are drilled in and either mechanically or chemically bonded to the inner and outer leaves of brickwork. The work can cause localised loosening of plaster, and the disturbance and associated costs can therefore be considerable. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Cavity wall ties not seen (1)
standard_paragraphs.text: It has not been possible to inspect the ties holding together the inner and outer leaves of the cavity walls. Metal wall ties can suffer gradual corrosion with time. With some types of ties, this corrosion is sometimes accompanied by rust expansion, causing horizontal cracks to appear at intervals in the external wall surfaces. With ties of the 'butterfly wire' type, such evidence of failure may not be evident, and the absence of cracks in the mortar joints is not therefore a guarantee the ties are in good condition. At the time of inspection, there was no evidence of such problems occurring. Condition Rating 1.

standard_paragraphs.label: Cavity Wall Insulation, Drill holes noted NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: Based on a visual inspection, it appears that there are historic drill holes in the external walls, which are typically associated with the installation of cavity wall insulation. These holes are made to inject insulation into the wall cavity. However, without intrusive investigations, we cannot confirm whether cavity insulation has been installed throughout all areas of the external walls or if it is indeed present. Older types of cavity wall insulation could possibly be urea formaldehyde. Your legal advisor should be asked to investigate whether cavity insulation has been installed, the type of insulation used, and whether any guarantees exist for the work. It is important to note that cavity foam insulation can adhere to mortar droppings on wall ties, potentially creating a bridge across the cavity and leading to localised damp spots on internal walls. We recommend obtaining any relevant guarantees related to this work and ensuring that the benefit of such guarantees is transferred upon completion of the sale (see sections H2 & I3).

standard_paragraphs.label: Cavity trays - wall extensions
standard_paragraphs.text: The property has been extended. When an extension/conservatory is added to existing cavity walls, it is very important to ensure a cavity tray is fitted within the cavity of the original part of the building,above the line of the extension roof. This is to ensure any water running down the cavity is prevented from passing into the internal areas of the building. It is good practice to include weep holes (vertical slots in the perpendicular joints of the brickwork) immediately above the line of the cavity tray, to allow any water to escape. Cladding

standard_paragraphs.label: Front bay (AMEND)
standard_paragraphs.text: The external walls to the front bay have been clad with plain concrete tiles. Cladding involves applying one material over another to provide a protective layer or skin. In construction, cladding serves to offer thermal insulation, weather resistance, and aesthetic improvement to buildings. We observed that some of the cladding tiles at the lower level of the bay, particularly at the edges, have slipped. Additionally, there are gaps at the abutments of the bay with the external wall where the cladding tiles meet the front elevation. These tiles should be realigned, and any gaps should be filled and repaired by a competent contractor to prevent the risk of water ingress into the property. Since the external surfaces have been painted, ongoing decoration and maintenance will be necessary in the future. Condition Rating 2. The lead flashing underneath the window at first floor level to the front bay showed signs of deterioration. The paint applied to the surfaces of the lead has deteriorated. Lead should be left to oxidise and protect itself. Any coating may shorten the life of the lead by allowing it to degrade. However, where visible, no visible signs of defects such as internal dampness in the surrounding areas of the bay were noted, indicating the lead flashing is functional. Renewal in the future should be anticipated. The flashing should be checked closely by a competent contractor and cleaned/restored if possible. In some cases, lead flashings may deteriorate and there will be no option but to replace them. Lead is recyclable and has a life expectancy in excess of 100 years if installed correctly and kept in a good condition. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Cladding (A)

standard_paragraphs.label: Window Sills and surrounds have cracked and deteriorated
standard_paragraphs.text: The window sills and surrounds have been rendered and painted, as is typical of properties of this age and type. The render showed signs of cracks and deterioration, indicating that repairs will be required. Cracked and deteriorated areas of window sills and surrounds pose a risk of water ingress, which can lead to internal damage. When window sills and their surrounding structures are compromised, they create entry points for water during rain or snow. This water can seep into the building's interior walls, leading to issues such as dampness and mould growth. To prevent these issues, it is important to regularly inspect and maintain window sills and surrounds, promptly addressing any cracks or signs of wear with appropriate sealants or repairs to ensure a watertight barrier. Condition Rating 2. No Groove for window sills: There is no adequate drip throat (groove) beneath the window sub-sill to the windows. This is required to avoid the risk of water ingress internally. The drip throats beneath the window sub-sills should be kept clear of obstruction to prevent possible water ingress below and should be recut if necessary, which can usually be achieved by carefully running a grinder along a batten that has first been securely clamped to the underside. The dropped sub-sills should be recast or resurfaced to direct rain away from the property. The cracked sub-sills that haven’t dropped should be repaired/filled. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Spalled brickwork (CR2) NEW FULL PARA
standard_paragraphs.text: Some deterioration has occurred to the brick wall surfaces, including spalled brickwork and mortar joints. Spalling occurs when brickwork becomes wet due to rain. If freezing conditions occur before the bricks dry out, the entrapped moisture expands and forces off the hard face of the brick, thus exposing the softer inner core. Localised repair will be required as necessary when external redecoration is next undertaken. The new mortar should not be too weak, but conversely it should not be stronger than the bricks to which it is applied. A common misconception is that mortar requires a large proportion of cement in the mix, but too rich a cement content can cause serious problems. This work should only be entrusted to an experienced bricklayer. Condition Rating 2.
