standard_paragraphs.text: A number of the bricks at the ||describe|| of the building are damaged by spalling. Spalling occurs when brickwork becomes wet due to rain. If freezing conditions occur before the bricks dry out, the entrapped moisture expands and forces off the hard face of the brick,thus exposing the softer inner core. Repairs including repointing by a competent contractor will be required. Also, a number of spalled bricks have been patched with mortar. This is a temporary repair and proper cutting out and replacement with new bricks would be a better long term repair. The new mortar should not be too weak, but conversely it should not be stronger than the bricks to which it is applied. A common misconception is that mortar requires a large proportion of cement in the mix, but too rich a cement content can cause serious problems. This work should only be entrusted to an experienced bricklayer. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Mortar with high cement Ratio
standard_paragraphs.text: Some deterioration has occurred to the wall surfaces, including spalled brickwork and mortar joints. Over time, mortar joints in the brickwork have become eroded out by the weather and are now in need of re-pointing. Missing pointing will result in water penetration and further deterioration to the mortar bedding. The existing mortar appears to contain a high cement ratio which is not a good building practice for a property of this age, and over time over time can cause problems such as spalling of the bricks. The new mortar should not be too weak, but conversely it should not be stronger than the bricks to which it is applied. A common misconception is that mortar requires a large proportion of cement in the mix, but too rich a cement content can cause serious problems. Repointing with lime mortar should be carried out. It is essential the joints are raked out sufficiently, usually to a depth of not less than 15-20 mm so the new mortar is given sufficient key. Failure to do this can result in the new pointing simply cracking and falling out over a relatively short timescale. This work should only be entrusted to an experienced bricklayer to provide further advice and a cost estimate for remediation. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Wall plinths cracked
standard_paragraphs.text: A rendered wall plinth is a protective and decorative feature applied to the lower portion of a wall. It is a strip of wall coated with a layer of plaster or cement-based material that serves to protect and enhance the lower part of the wall. The wall plinth shields the wall from moisture, dirt, and damage caused by weather conditions, ground contact, or splashback from rain. This helps prevent the wall’s base from deteriorating, especially in areas prone to water ingress. Additionally, it provides a neat and finished appearance at the base of the wall, complementing the overall design of the building. The external wall plinths have cracked and deteriorated in various locations and repairs should be undertaken. All cracks require repair to avoid damaging water ingress into the walls. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Lead wall and lead roof DISCOLOURED NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted signs of discolouration to the lead claddings. Lead can become discoloured over time due to exposure to the elements. This discolouration is typically caused by oxidation, which occurs when lead reacts with oxygen, carbon dioxide, and other environmental pollutants. Acid rain and air pollution can accelerate this process, leading to uneven colouring and potential streaking. Regular cleaning and maintenance can help manage discolouration, but it is generally considered a natural and expected characteristic of aging lead. In some cases, specialised treatments can be applied to restore or preserve the appearance of the lead surface. However, in cases where lead deteriorate, there may be no option but to replace them. Lead is recyclable and has a life expectancy in excess of 100 years if installed correctly and kept in good condition. Although they remain functional, as we did not note any visible signs of dampness internally surrounding the dormers, the lead claddings and lead roof should be checked closely by a competent contractor and cleaned/restored if possible. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Dormer Ventilation point
standard_paragraphs.text: There seem to be ventilation points installed on the side walls of the dormers, presumably to provide ventilation for the voids within the dormers. However, we cannot confirm if these vents may be blocked internally. To limit interstitial condensation, site formed dormers should incorporate an air and vapour control layer to the walls. Proper ventilation for dormer walls is essential to maintain the overall health and efficiency of a building. Adequate ventilation helps prevent the buildup of moisture and condensation, which can lead to mould growth, wood rot, and deterioration of building materials. To ensure effective ventilation, dormer walls should be equipped with vents that allow for continuous airflow. These vents can facilitate the escape of warm, moist air and the entry of fresh air. Additionally, ensuring that insulation does not obstruct airflow is crucial. Regular maintenance and inspection of the vents are necessary to keep them clear of debris and functioning properly. By maintaining proper ventilation, the structural integrity of the dormer walls can be preserved, and the indoor air quality can be improved, ultimately extending the lifespan of the building.

On the other hand, during colder months, these structures are prone to heat loss and may feel colder compared to solid or cavity brick walls, as they are considered a lightweight structure. The strength and stability of the structure depend largely on how well the inner and outer layers are connected, but since the fixings are concealed, they cannot be inspected. Similarly, the weatherproofing depends on the completeness of the waterproof membranes, which are not visible during a surface inspection. Additionally, in areas where the external walls are tile-hung or cladded, it is important to understand that this is generally considered a less durable form of construction, which may require more frequent maintenance and repairs. Additionally, the timber decking is currently at the same level as the internal floor and above the potential damp proof course (DPC). This practice is not ideal, as during heavy rainfall, rainwater splashback can breach the DPC and increase the risk of damp penetration. To comply with current building regulations, the decking should be lowered so that its top level is at least 150 mm below the DPC. When replacing the decking, you should ensure it is installed at this recommended level. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: DPC Injection at ground floor neighbour (Shared maybe) NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: A damp proof course (DPC) is a water proof layer built in or formed within the walls to prevent ground dampness from rising. Impervious horizontal barriers called Damp Proof Courses (DPC’s) which are intended to prevent moisture originating in the ground rising into a wall by a process known as capillarity have been mandatory in walls of buildings in London since about 1877 as a result of model bye-laws which in this instance is likely to be slate to the original walls which is usually located about 175 mm beneath the floorboards and at about the height of a solid floor although this isn’t always the case. It is considered likely that a damp proof course (DPC) would have been incorporated within the structure but the type of DPC could not be ascertained as it is concealed by internal and external wall finishes. The original Damp Proof Course should not be bridged externally or internally and the external ground levels kept to at least 150mm below it to prevent rain from splashing over it. Items should not be stored against the outside walls that might trap rain behind or that might direct it over the Damp Proof Course. There is evidence that a remedial damp-proof course has been installed at the rear of the building, partially visible near flat 57B through the passageway, where we were able to conduct a limited observation of the external walls. We noted the presence of chemical damp-proofing holes at ground level on the external wall. However, this does not necessarily mean that a chemical damp-proof course (DPC) was required in this area. As the inspection of neighbouring flats is beyond the scope of this survey, we cannot confirm whether the treatment was successful or whether ground-floor properties may also be experiencing damp issues. Additionally, we are unaware if the DPC treatment is limited to this area or extends to other parts of the building. Therefore, there remains the possibility that neighbouring properties at ground-floor level may be affected by dampness. Any defects to the DPC will not affect the subject flat, but the neighbouring properties at ground floor level. It is essential that your legal advisor investigates further to determine whether any dampness issues in neighbouring properties could fall under shared maintenance responsibilities. If such damp issues are confirmed, you may be liable for future repair costs as part of your shared management responsibilities. Your solicitor should verify this, as we have not examined the lease agreements. If shared management applies, your legal advisor should also enquire whether any guarantees were issued for the damp-proofing works carried out at ground-floor level. It is important to note that if a guarantee exists, it would only cover the areas treated and would not provide comprehensive coverage for the entire building. Additionally, if the property is subject to shared management, you should ensure that the guarantee is transferable to you and offers meaningful protection. For further advice, please consult your solicitor, as we cannot provide additional commentary on this matter (see Section H2).

standard_paragraphs.label: Timber decking high (AMEND)
standard_paragraphs.text: External ground levels to the rear are too high, particularly on the side of the kitchen area. A distance of 150mm (6 inches) should be maintained between external levels and the damp proof course and internal floor levels in order to prevent the risk of damp penetration. When the external timber decking is replaced, it is important to ensure the ground is lowered. When installing external timber decking close to an external wall, it is crucial to consider the risk of splash back and water ingress. Timber decking situated too close to a wall can lead to water being splashed onto the wall's surface during rainfall or cleaning, increasing the likelihood of moisture seeping into the wall structure. This can cause dampness, mould growth, and potential structural damage over time. Therefore, it is important to ensure an adequate gap, typically between 10-15mm, between the decking and the wall to mitigate these risks. This gap allows for proper drainage and ventilation, thereby protecting both the decking and the building from water-related issues. Additionally, timber decking should be lower than the internal floor level. Keeping the decking lower than the internal floor level helps prevent water from entering the building during heavy rain or when cleaning the deck. It reduces the risk of moisture-related problems, such as mould or rot, in the internal flooring and structure. Typically, a height difference of 150mm (about 6 inches) between the external decking and the internal floor level is recommended to ensure proper drainage and protection against water ingress. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Foliage/plant Standard
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted the presence of plants growing on the external walls of the property. Walls should be kept free of plants and foliage, as this can impair their efficiency and potentially damage the wall structure. Plants growing in close proximity to walls can cause problems to structures and services, particularly on shrinkable subsoil. These plants can absorb and retain moisture, which, during winter, can freeze and lead to the deterioration of brick surfaces. Trees with high water demands, such as poplar, oak, willow, and elm, should be discouraged within 10 metres of the building, and other trees should be kept at least 5 metres away. Any climbing plants present on the walls should be well-pruned if they are to be retained. They should not be allowed to exceed eaves height, as they can damage or dislodge rainwater goods, roofing slates, and tiles. Condition Rating 2. Gaps

Therefore, as part of routine maintenance, future repairs should be anticipated. Cracks and defective areas in the mortar fillings can allow water to penetrate, posing a risk of internal dampness and decay to timbers and internal plaster. When repairs are undertaken in the future, raking out and replacement with a lime-rich mortar will be required. Condition Rating 2.

Ideally, a small trench should be dug around the external walls of the property. This need only be approximately 150 mm width from the wall and infilled with stones, ideally with a French Drain (perforated pipe) beneath this, channelling the water away to a suitable outlet. The previous recommendations for infilling with Pea Shingle have now been superseded as it has been found that this finer material in fact holds moisture. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Staining under coping stones
standard_paragraphs.text: We observed signs of staining at the upper level of the front elevation, specifically on the front parapet wall below the coping stone. This suggests that the area is not fully watertight, and the detailing is inadequate. To address this, it is essential to ensure a 25-35mm overhang on each side of the coping stone, with proper drip channels to direct water away from the structure. A competent contractor should be engaged to thoroughly inspect the front parapet wall and coping stones to confirm that sufficient measures are in place to allow water to run off freely. It is also crucial to provide adequate drip channels to prevent water from seeping into the wall. Additionally, a flexible Damp Proof Course (DPC) should be installed beneath the coping stone to prevent moisture from penetrating downward into the wall. This DPC should be bedded on both sides, sandwiched within the joint, and should project 5mm beyond each face of the wall below. Condition Rating 3.

A common misconception is that mortar requires a large proportion of cement in the mix, but too rich a cement content can cause serious problems. Unfortunately, this damage has already been done to the bricks and removing the existing pointing may cause even further damage to the bricks, therefore at this stage, it is advisable to just undertake localised repointing including the replacement of all damaged bricks. The parapet walls then should be monitored on a regular basis and in the case of any future spalling noted, the existing mortar should be raked out and replaced with lime mortar. Some bricks may have to be replaced as this work can be destructive to an old building. In this case, it will be essential for the joints to be raked out sufficiently, usually to a depth of not less than 15-20 mm so the new mortar is given sufficient key. Failure to do this can result in the new pointing simply cracking and falling out over a relatively short timescale. Any work will have to be entrusted to an experienced bricklayer to provide further advice and a cost estimate for remediation should be obtained before a commitment to a purchase is made. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Spalled brickwork

standard_paragraphs.label: Spalled brickwork and cracked render

Localised repairs will be required as necessary when external redecoration is next undertaken. Condition Rating 2. No coping stones ( Mineral Felt): There are no coping stones on the parapet walls and mineral felt have been used as a way of waterproofing which is poor building practice. The top of a parapet wall is vulnerable to moisture penetration problems. Choosing an appropriate cap is an effective way to eliminate this condition. Coping stones are important to protect walls from weather damage. Coping stones are manufactured from high-strength concrete and provide an aesthetically-pleasing finish. A variety of materials are available to cap off the wall, with limestone, terracotta, hard-fired clay, or precast concrete preferred. When selecting your coping, you should allow a 25-35mm overhang on each side for the drip channels. Adequate drip channels should be provided to keep water away from the wall. Also, a flexible Damp Proof Course (DPC) will be required below a coping unit to prevent the downward transfer of moisture into the wall. This DPC should be bedded on both sides, so that it is sandwiched in the joint, and projecting 5mm beyond each face of the wall below. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: External Wall Insulation NEW AMEND
standard_paragraphs.text: The original building's main walls are believed to have been constructed with solid brickwork. In properties of this type and age, the thickness of a solid brick wall typically measures approximately around 250 to 270 millimeters. However, due to the addition of external insulation and rendering to the front elevation walls on both the ground and first floors, as well as the rear elevation walls on the first floor, the wall thickness through openings has increased to approximately 370 millimeters. External wall insulation can be an effective way to improve energy efficiency and reduce heat loss, but it also carries certain risks and implications that should be carefully considered. One of the main concerns is that external wall insulation can disrupt the natural "breathing" cycle of older buildings, particularly those originally constructed with breathable materials like lime mortar. This disruption may trap moisture within the walls, potentially leading to issues such as dampness, mould growth, and interstitial condensation. Additionally, external wall insulation can conceal movement cracks or defects in the underlying structure, making it difficult to identify and address these issues. Maintenance is also more complex, as any future repairs or modifications to the walls may require specialised techniques or materials. Insulating the walls of a solid-walled structure is often considered controversial and technically challenging. Much of the charm and character of older buildings comes from the natural imperfections and undulating surfaces of old lime plaster. Covering or replacing this with flat, modern insulation materials can strip away the aesthetic qualities that have developed over centuries. Additionally, many historic buildings have unique external finishes and details that may be lost when insulation is applied to the exterior. Even in cases where insulating the internal or external surfaces of a wall is deemed acceptable, there is considerable debate about the best approach. Some experts warn that many modern insulation products can lead to future problems, including mould growth, trapped moisture, and decay. Predicting the long-term effects of insulation on solid walls is inherently difficult, as outcomes depend on numerous factors that are unique to each building. The vendor mentioned that insulation was applied only to the external walls, which is visually evident, and it seems there is no internal insulation. External wall insulation can be problematic in areas with complex features, such as around windows or in hard-to-reach places. Incomplete coverage may lead to thermal bridging, which can cause internal condensation and mould growth, though these issues may take years to manifest. Poor installation can lead to thermal bridging, where gaps in insulation allow heat to escape, undermining the insulation's effectiveness. It is essential that insulation work is carried out by reputable companies with proper supervision from professionals experienced in dealing with older buildings. Unfortunately, we are unable to comment on the quality of the insulation that has been installed. Whilst ideally, external wall insulation should be avoided in older buildings due to the increased risk of future complications, if installed adequately and correctly by competent professionals, it would bring thermal comfort to the house, however, as mentioned before this can only be determined in time. At the time of our inspection, no significant issues were identified, aside from some dampness at ground floor level, as mentioned in Section E3 of the report. However, we cannot conclusively determine if this dampness is related to the external wall insulation. The vendor indicated that the external wall insulation was installed around 2015, making it nearly 10 years old. Typically, any defects caused by poor installation or substandard materials would have likely surfaced by now, as a decade is generally considered sufficient time to assess the insulation's effectiveness. That said, a single inspection cannot completely rule out the possibility of future issues, especially if recent redecorations, such as painting or renovations by the vendor, may have concealed any existing defects. Ultimately, the effectiveness of the external wall insulation can only be assessed by monitoring the performance of the building over the coming years to determine whether any complications arise. You should ensure that proper ventilation is maintained. In addition, your solicitor should obtain any available guarantees related to this insulation work. It is important that your solicitor makes enquiries with the vendor to verify whether adequate and comprehensive guarantees are in place, the scope of those guarantees, and whether they cover any defects arising from the insulation. Additionally, your solicitor should confirm whether these guarantees can be legally transferred to you as the new owner. NOTE: We understand that Government planning regulations generally allow for external wall insulation on domestic properties without the need for planning permission, provided there is no material change to the external appearance of the property. To assist the client, we have made the following comments. However, it is important to note that we are not legal advisors, and your solicitor should investigate this matter further and confirm any implications. Your solicitor should verify our understanding and provide additional advice. External wall insulation involves applying a decorative, weatherproof insulating treatment to the exterior of the property, with a typical thickness of between 50mm and 100mm. Based on our visual inspection, we could not confirm whether the thickness of the insulation, particularly at upper levels, exceeds 100mm, which may surpass the permitted limits. Therefore, your solicitor should obtain the necessary paperwork and information regarding the insulation, if available, to determine its thickness. If the insulation is less than 100mm, it may be considered permitted development; however, there are important limits and conditions to these rights.

standard_paragraphs.label: Planning permission may be required if
standard_paragraphs.text: - The external wall insulation extends more than 100mm beyond the original wall, as this could be considered a significant alteration to the building's appearance. - The property is subject to an Article 4 Direction, which restricts certain development rights. Your solicitor should investigate this and provide further advice. If there is any uncertainty about whether the insulation meets the permitted development criteria, we recommend asking the current vendor to apply for a Lawful Development Certificate (LDC). Even if the works are believed to be lawful under permitted development rights, having written confirmation from the council that planning permission was not required can be valuable. An LDC is not the same as planning permission but serves as proof that the work complies with the law. Obtaining an LDC is particularly helpful when selling the property in the future, as it provides clarity for potential buyers and their legal representatives. The vendor can apply for an LDC through the local council using the Planning Portal’s secure online application service, although a fee will be required. If requesting an LDC from the vendor might delay the sale process, you could apply for it yourself after purchasing the property, though this carries some risk. Should the insulation require planning permission, there is the potential for enforcement action. Your solicitor can advise you on this matter. We are also aware that solicitors often obtain indemnity insurance to cover the lack of planning or Building Regulations approval, but we cannot comment further on this; your solicitor can provide additional guidance on the implications of such insurance.

standard_paragraphs.label: Building Regulations Approval
standard_paragraphs.text: Building regulations approval is typically required for external wall insulation because it alters the thermal performance of the building. This ensures that the insulation meets standards for energy efficiency, fire safety, and weather resistance. The regulations also address how the insulation integrates with the structure, ensuring that it does not pose risks of condensation, damp, or other structural issues. Regarding indemnity policies for the lack of Building Regulations approval, these are generally considered a last resort. Whilst they may offer protection against enforcement actions, to our knowledge, they do not cover losses related to defects in the work itself. The primary purpose of Building Regulations is to ensure that work is carried out to an acceptable standard. If approval has not been obtained, there is always a risk that the work is substandard, which could impact the future saleability of the property. Therefore, your solicitor should make further enquiries to determine whether Building Regulations approval was obtained for the external wall insulation, as well as for any other alterations to the property, as outlined in Section H1 of the report, and confirm the implications of this matter for you.

standard_paragraphs.label: External wall re-rendered NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: It is important to note that, as the external front wall appears to have been recently rendered or re-rendered, Building Regulations approval would likely have been required. This is based on information from the Planning Portal, which indicates that regulations apply when external walls are significantly altered, such as re-rendering, particularly if it affects 25% or more of the wall's surface. Approval ensures that the work meets safety, structural stability, and insulation standards. Your solicitor should confirm this with the local authority’s Building Control Body. Additionally, planning permission may also be necessary, especially if the property is in a conservation area or if an Article 4 Direction restricts permitted development rights. Your solicitor should verify this with both the planning department and Building Control. We cannot provide legal advice on this matter.

standard_paragraphs.label: Lintel replaced appeared old
standard_paragraphs.text: The small beams spanning across the tops of windows and doors are known as lintels. The lintels above the rear patio door and the garden door from the kitchen appear to have been replaced at some point in the past with concrete lintels. No significant defects were observed. However, it is important to note that lintel replacements typically require approval under Building Regulations. The exact date of the lintel replacement is not known to us (see Section H1). Render

standard_paragraphs.label: Spar dash cracked and old NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: In 1930s houses, “spar dash render" consists of a mixture of small stones or chippings (spar) embedded in a cementitious or lime-based render. The render itself is usually made from a mix of sand, cement, and sometimes lime. This combination creates a textured finish on the exterior walls, providing both weather protection and aesthetic appeal. The stones or chippings in the spar dash render contribute to its distinctive rough texture and can vary in size depending on the desired finish. Cracks have appeared in the rendered walls at various locations. Future monitoring is required, and all cracks should be repaired to prevent water ingress and subsequent damage. The spar dash render on the walls appears to be an original feature of the property and is very old. Whilst it can be patch repaired, it may be more cost-effective to re-render the entire property in the future. It is important that this work be carried out by a competent building contractor familiar with old buildings and using like for like style and with correct ratio of lime mortar, which not only preserves the architectural appeal but also allows for the natural breathing cycle of the building. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Paint blister/bubble (CR2)
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted evidence of paint blisters/ bubbles to some areas of external wall render in several locations. This was particularly more evident to ||SPECIFY||. Spalling to render occurs when the plaster loses its bond to the underlying surface, leading to sections of the plaster detaching and falling away. This can be caused by various factors, including water infiltration, freeze-thaw cycles, poor initial application, or the natural aging of materials. The paint film lifts from the underlying surface due to heat, moisture, or a combination of both, which eventually leads to peeling. Repairs should be anticipated. It is recommended that the render be regularly coated with good quality masonry paint. The integrity of the render is vital; once water penetrates the external surface, dampness is likely to occur internally, and the render itself will continue to deteriorate. As the external surfaces have been painted, this will be an ongoing decoration and maintenance burden in the future. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Cracked render, clay geology regular maintenance
standard_paragraphs.text: Cracks have occurred in various locations of the render due to thermal movement within the fabric of the building. As this property is located on a subsoil with clay geology, this may become a regular maintenance issue in the future and cracks are likely to reappear again when repairs are undertaken. Whilst such cracking do not appear to be structural, future monitoring is required and all cracks require repair to avoid damaging water ingress into the walls. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Timber decking hiding render
standard_paragraphs.text: The rendering to the external walls in front of the main entrance have been carried down to ground level. There is timber decking to the rear which restricted our inspection of external walls at lower levels. However, where visible through the gaps, it is apparent that the render to the rear is also carried down to ground level. (See also our comments with regards to timber decking at sections H3 & J3). This is not good practice as it can conduct moisture up from the ground, bypassing the damp proof course. We noted evidence of dampness internally. (See section F3). The render should be neatly cut back to a horizontal line 150 mm above ground level and a bellmouth profile formed. Ideally, this should be finished off with a stainless steel trim designed for the purpose, to provide a neat appearance. Any defective brickwork revealed by this work should be repaired as found to be necessary. (See also section F4). Condition Rating 3.

This is not good practice as it can conduct moisture up from the ground, bypassing the damp proof course, and this may cause internal dampness. The render should be neatly cut back to a horizontal line 150 mm above ground level and a bellmouth profile formed. Ideally, this should be finished off with a stainless steel trim designed for the purpose, to provide a neat appearance. Any defective brickwork revealed by this work should be repaired as found to be necessary. Condition Rating ||*2/3.*||

standard_paragraphs.label: Overflow pipe statining with hole

standard_paragraphs.label: Efflorescence (A)
standard_paragraphs.text: Efflorescence can be seen on the external wall surfaces. This is an accumulation of naturally occurring salts in the bricks which are drawn to the external surface when wetted by rain and remain thereupon drying out. The efflorescence does not cause any particular damage to the brickwork. Left alone, these deposits will gradually disappear. Cleaning off, if desired, can be done by dry brushing, taking care not to scour the surface of the brickwork. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: White staining as a result of overflow pipe

This should not cause any particular damage to the brickwork. Cleaning off, if desired, can be done by dry brushing, taking care not to scour the surface of the brickwork. Condition Rating 2. Structural movements

standard_paragraphs.label: Solicitor confirm if insurance claim is made
standard_paragraphs.text: We advise that your solicitor makes further enquiries with the vendor to determine if they are aware of any previous structural movement or if there have been any insurance claims related to movement that should be disclosed.

standard_paragraphs.label: Retro Reflective Targets
standard_paragraphs.text: During our inspection, we observed several Retro Reflective Targets located on the rear façade of the building and on the adjoining neighbouring property to the right. Retro Reflective Targets are small markers typically used to monitor and measure any structural movement within a building. These targets are generally installed to detect movement or settlement within the structure. They are often used in conjunction with monitoring equipment to track any shifts or changes in the building's position over time. The data collected from these targets can help assess any potential issues regarding the stability or settlement of the structure. In properties undergoing conversion or significant renovation, particularly those of older construction such as Victorian-style buildings, it is common practice to install such targets. This is especially relevant when alterations have been made to the structural components of the building. The installation of Retro Reflective Targets allows engineers to track changes in the building's alignment or position in relation to neighbouring structures, which can help identify any potential concerns regarding its structural integrity. These targets may be part of a monitoring system established to ensure that the building remains structurally sound following the completion of any conversion or renovation works. However, it is important to note that the use of such monitoring systems is sometimes recommended by insurance companies, block management companies, or local authorities, particularly when there are claims of structural movement made by current or previous owners. That said, the targets may have been installed during the building’s alteration project purely to monitor the structure’s verticality during construction. To clarify the purpose of these targets, we strongly recommend that you instruct your solicitor to make further enquiries and, if applicable, obtain any relevant documentation or structural engineer’s reports pertaining to this work. Based on the findings from our single inspection, we did not observe any visible signs of active structural movement. However, it is crucial that you do not proceed with the purchase until all relevant information is disclosed to you, confirming that no active structural movement is occurring. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Underpinning No doc Amend
standard_paragraphs.text: As mentioned above, we undertook an online search of publicly available records via the London Borough of Haringey’s planning and building control portal. We identified a Building Control Regularisation application under reference RGE/0011/7461, relating to “underpinning to party wall with No. 33.” The application status is recorded as ‘accepted’ and dates back to July 2015. However, no further documentation, such as completion certificates, structural engineer’s reports, or approved plans, is available from the public record. Based on our visual inspection, we were unable to verify whether these works were actually implemented, nor could we or assess their quality, as such matters fall outside the scope of a non-intrusive survey. Please find below important considerations and risks associated with purchasing a property that has a known or suspected history of underpinning:

standard_paragraphs.label: Technical and Risk Considerations
standard_paragraphs.text: Properties that have undergone underpinning works often carry a residual stigma in the property market. Whilst underpinning is typically undertaken to stabilise subsidence or structural movement, it also suggests that the property has previously suffered from structural concerns, such as foundation failure, soil shrinkage, or ground movement, particularly in areas with clay subsoil or a history of underground water level fluctuation. Although we would expect such works to have been carried out under the direction of a qualified structural engineer, it is not possible to confirm the adequacy or long-term effectiveness of the underpinning without intrusive investigations, which lie beyond the scope of this report. In the absence of full supporting documentation (e.g. structural warranties, engineer’s calculations, completion certificates), the presence of underpinning introduces an element of uncertainty regarding the property's structural integrity. It is also important to note that, whilst underpinning may stabilise the foundations, it does not guarantee that further movement will not occur. From a mortgage and resale perspective, it is important to be aware that lenders adopt differing policies towards underpinned properties. Some lenders may require:  A 10- or 20-year structural warranty backed by an insurance indemnity policy;  Evidence of Building Regulations compliance and approval for the works;  Confirmation from a Chartered Structural Engineer that no ongoing movement is present;  A favourable valuation confirming the property is suitable security. Certain lenders may decline applications outright for properties underpinned in the past three years, or may only consider terraced or semi-detached dwellings where the entire terrace has been subject to similar remedial works, thereby reducing the perceived risk of neighbouring ground movement. This can affect both mortgage availability and future marketability of the property, particularly if the documentation is incomplete or outdated. We strongly advise that your legal adviser makes full enquiries into the circumstances surrounding the underpinning works, and requests:  A copy of the Building Regulations approval;  Structural engineer’s reports and specifications for the underpinning;  Completion certificates and any insurance-backed guarantees;  Details of any ongoing monitoring or follow-up assessments. It is essential that any guarantee is both long-term and transferrable, ideally with an associated insurance indemnity policy in place. Additionally, even where such documentation is obtained, there remains long-term uncertainty regarding how future lenders may treat underpinned properties, especially once any warranties expire. This could affect the property’s future value and saleability, particularly if you intend to retain the property for a number of years. Furthermore, the durability of the underpinning and its long-term effect on the property's structural performance remain unknown without continuous monitoring or invasive investigation. Furthermore, it is important to be aware that many mainstream building insurers may be unwilling to provide cover for properties with a history of underpinning, regardless of whether the works were completed and certified. In such cases, insurance may need to be sourced through a specialist provider, which can prove both challenging and costly. Premiums are typically higher due to the perceived increased risk. This may also impact the future marketability and desirability of the property, as prospective purchasers and their lenders may be deterred by the associated insurance implications. As a general notion, properties that have been underpinned often carry a stigma, even if the original issue has been resolved. In the absence of full documentation, it is unclear why the underpinning was undertaken or whether it fully addressed the underlying problem. This may raise concerns for future buyers and mortgage lenders, and can affect both marketability and perceived value. Based on a single visual inspection of the property, we did not observe any signs of active structural movement or defects suggestive of foundation-related issues. However, this should not be interpreted as an absolute confirmation that future movement will not occur. That said, the visual inspection did not reveal any substantial cracking or visible defects typically associated with structural instability. Unfortunately, it is not possible to provide absolute assurance or certainty on this matter based solely on a single visual inspection. These are material risks which you should be aware of when considering the purchase of a property with a history of structural movement and remedial works

standard_paragraphs.label: Repair and Monitor and if reappeared Helfix NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted a crack above the kitchen window, beneath the boiler flue pipe. This crack should be repaired and monitored, and in the case of future cracks, repairs can be undertaken by inserting Helifix bars. Regarding repair of the cracks, that may be subject to further minor movement, it is standard practice to recommend that the external wall cracks are strengthened with the installation of ‘Helifix’ bars & resin injection repairs. This consists of 6 mm diameter stainless steel bars inserted into the bed joints at approx. 500 mm each side of the crack. The crack in the bricks can either be replaced or resin grouted with low viscosity grout such a ‘Nitokit LV’ by Fosroc. The bars are inserted every 2 – 3 courses of brick. A well installed ‘Helifix’ bar repair should blend into the façade wall & not visibly stand out.

standard_paragraphs.label: 4 Options AMEND
standard_paragraphs.text: The wall on the side of the green area is of solid construction; however, this wall has not been constructed to the standards expected from solid walls, which usually have a measurement through opening of 250 mm or more. The wall on the side of front addition has been partially rendered and painted. We noted signs of cracks and undulation in the external walls in this area, and a section of the wall to the left appeared to have slipped and moved near the ground level. The wall on the left side was out of plumb and undulated, and the rendered areas showed signs of cracks. Internally, the presence of kitchen fittings limited our inspection, and we could not ascertain if the cracking may be present on the inside walls as well. This appeared to be a design issue, as the neighboring properties in the same row of terraces also appeared to suffer from similar movements at their front addition walls. Without intrusive investigations, which are outside the scope of our survey, it is not possible to ascertain if the foundation of the walls in this area has sufficient depth. The property is constructed on a slope, and if the foundations are not designed properly, movement is inevitable. Unfortunately, in a single inspection, we cannot rule out the possibility that the movement may be progressive. Therefore, we offer the following options, out of which option 4 is not preferable, meaning any investigations should be concluded before a commitment to purchase. In a single inspection, we will not be able to rule out the possibility that these cracks may worsen over time without more in-depth investigations. **Option 1:** You should discuss this with your solicitor and the vendor to ask the current vendor to make a claim under their building insurance. In these instances, the insurers will usually assess the movement in more detail, which may or may not include assessing the subsoil and foundations by digging "trial pits/boreholes" to establish the cause and remedy required. Your solicitor should provide further advice on the implications of this approach to you. You must ask the seller to notify their buildings insurers to investigate the movement and obtain quotations for any necessary repairs. Your solicitor should provide further advice on the implications of this approach to you. **Option 2:** If this option is not available, it is advisable that you and the vendor jointly instruct a structural engineer to commission a full survey relating to the movement noted and general observations concerning the structural integrity of the property as a whole. The benefit of the report can be transferred to you on completion if there is a period of monitoring required. **Option 3:** Out of experience, the majority of structural engineers may not be willing to produce a report for the benefit of both seller and buyer, as stated in option 2 above. If you cannot find a structural engineer to agree on option 2, you should then obtain your own structural engineer’s report specifically relating to the movement noted for further investigations. **Option 4:** As the extent of these cracks is not excessive and also only limited to the front addition, you may wish to postpone the in-depth investigations if the above may cause delays to the sale and you have time constraints. However, we do not recommend this option and advise you, if possible, to try the above options. In that case, you may wish to undertake localised repairs and monitor the affected areas. The cracking should be repaired and monitored regularly. We recommend localised repairs be undertaken by re-bonding/re-toothing the masonry joints or reinforcing with bed-joint reinforcement. Regarding the repair of the cracks, which may be subject to further minor movement, it is standard practice to recommend that the external wall cracks are strengthened with the installation of ‘Helifix’ bars and resin injection repairs. This consists of 6 mm diameter stainless steel bars inserted into the bed joints at approximately 500 mm each side of the crack. The crack in the bricks can either be replaced or resin grouted with low viscosity grout such as ‘Nitokit LV’ by Fosroc. The bars are inserted every 2-3 courses of brick. A well-installed ‘Helifix’ bar repair should blend into the façade wall and not visibly stand out. Some sections may require partial reconstruction, and some of the brickwork will need to be replaced. You should obtain full cost estimates before a legal commitment to purchase is made. We recommend that the cracking, once repaired, be monitored regularly. In the event of further movement being identified in the future, the matter should be referred immediately to a Chartered Structural Engineer, who should undertake a more detailed investigation on your behalf. As this property is located on a subsoil with clay geology, this may become a regular maintenance issue in the future, and minor cracks may reappear after repairs are undertaken. In any case, future monitoring is required, and all cracks require repair to avoid water ingress into the walls, which is damaging. Condition Rating 3. We cannot confirm the condition of the underground drain lines between the manhole covers. Given the age of the property and the movement noted, we advise you to have a drains test carried out using CCTV. Any such test should be carried out prior to exchange of contracts for purchase.

standard_paragraphs.label: Bay movement cracks-Helifix Repair and injection NEW (AMEND)
standard_paragraphs.text: The mortar joints at the abutment of the front bay and the main wall have cracked. Also, there is a gap to the left side of the bay. These cracks have appeared since apparent fairly recent repointing works were carried out, indicating there to be progressive movements occurring. The external lintels were seen to be intact without any through or surface cracking visible. OR: Movement was noted in the front bay, as evidenced by cracks in the external walls in various locations, both externally and internally (see also Section E3). It appears that movement in the front bay has occurred after re-rendering works were undertaken at some point in the past, the exact date of which could not be ascertained. Therefore, we cannot guarantee that further movement will not occur in the future. It is often the case that the foundations of bays are shallower than those of the remainder of the house, making the bay more susceptible to structural movement. Due to the clayey nature of the soil, it typically experiences seasonal expansion and shrinkage cycles, contributing to the visibility of cracks and their reappearance. Given the size of the cracks and the typical clayey nature of the soil in this area, it is recommended to increase the tensile strength of the masonry fabric by installing stainless steel HeliFix bars between the bay structure and the main building walls to ensure that the abutment connection is strengthened and potential future movement is arrested. Regarding the repair of the cracks, which may be subject to further minor movement, it is standard practice to recommend that the external wall cracks are reinforced with the installation of Helifix bars and resin injection repairs. This involves inserting 6 mm diameter stainless steel bars into the bed joints at approximately 500 mm intervals on each side of the crack. The cracks in the bricks can either be replaced or resin grouted with a low viscosity grout such as Nitokit LV by Fosroc. The bars should be inserted every 2–3 courses of brick. A well-installed Helifix bar repair should blend into the façade and not be visibly prominent. If further assurance is required to reduce the expansive nature of the clayey soil below, the client could consider local resin injection beneath the bay window to fill any potential void pockets and increase the bearing capacity of the soil in this area. This method involves injecting grout or resin into the soil beneath the property footings at strategic locations to displace any voids or water, bind the soil into a solid mass, and stabilise the ground. Additionally, the injected resin typically lifts the structure back to its previous level, usually closing any cracks in the internal or external walls that may have formed. This solution is relatively quick and can be completed in approximately 1–2 days, avoiding extensive excavation works and minimising disruption. When undertaken by a reputable company, 10- to 20-year product warranties are provided as standard. Mainmark, Geobear, and other companies offer this solution in the UK. Once repaired, the cracks should be sealed to prevent possible water ingress into the property. Underpinning is not considered a suitable option at this stage. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Bay movement minor, Injection only
standard_paragraphs.text: Movement was noted in the front bay, evidenced by cracks in the external walls at various locations. Based on this single inspection, the movement appeared minor and within acceptable tolerances. It is common for bay foundations to be shallower than those of the rest of the house, which can make the bay more susceptible to structural movement. Due to the clayey nature of the soil, it typically undergoes seasonal expansion and shrinkage cycles, contributing to the visibility of cracks and their reappearance. Given the size of the cracks and the typical clayey nature of the soil in this area, to reduce the expansive nature of the clayey soil below, if cracks reappear after repairs to the cracked areas of the render by a competent contractor, the client could consider a local resin injection below the front bay are to fill any potential void pockets and increase the bearing capacity of the soil in this area. This method uses a technique where grout/resin is injected into the soil below the property footings at strategic locations, such that it displaces any voids or water, binds the soil into a solid mass and stabilises the ground. Additionally, the injected resin typically lifts the structure back to its previous level, normally closing any cracks in the internal/external walls of a house that may have formed. This solution is relatively quick and can be completed in approximately 1-2 days. Additionally, this method avoids extensive excavation works and does not cause heavy disruption. Where undertaken by a reputable company, 10-20 year+ certificates/product warranties are provided as standard. Mainmark, Geobear, and other companies offer this solution in the UK. Once repaired, the cracks should be sealed to prevent possible water ingress into the property. Underpinning is not considered a suitable option at this stage. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Bay active movement due to trees (LONG PARA)
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted signs of movement cracking to the front bay in various locations at ground and first floor level, and also to the right flank wall towards the front section of the building. These cracks have appeared since apparent fairly recent repointing and re-rendering/paint works were carried out indicating there to be progressive movement occurring. We also noted that crack monitoring measures have been undertaken at some point in the past by way of inserting two metal “Demec Studs”. Demec studs are installed either side of a crack and secured using a high strength adhesive. A high quality measuring caliper is recommended to ensure you reliably and accurately record the distance between the 2 disks. The disadvantage of this type of monitoring system is that these are particularly difficult tools to work with as cracks can be monitored in one direction only, also these are not suitable for cracks in corners. The existing Studs are only in one area of the bay and do not cover all areas of the front elevation where we noted signs of movement. Your solicitor should make further enquiries to establish if the vendor may have any information or data regarding the crack monitoring measures that have been undertaken to the front bay, however we assume any data may not be very useful as it is clearly evident the cracks have reopened again indicating there is a progressive movement at the property. Subsidence cracks are often caused by tree roots extracting moisture from shrinkable clays under shallow footings. However, unfortunately, it is not possible in one single inspection to ascertain the exact cause of the movement. Many different factors may have caused or contributed to this movement. The presence of trees or faulty drainage trenches are the most common cause of cracking, although in the case of this property, extensive structural alterations that could have increased loads, use of strong mortar, replacement of the windows, and expansion and contraction of materials in the building may also have contributed to the movement noted. The complexity here is that you may not be able to rule out the possibility that these cracks may get worse over time without more in-depth investigations. I am not sure if the vendor would be willing to allow for intrusive investigations by a structural engineer at this stage. However, one option that you may have, and you may like to discuss this with your solicitor and the vendor, is to ask the current vendor to make a claim under their Building insurance. In these instances, the insurers will usually assess the movement in more detail which may or may not include assessing the subsoil and foundations by digging "trial pits/boreholes" to establish the cause and remedy required. Your solicitor should provide further advice on the implications of this approach to you. The surveyor’s view is that this defect must be resolved by elimination of all potential causes. If the trees are the main cause of movement, the problem could potentially be resolved by removal of the vegetation, whose roots are beneath the foundations. However, again, this will have to be followed by a period of monitoring by a Chartered Structural Engineer (probably 3-year period or more of monitoring) and the trees will have to be cut down in stages to avoid the risk of heave. Any permanent repairs should be postponed until it has been established that the cracking is not progressive – or likely to start again as soon as there is a spell of dry weather. In removing the trees, they should be reduced in size progressively over several years (depending on the size and species of the tree). This will help to control ground heave when a clay subsoil, that has been dried out by a tree, expands as it starts to take up water again. Therefore it is important to obtain a report from an Arborist to advise on this matter. You should be mindful that the Cypress tree is located at the neighbouring property to the right, therefore one complexity here would be to obtain permission from the neighbouring property and your solicitor should advise you on the implications of this matter. The vital issue is whether the cracking is progressive. If the cause of cracking can be removed, the wall can either be repaired or stitched together, or, if this proves impracticable, displaced walling can be rebuilt. In extreme cases, parts of the buildings may have to be demolished to avoid excessively expensive repairs. We cannot confirm the condition of the underground drain lines between the manhole covers. Given the age of the property and the movement noted, we advise you to have a drains test carried out using CCTV. Any such test should be carried out prior to exchange of contracts for purchase. The ground floor level spandrel of the bay is usually masonry, and a crack at this level is usually due to subsidence of the bay foundation which may be shallower and more vulnerable to clay shrinkage during droughts. In extreme cases, underpinning or a pad and beam foundation is likely to be needed to support a ground floor bay spandrel that has cracked away. The cracked brickwork should be cut out and made good. We cannot rule out the possibility that the bay may require underpinning in the future. However, this will have to be confirmed by a Chartered Structural Engineer once all the potential causes of movement have been identified and eliminated which may well take several years. Once observation shows that the cracks are no longer developing, it should be made good. As mentioned before, no permanent repairs to cracked walls should be carried out until the movement of the soil has virtually finished. The small daily fluctuations in the width of the cracks, caused by thermal expansion and contraction must be ignored. Fine cracks can be left alone, unless they allow water to penetrate into the building, in which case they might be made watertight. The extent of the making good will depend on the extent of the crack and on the displacement of the brickwork. It is important to ensure that strong mortar is not used (see our comments below). Any repairs must be undertaken by a Chartered Structural Engineer and after a period of monitoring when it is ensured there is no progressive movement occurring. You may obtain cost estimates of repairs from a Chartered Structural Engineer before a commitment to a purchase is made. Unfortunately, there is a stigma attached to cracking in buildings and the majority of high street lenders may not welcome this in the future without solid confirmation that the cracking is not a subsidence crack and it is longstanding, usually after a period of monitoring. I doubt if there would be many professionals willing to give 100% assurance to any lender that further movement will not happen in the future. It is important to note that different lenders may have different policies and approaches towards properties with a history of underpinning. For example, some high street lenders state that properties that have been subject to underpinning must have the residue of a 10 (some 20) year guarantee, evidence of full Building Regulations approval and be given a supportive valuation to be acceptable security to the Bank. Some state that in some cases it may be prudent only to accept underpinned terraced or semi-detached dwellings if the abutting ones have been similarly treated, or where it has been proved that the proposed security is unaffected by a local or inherent individual problem. Also, some lenders do not accept properties which have been underpinned within the last 3 years. This may have an impact on the future saleability of the property and your solicitor should provide further advice. As you may have noticed, you should appreciate that unfortunately there is no Yes/No answer to situations like this and as your surveyor, we can only highlight all the potential future risks involved in your investment. We must reiterate that the above information is based on one single visual inspection and does not provide a conclusive answer or remedy. You should be aware of the risks involved in the purchase of this property and be mindful of complexities and costs that could be involved surrounding the movement until such times the matter is fully investigated and monitored under strict supervision by a Chartered Structural Engineer, who should provide a cost of repairs, full diagnosis and remedy. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Timber 2
standard_paragraphs.text: Timber framed homes when built are invariably insulated to a higher than normal standard required by building regulation at the time of construction. standard_paragraphs.label: On glazing
standard_paragraphs.text: There is a cat flap in the rear patio door. This appears unsightly, and you may wish to remove this. Removing a cat flap from patio door glazing without replacing the glazing is generally not possible. Cutting a hole in the glass for a cat flap compromises the structural integrity of the glass. Once a hole is made, the glass is permanently weakened, and removing the cat flap leaves an unrepairable hole. Cutting a hole for a cat flap can break the vacuum seal between the glass panes. This seal is critical for the insulation properties of the glazing, and once broken, it cannot be restored without replacing the glazing unit. Also, the resulting hole would be unsightly and could let in drafts, reducing the energy efficiency of the door. The most practical solution is to replace the entire glazing panel. This will restore the door to its original condition, maintaining its structural integrity, insulation properties, and aesthetic appearance. Condition

If this is the case, we consider it possible that areas of hidden wet rot may exist in timber fascia boards hidden behind the gutter brackets. Condition Rating NI.

standard_paragraphs.label: Redecorate Advice
standard_paragraphs.text: Outside decorations help keep the property in satisfactory condition. Without a protective finish, parts will quickly deteriorate requiring extensive repairs. To prevent this, the external surfaces should be redecorated soon. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Repairing Safely General
standard_paragraphs.text: To safely repair parts of the property at higher levels, contractors will have to use appropriate access equipment (for example scaffolding, hydraulic platforms, etc.).

standard_paragraphs.label: Surface rot and deterioration
standard_paragraphs.text: From ground level, we noted evidence of surface rot, deterioration and discolouration to timber fascia and soffit boards. On-going maintenance will be required to slight rot, softness, open jointing, flaking paintwork and other minor defects. Regular upkeep of decorations is particularly important with softwood as this type of timber is prone to fungal attack. Condition rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Mandatory
standard_paragraphs.text: All exterior timber work should be carefully checked for decay when redecoration is carried out, and repairs undertaken as found to be necessary. The external paint work should be maintained to a good standard to reduce the dangers of timber decay. Woodwork at roof or eaves level is commonly affected by weathering and rot and the need for repairs must be anticipated.

standard_paragraphs.label: General condition (1/2/3)
standard_paragraphs.text: The external decorations are in an overall ||poor/fair/good||condition. Regular upkeep of decorations is particularly important with softwood as this type of timber is prone to fungal attack.Condition Rating ||3/2/1||. Gutters

standard_paragraphs.label: Hidden wet rot (A)
standard_paragraphs.text: In view of the age and condition of the gutters we consider it possible that areas of hidden wet rot may well exist in fascia boards hidden behind the gutter brackets. Soffit boards

standard_paragraphs.label: UPVC through gaps timber is present NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: The fascia and soffit boards are made of UPVC. Where partially visible through gaps from the upper floor bedrooms, it appears that the timber fascia boards are still in place. Therefore, we consider it likely that the UPVC soffits are cappings over the original softwood, at least in some areas, if not all. This can only be confirmed with intrusive investigations, which are outside the scope of a home survey. If softwood fascias are still in place, they could be subject to decay. Where partially visible, no significant defects to the UPVC sections were noted. However, the exposed areas of timber showed signs of surface rot and deterioration. This arrangement remains functional for now, and there is no need for intrusive investigations at this stage. Condition rating: 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: UPVS ONLY MODERN
standard_paragraphs.text: The fascia and soffit boards are of modern UPVC construction. Where visible, no significant defects were noted. Condition rating 1.

If softwood fascias are still in place, they could be subject to decay. Where visible, no significant defects were noted. Condition rating 1.

standard_paragraphs.label: UPVC clad soffits (1)
standard_paragraphs.text: The soffit boards under the bottom edges of the front and rear roof slopes are clad in UPVC. They are flat and even, and in satisfactory condition. These boards may mask the original soffits which could contain asbestos (see Section I3). According to the Institute for Environment and Health this asbestos based product should not be a cause for concern, however it should not be disturbed or drilled without taking suitable safety precautions. Condition Rating 1.

standard_paragraphs.label: Timber condition
standard_paragraphs.text: Timber fascia boards and soffit boards appear to be in||poor/satisfactory|| condition. Condition Rating ||3/2/1||.

standard_paragraphs.label: Asbestos soffits
standard_paragraphs.text: The soffit boards may contain asbestos. However, we are not asbestos surveyors and this could not be ascertained without specialist’s test. You must treat them as though they contain asbestos unless it could be confirmed through testing that they are safe. (See section I3). D9 Other

standard_paragraphs.label: possibly poor sound insulation
standard_paragraphs.text: We inspected the property during the day. At the time of our inspection no significant sound from adjacent properties was noted. Having regard to the age of the property it is unlikely that any effective sound insulation was provided between adjacent properties at the time of construction. Therefore it is possible, dependent upon the lifestyle of the neighbours, that sound transmission will be encountered during your occupation of the property and which in the extreme could affect your quiet enjoyment.

standard_paragraphs.label: Visit again before purchase
standard_paragraphs.text: We strongly advise that prior to exchange of contracts you should return to the property on a number of occasions, particularly in the evening and at weekends, in an attempt to establish who your neighbours are and whether the way in which they use and occupy their property will produce unreasonable levels of sound transmission which could affect your quiet enjoyment, such that, if known to you prior to purchase, would lead you to reconsider your proposal to purchase the property.

standard_paragraphs.label: Mandatory
standard_paragraphs.text: No site investigations or specific enquiries have been undertaken to determine whether the property is situated on made ground or land that may be contaminated. For the purposes of this report, it has been assumed that the site is free from any such contamination and that no deleterious materials are present which would adversely affect the structure, occupation, or quiet enjoyment of the property. We have not made any enquiries with the Local Authority, building management, or other relevant bodies regarding the historical use of the land, the potential for previous industrial activity, or any known environmental or ground condition concerns which may impact the property. You are therefore advised to instruct your legal adviser to carry out appropriate due diligence, including environmental searches and enquiries with the Local Authority, to establish whether any historical or current factors exist which may affect the property’s suitability for continued residential use or impose future liabilities.

standard_paragraphs.text: There are various minor defects which, like those noted above, are not urgent and individually will not be costly to repair. These items could lead to significant expenditure if regular maintenance is not undertaken.

standard_paragraphs.text: Small sections of the roof voids at the front and front left were partially visible through the eaves cupboards, offering a view of the roof void at the rear of the roof slope. However, these areas are boarded on both the floor and the underside of the sloping roofs beneath the rafters, which limited our ability to inspect the insulation (if any) between the ceiling joists on the floors of the eaves cupboards. standard_paragraphs.text: The roof space was not adequately covered with floor boards and we carried out a head and shoulder inspection through the loft hatch. E1 Roof structure

standard_paragraphs.label: Stored items including redundant water tank
standard_paragraphs.text: Stored items and personal belongings were present within the loft, including a redundant water tank. You should obtain confirmation from the vendor as to whether these items will be removed prior to completion of the sale.

standard_paragraphs.label: Does not serve the flat, lower level flat, Heavy tiles
standard_paragraphs.text: Your legal adviser should make further enquiries to ascertain the exact liabilities under the terms of the lease. We have not studied the lease. In any event, the rights and responsibilities for repair and maintenance should be thoroughly investigated by your legal adviser. The roof structure serves the neighbouring property above and has therefore not been inspected. We are not aware of any existing defects to the roof structure. It is important to note that, in a building of this age, the original roof coverings would likely have consisted of either slate or clay tiles, both of which are lighter in weight compared to modern interlocking concrete tiles. The replacement of original tiles with heavier alternatives can, in some cases, lead to stress or deflection within the roof structure. This can only be determined through an internal visual inspection of the roof structure to assess its condition and confirm whether adequate support is in place. As such an inspection falls outside the scope of our survey, we cannot confirm the presence or absence of structural defects. However, based on our external visual inspection of the roof coverings, no signs of deflection or distortion were observed, suggesting that the current arrangement remains functional. Nonetheless, the possibility of concealed defects cannot be entirely ruled out.

standard_paragraphs.label: Stored items removed
standard_paragraphs.text: There are stored items and personal belongings inside the loft. You should ensure that the vendor removes these items before completion of the sale.

standard_paragraphs.label: Rubble/broken pieces May contain ASBESTOS
standard_paragraphs.text: We observed loose rubble and broken materials that may contain asbestos. However, we are not asbestos specialists, and the presence of asbestos can only be confirmed through specialist testing, which falls outside the scope of our survey. For more detailed information, please refer to our comments in Section I3 of the report. Until confirmed otherwise through specialist testing, you should assume that the broken and loose rubble in the roof space contains asbestos. You must exercise extra caution when opening and closing the loft hatch, and take particular care if you plan to put insulation in the loft. Any disturbance could release dust, which poses serious health and safety risks if asbestos is present. We recommend obtaining an asbestos report to verify its presence, particularly in this area. If asbestos is confirmed, you should also obtain cost estimates for its safe removal.

standard_paragraphs.label: Small wasp nests
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted evidence of a few small wasp nests in the roof space, however no evidence of current activity was identified. We recommend that you monitor this section and in case of noticing any activity refer the matter to a reputable Wasp Nest Control Specialist for further investigation. Condition Rating 2.
