standard_paragraphs.text: I found that minor parts of the original structure are too small ||Describe|| and these should be replaced.

standard_paragraphs.label: Fire Check Wall Repair
standard_paragraphs.text: The wall between this and the neighbouring dwelling (called the party wall) is partly missing and could allow fire to pass from one property to another (see section J3 Risks). The wall should be built up and any gaps to the underside of the roof covering sealed soon. The owner of the neighbouring property has a number of legal rights over this party wall. You should check with your legal adviser before you organise any work (see section I2).Condition rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Chimney Breast Part Removed (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: Part of the chimney breast within the roof space of this property has been removed and the remaining structure is not properly supported and is at risk of collapse (see section J1 Risks). This is a safety hazard (see section J3 Risks).You should ask your legal adviser to check if the local authority gave permission for this work (see section I1). If not, you should ask an appropriately qualified professional to inspect the structure, and provide a report with recommendations. Condition rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Gallows Brackets
standard_paragraphs.text: The chimney breasts from the rear of the chimney stack have been removed. Gallows brackets, which are right-angled steel supports, are used to support the remaining chimney breast or stack above and are installed onto the party wall directly beneath the remaining element of the chimney breast or stack. Gallows brackets have been used as a form of support to withstand the remaining load of the chimney stack above. Your legal adviser should confirm if Building Regulations approval has been obtained (see also sections E5 & H1).

standard_paragraphs.label: Serious Beetle Advice
standard_paragraphs.text: I found an active and extensive infestation of wood-boring insects in parts of the roof structure. This is serious and you should ask an appropriately qualified and experienced person to repair this problem now.

standard_paragraphs.label: Roof Covering Too Heavy
standard_paragraphs.text: The roof covering is too heavy and has caused the roof structure to distort and sag.You should ask an appropriately qualified person to inspect the roof and recommend a repair scheme. Condition Rating||* 2/3.*||

standard_paragraphs.label: Down lighters without Fire hoods
standard_paragraphs.text: We observed that the downlighters in the loft are not equipped with fire protective safety hoods, which poses a potential fire hazard. To ensure the ceiling is fire-safe and to prevent the accumulation of dust and other flammable particles, it is essential to fit protective fire hoods to all downlighters within the roof structure. Failure to do so could compromise the safety of the property in the event of a fire. Condition Rating ||*2/3*||.

standard_paragraphs.label: Fire collar
standard_paragraphs.text: There is no adequate intumescent fire collar where the boiler flue pipe penetrates inside the roof space. A fire collar is a type of fire-resistant fitting that maintains the integrity and fire insulating rating of a building element which has been penetrated by building services. Typically, fire collars comprise a retaining ring which contains an intumescent material that expands when heated rapidly. The strong compressive force exerted by the expanded material forms a fire-resistant seal, closing off the service component and creating an insulating barrier. An intumescent pipe collar should be installed. Condition Rating 2. No access but no distortion: There was no available access to the roof void, however externally there were no signs of significant distortion.

standard_paragraphs.label: Modern wood (A)
standard_paragraphs.text: The roof timbers are of modern kiln dried softwood. No bracing to trusses (3): Roof trusses should be provided with bracing timbers to prevent further movement or distortion in the roof structure. Bracing timbers should be provided laterally and diagonally across the underside of the rafters throughout the length of the roof. Each of the plate fixing joints to the trusses should be carefully checked to ensure they are secure. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Overstressed roof (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: The roof timbers appear to be over stressed and deflection is taking place. Strengthening is required and a specification should be provided by a Structural Engineer. Condition Rating 3. No firewall (3): There is no fire break wall in the roof void, the omission of which is causing potential fire and security hazards. Many lending institutions require an adequate firebreak wall to be created as a condition of their mortgage, whilst the omission or inadequacy of the fire breakwall can lead to potential difficulties if a claim for insurance is made.We therefore consider an adequate fire break wall should be created at the earliest possible date. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Bad condensation (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: There is increasing evidence of condensation staining to a number of the roof timbers. This represents a significant risk to the roof timbers.Ventilation should be improved by fitting vents in the eaves and roof slopes to ensure long term damage is not caused to the roofing timber or underfelt. A reputable roofing contractor will be able to undertake this work, and it is recommended that quotations should be obtained prior to legal commitment to purchase. Condition Rating3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Repoint chimney breasts (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: The mortar joints in the chimney breast are deteriorating. This may allow escape of smoke and flue gases into the roof space. The soft and recessed areas of mortar need to be thoroughly raked out to a depth of at least 15mm and repointed with sulphate resistant mortar.Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Gaps in party wall (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: There are gaps within the party walls. These should be sealed with fireproof material. This may be a requirement of your insurance policy. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Woodworm found (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted evidence of wood boring beetle infestation in ||describe location||. In view of the presence of this infestation, which could extend into other areas hidden from our view, we recommend a suitably qualified firm is employed to inspect the property and report upon the extent of such beetle infestation and to provide an estimate for treatment of the work. Ideally this firm should be a member of the Property Care Association. We recommend a copy of the specialist report be provided to us, at which time we can give it consideration and make such further recommendations or provide such further advice as we consider appropriate. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Vermin in loft (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: There is evidence of vermin in the roof space. Mice, rats and squirrels can cause serious damage, particularly if they chew through electrical cables. It is recommended you engage the services of a pest control specialist to inspect and report on control measures and cost.Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Bird nests (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: There is evidence of birds' nesting materials and droppings within the roof void area. These materials are hazardous to health. It is recommended they are removed under controlled conditions.Further advice should be sought from the Environmental Health Department of the Local Authority. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Sheeting under rafters (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: The material which has been fixed to the underside of the rafters should be removed as it prevents ventilation and directs any penetrating moisture to discharge at the eaves, or penetrate timbers resulting in decay. Possible hidden defects may be found. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Truss storage of goods (A)
standard_paragraphs.text: Any items stored in the roof should be of lightweight nature and spread evenly in the roof void to avoid the possibility of damage to the ceilings thereunder. Truss roof construction was not designed to allow for excess weight, therefore the storage of items is discouraged. No bracing but ok cond (1): The trussed roof construction is built in accordance with regulations and building controls current at the time of construction. Since that date building regulations have been amended and now provide for bracing at top, fixing points and diagonal bracing across the underside of rafters, and throughout the length of the roof. This property roof lacks such bracing but there was no indication of significant deflection or other roof timber damage at the time of our inspection. Condition Rating 1.

standard_paragraphs.label: Cable damage
standard_paragraphs.text: Signs of damage were found to the electrical cables in the loft, and a full inspection and test of the electrical installation is recommended to assess the extent of the damage and costs to carry out repairs.Condition Rating 3. Condition

standard_paragraphs.label: NEW-Shakes with new strutting, Heavier roof tiles
standard_paragraphs.text: Longitudinal cracks, known as ‘shakes’, were observed in some of the roof timbers, particularly the rear purlin. Shakes are natural splits that occur due to timber shrinkage. Rafters are typically supported at mid-span by purlins, which in this property run from party wall to party wall, providing both support to the rafters and lateral stability to the gable end walls. The purlins are supported on corbelled brick projections, which is also the case here. Additional strutting supports have been installed, some of which appear to have been added in recent years. These may have been introduced following the removal of chimney breasts, to strengthen the purlins and mitigate the effects of the shakes (refer to Section H1 for comments on relevant regulations). As previously noted in Section D2, the roof coverings appear to have been renewed at some point, although the exact date is unknown. The original covering was likely clay or slate tiles. The current interlocking concrete tiles are significantly heavier than traditional clay or slate, which may place additional strain on the roof timbers. The presence of shakes and added strutting supports suggests some minor historical movement; however, during this inspection the roof structure appeared generally stable. The extent of the shakes was not excessive and is considered within acceptable tolerances. There is no immediate need for repair, and they are unlikely to affect the structural performance of the roof. Annual inspections are advised to monitor the condition and address any future deterioration or splitting. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Timber ok - shakes present (1)
standard_paragraphs.text: The roof timbers are in sound condition where visible. There are some longitudinal cracks in the roof timbers, which are known as 'shakes'. These occur naturally in timbers and are caused by shrinkage. They are not serious and do not detrimentally affect the performance of the timbers. Nevertheless, annual inspections are recommended to monitor the condition of the timbers so that any deterioration or further splitting can be dealt with. No comment can be made on the concealed roof timbers. It is possible these may have suffered decay such as an outbreak of dry rot or wet rot, or they have been weakened from attack by wood boring beetles. Concealed timbers include the bottom ends of the rafters, wall plates and purlin ends. Condition Rating 1.

standard_paragraphs.label: Significant distortion due to alterations (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: The roof structure has been altered by the removal of the supporting timber struts beneath the purlins. This has resulted in weakening of the roof structure and dishing to the roof. You should engage the services of a structural engineer who will be able to provide guidance on strengthening the roof structure. Condition Rating 3. No significant defects (1): The roof slopes are reasonably aligned and free of any significant deflection or structural defect. Condition Rating 1.

standard_paragraphs.label: Good roof (1)
standard_paragraphs.text: The visible areas of the roof frame are of traditional timber design for this type of building. There is no evidence of significant distortion although there is some slight deflection considered normal in a property of this age and type and to be within acceptable tolerances.Condition Rating 1. No condensation (1): There was no evidence of condensation or rot damage on the date of inspection but the situation should be monitored. Condition Rating 1. No distortion (1): There is no evidence of significant distortion. Condition Rating 1. No woodworm (1): Whilst there was no evidence of frass (powdered wood) to indicate ongoing wood-boring beetle activity, roof voids are intrinsically dusty places and it is possible that evidence may be concealed. Condition Rating 1. Insulation

standard_paragraphs.label: All boarded not ascertained NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: As the loft floor was all boarded, we could not ascertain if there was adequate insulation provided in all areas of the roof between the ceiling joists. We recommend a sample of the floorboards be lifted by a competent contractor to establish if adequate insulation is provided. The roof void insulation should be a minimum of 270 mm of fibre quilting, laid between and over the joists (the timbers onto which the ceilings are fixed). Care should be taken to ensure that any wiring and electrical fittings are not unduly covered. In any case, any roof insulation, if present, is likely to have been compressed by the floorboards. It is worth noting that when floorboards are placed directly onto the joists, this would compress the insulation and not meet Building Regulations guidelines because you wouldn’t have the full 270 mm depth of insulation required by regulations. Should you decide to place loft boards on top of the insulation, a raised loft floor should be built above the insulation to avoid the risk of interstitial condensation and rot to roof timbers. It is worth noting that should you place loft boards directly onto the joists, this would squash the insulation down and it would not meet Building Regulations guidelines because you wouldn’t have the full 270 mm depth of insulation required by regulations. Condition Rating 2. NOTE: Boarding the loft may change the load-bearing characteristics of the ceiling below and could be considered a change of use if the space is being converted for storage or living purposes. This often requires Building Regulations approval to ensure the floor can support the additional load and that other safety standards are met. Therefore, you should consult the Building Control Body of the local authority first. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Inside walls of eaves
standard_paragraphs.text: The inside walls of the eaves cupboard are covered with insulation boards. Condition Rating 1.

standard_paragraphs.label: New-Boarded, where visible fibre quilt Insufficient depth
standard_paragraphs.text: Where partially visible, the insulation in the roof space consists of fiber quilting laid between the ceiling joists. However, as the majority of the loft space is boarded, we could not ascertain if there is adequate insulation provided in all areas of the roof between the ceiling joists. Where visible, the insulation does not have adequate depth. We recommend increasing the roof void insulation to a minimum of 270 mm, laid between and over the joists (the timbers onto which the ceilings are fixed). Additionally, the roof insulation has been partially compressed by the floorboards. A raised loft floor should be built above the insulation to avoid the risk of interstitial condensation and rot to roof timbers. It is worth noting that when floorboards are placed directly onto the joists, the insulation is compressed, which does not meet Building Regulations guidelines, as the full 270 mm depth of insulation required by regulations is not achieved. Care should be taken to ensure any electrical fittings are not unduly covered. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: All boarded, visible through gaos fibre quilt Compressed NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: Where partially visible through gaps, insulation in the roof space is of fibre quilting, laid between the ceiling joists. However, as the roof space was boarded, we could not ascertain if there was adequate insulation provided in all areas of the roof between the ceiling joists. The roof void insulation should be a minimum of 270 mm of fibre quilting, laid between and over the joists (the timbers onto which the ceilings are fixed). In any case, any roof insulation has been compressed by the floorboards. A raised loft floor should be built above the insulation to avoid the risk of interstitial condensation and rot to roof timbers. It is worth noting that when floorboards are placed directly onto the joists, this would compress the insulation and not meet Building Regulations guidelines because you wouldn’t have the full 270 mm depth of insulation required by regulations. Care should be taken to ensure any electrical fittings are not unduly covered. However, this work is not urgent as the removal of boardings and raising a floor can be intrusive and expensive. The vendor mentioned they have not obtained any Building Regulations approvals. Condition Rating 2. No insulation NEW: There is no insulation in the roof space. The roof loft should be insulated to a minimum of 270 mm of fibre quilting, laid between and over the joists (the timbers onto which the ceilings are fixed). standard_paragraphs.label: SPRAY FOAM INSULATION
standard_paragraphs.text: We observed the presence of spray foam insulation within the roof structure. There is stigma associated with spray foam and its associated risks. Therefore, it is important to carefully consider our comments below before making a purchase decision. In 2022, an investigation conducted by the Property Care Association revealed a concerning trend: the majority of spray foam installations lacked adequate preparation, leaving structural roof timbers vulnerable to severe weakening due to rot and other defects. When considering properties with spray foam roof insulation in relation to your mortgage application, it’s crucial to be aware of potential complications. Whilst different lenders adopt varying approaches, the presence of spray foam can pose obstacles during the mortgage process. Hence, it is imperative to inform your solicitor about this aspect.

standard_paragraphs.label: Several concerns arise regarding spray foam insulation
standard_paragraphs.text:  Spray foam, or SPF, expands and solidifies upon application, effectively sealing the roof space. However, this significantly limits air circulation.  Restricted airflow results in condensation build-up, potentially leading to weakened or rotted roof supports over time.  Spray foam can obscure visual inspections, making it difficult to assess the condition of roof timbers. Over time, hidden defects, such as wood rot or decay, may go unnoticed, leading to structural failures. Regrettably, there is insufficient evidence to assess the future performance of the roof structure. Based on our assessment, we believe that the risks associated with this roof could be significantly mitigated by the removal of the foam insulation. Therefore, it is advisable to seek further guidance from a qualified roofing contractor. They can conduct a thorough inspection of the roof and provide detailed advice, along with a quotation for the removal of the foam. If you decide to proceed with the property purchase, it is important to be aware of the potential risks involved. However, it is essential to note that the presence of these risks does not necessarily indicate that the roof has serious defects. Confirmation would require intrusive investigations beyond the scope of a standard home survey. You may want to ask your solicitor to obtain any valid guarantees issued by the installation company. Additionally, ensure they confirm whether the company is accredited. If available, verify that you would be able to pass on such guarantees to future buyers when you decide to resell the property. However, it is crucial to note that the existence of any guarantee does not offer complete assurance regarding the potential impact of foam insulation on the future saleability of the property, as mentioned above, particularly for secured lending purposes. Furthermore, there remains the possibility of hidden defects that may not be covered by the guarantee. Therefore, it is essential for the client to understand and acknowledge these risks before committing to a purchase. Whilst a guarantee may provide some level of protection, it cannot guarantee immunity from all potential issues related to the foam insulation, as noted above. Future buyers and lenders may still have concerns about the presence of foam and any associated risks, which could affect the property’s marketability. Moreover, hidden defects, such as underlying structural issues, may not be apparent even with the presence of a guarantee. Additionally, some lenders and insurers may refuse to provide services for properties with spray foam insulation due to potential risks and difficulties in assessing structural integrity. Given these considerations, it is imperative for the client to carefully weigh the risks associated with the property, taking into account the presence of foam insulation. Condition Rating 3.

It is important that gaps are maintained between the insulation and the underside of the roof coverings or underfelt, which can be achieved by sliding rigid foam insulation slabs between the rafters. Condition Rating 3. No Corbelled brick for main roof: To help keep the rafters to a sensible size they are usually supported mid-span by a purlin. A purlin is a timber beam which generally supports the rafters mid span thus preventing deflection. The purlin spans from party wall to party wall and, besides supporting the rafters, provides lateral stability to the gable end walls i.e. at each end of the terraced house. They are usually built into the gable or party walls. Purlins often rest on a small projection of corbelled brickwork. However, this is not the case here and the purlins’ ends are not adequately supported. standard_paragraphs.label: Alterations AMEND NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: Repairs and some structural modifications have been undertaken in the roof structure. It appears that new strutting supports have been installed, and the location of the loft hatch has been repositioned from above the staircase to the bedroom. Additionally, the loft has been insulated and boarded on top. Adding new strutting, repositioning a loft hatch, and boarding the loft involve structural changes and alterations to the use of the space, which are different from simply repairing or re-covering the roof. Adding structural elements such as struts often affects the building's structural integrity and usually requires approval under Building Regulations to ensure the work complies with safety standards. Also, changing and repositioning the location of the loft hatch could involve alterations to the structural framework of the ceiling or roof. This kind of work typically needs Building Regulations approval to confirm that the new hatch is safely integrated into the structure. In addition, boarding the loft may change the load-bearing characteristics of the ceiling below and could be considered a change of use if the space is being converted for storage or living purposes. This often requires Building Regulations approval to ensure the floor can support the additional load and that other safety standards are met. Moreover, the chimney breasts from the chimney stack have been removed. The vendor mentioned this work was undertaken by the previous owner; however, we cannot comment on the accuracy of this statement. Gallows brackets, which are right-angled steel supports, are used to support the remaining chimney breast or stack above and are installed onto the party wall directly beneath the remaining element of the chimney breast or stack. Gallows brackets have been used as a form of support to withstand the remaining load of the chimney stack above. Your legal adviser should confirm if Building Regulations approval has been obtained (see sections E5 & H1).

standard_paragraphs.label: IMPORTANT REGULATION NOTE
standard_paragraphs.text: VERSION 1: As the rear dormer and Velux-style window are situated on the rear roof slope, and given the relatively modest scale of these additions, it is our understanding that the loft conversion falls within permitted development rights. However, we are not aware whether such rights may have been removed by the local authority, for example, through an Article 4 Direction or other planning restrictions. Your solicitor should therefore confirm whether our understanding is correct. Your legal adviser must seek confirmation that this work was carried out in compliance with Building Regulations and Planning Consent (see Section H1). VERSION 2: The roof space has been converted to create two bedrooms and a bathroom, including the installation of Velux-type windows on both the front and rear roof slopes. As a result, the majority of the main roof frame is concealed from view due to the loft conversion. Your legal adviser must seek confirmation that this work was carried out in compliance with Building Regulations and Planning Consent (see Section H1). As the roof space has been converted and all areas of the roof voids are concealed from view, without intrusive investigations and opening up the structure, which is outside the scope of a home survey, we cannot confirm whether adequate insulation or ventilation has been provided in the roof voids, nor can we confirm the adequacy of the structure. It is important to ensure that adequate consents have been obtained, including Building Regulations approval. This is particularly crucial, as in recent years, it has come to our attention that some high street lenders, during the process of secured lending valuation, have stated that the valuer has been unable to provide a valuation figure for the property due to fire safety risks. Before proceeding, they require more information to be provided, including either the original Building Regulations completion certificate for the works, a Regularisation Certificate, or a Chartered Building Surveyor’s report with specific comments on the structural integrity of the conversion, means of escape, and provision of an adequate pre-warning alarm system, including any necessary recommended works to improve the safety of the conversion, along with an estimated cost. Alternatively, if these cannot be obtained, the lender will require confirmation from the mortgage applicant, acknowledging that health and safety, and fire risk concerns mean the attic room can never be used as habitable accommodation. Where this option is chosen, the applicant must acknowledge that the valuer, completing an inspection on behalf of the mortgage lender, has identified shortcomings in the design, specification, and construction of the attic room/ loft conversion, with associated concerns regarding health and fire safety, neither a Building Regulation completion certificate nor a Regularisation Certificate is available, and hence, the loft room cannot be used for living or sleeping purposes and it should only be used for storage, and the valuation for mortgage purposes will reflect this situation. We are unable to specifically comment on the rationale of mortgage lenders and valuers or the suitability of their advice, as each lender has different policies regarding secured lending. From our experience, applying to different mortgage providers can lead to varying results or evaluations. In such cases, we cannot provide further commentary. If any potential future requests arise from your lender (if applicable) or from prospective purchasers of the property once you own it, this issue may come up, and lenders may require the criteria mentioned above to be met before approving a mortgage application. Since the conversion was presumably completed many years ago, it is likely that it does not meet current regulations unless improvements have been made, such as in insulation and ventilation. However, this cannot be confirmed without intrusive investigations, which are beyond the scope of a home survey. Older structures often fall short of modern building standards regarding structural soundness, ventilation, or insulation, and some upgrades are usually expected. Confirming these conditions would require intrusive investigations and opening up the structure, which, as mentioned, is outside the scope of our survey. It is important to note that finding a qualified professional to undertake such an inspection may be challenging, and it is not a service our company offers. Therefore, the best approach would be to obtain Building Regulations approval or a Regularisation Certificate, if possible. However, be mindful that this process may involve property inspections and potential delays due to necessary structural investigations. Unfortunately, commenting further on this matter is outside the scope of our survey engagement. In summary, obtaining Building Regulations approval or, if not available, a Regularisation Certificate would be the best documentation for you should you decide to sell your property in the future. If not, you may risk future buyers finding it difficult to obtain a mortgage unless the above requirements are met, which may not be easily achievable (see Section H1).

standard_paragraphs.label: Butterfly roof
standard_paragraphs.text: The roof frames are of traditional design typical for this type of building. Butterfly roofs are also commonly known as inverted pitch roofs, or London roofs. They consist of two V shaped roof slopes and consists of a central valley beam which supports the rafters which in turn bear onto the party walls at the top. The V shape roofs meet at the base of the V in a central valley gutter, supported on a timber beam resting on internal walls, running from front to rear of the property.

standard_paragraphs.label: Sarking Boarding No felt(staining noted) CR2 NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: The underside of the roof tiles is lined with timber sarking boards (horizontal planks of wood) fixed over the rafters. This traditional method, commonly used in the 1930s, provided structural support as well as secondary protection against driving rain and snow before the introduction of modern roofing felt. The sarking boards conceal the roofing tiles and battens from view. Where partially visible through the gaps between the boards, the underside of the roof slopes did not appear to be lined with a modern waterproof underfelt, meaning no additional secondary defence against water penetration was noted. The top side of the boards is vulnerable to rot and decay from damp ingress. It is likely that the upper surfaces have been exposed to rain over time and may have deteriorated. Outbreaks of rot are known to occur in such timbers, and the sarking boarding should be inspected regularly, ideally every six months, as part of routine maintenance, for any signs of leakage or damage. As mentioned above, the top side of the boards is vulnerable to rot and decay. The presence of hidden defects in concealed areas cannot be ruled out. We noted signs of minor staining, localised surface rot, and water damage to sections of the sarking boards within the eaves areas. A damp test was carried out using an electronic moisture meter. Although no high readings were recorded, the inspection took place on a hot, dry day following a period of dry weather. Therefore, the possibility of occasional rainwater ingress cannot be excluded. As previously mentioned, there is no underfelt present beneath the roof tiles, and occasional rain penetration is to be expected. This is not unusual and typically dries out over time without causing significant concern. However, as noted in Section D2, some of the tiles have lifted and will need to be re-laid flat to reduce the risk of wind-driven rain entering the roof space. All gaps should be addressed to minimise water ingress. The roof should be monitored during periods of rainfall, and if any localised water penetration is observed, prompt repairs should be undertaken. As a longer-term improvement, if the roof is ever replaced, the sarking boards should ideally be removed and replaced with a suitable breather membrane. This would provide both a waterproof barrier and natural ventilation for the roof void. Condition Rating 2. standard_paragraphs.label: Fan discharge into the loft space
standard_paragraphs.text: The ventilation fan inside of the top floor bathroom is discharging into the loft space. The air removed by every mechanical exhaust system shall be discharged to the outdoors. Air shall not be exhausted into a roof space as discharging bathroom exhausts inside your home can allow for condensing and the spread of mould and contaminants. In order to discharge the vent to the exterior you technically have to put a hole in a roof, flash it properly, and ensure it does not leak. This can be achieved by venting the fan to a soffit vent or to the ridge vent. Further advice and a quotation from a competent contractor will be required. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Underside all boarded NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: The underside of the rafters is covered with boardings attached to the rafters, which limited our inspection. These boardings prevented a detailed examination of the battens and the underside of the roof coverings. Since these are attached to the underside of the rafters, it is likely that there is a sufficient gap between the rafters and the underside of the roof tiles. However, we are not aware if there is any insulation between the rafters or if adequate ventilation has been provided. If the gaps are maintained, this is unlikely to cause condensation problems with the roof timbers. If there is insulation present between the rafters, it should be insulation boards. The space between the rafters above the sloping ceilings requires a different type of insulation from the loft floor, which usually uses fiber quilt insulation. It is important that if insulation boards are present, gaps should be maintained between the insulation and the underside of the roof coverings or underfelt. This can be achieved by sliding rigid foam insulation slabs between the rafters. Ideally, these slabs should be 100mm thick, but it is important to maintain a 50mm ventilation gap above the slabs, so their thickness is restricted by the size of the rafters. Additionally, we are not aware if the undersides of the roof slopes have been lined with a waterproof underfelt to provide a secondary defense against water penetration. If there is no underfelt, occasional entry of driving rain and snow must be anticipated in severe weather conditions. Without underfelt, it is quite probable that the upper surfaces of the boarding and any potential insulation may have been exposed to rain penetration over the years and may have deteriorated as a result. Unfortunately, this cannot be determined without removing the boarding, which is outside the scope of a home survey. Having boardings installed on the underside of the roof rafters without adequate underfelt and provisions for ventilation is not appropriate. The boardings can restrict airflow inside the roof structure, which, in the long term, may cause condensation problems and rot in the timbers. We recommend, as a precaution, that a sample of the boarding attached to the other side of the rafters be opened to ascertain if underfelt and/or insulation is present. A competent roofing contractor should remove a sample of these boardings to ensure these provisions are in place. However, as there was no evidence of serious rain penetration to the boardings when viewed from beneath and no signs of damp entry or smell of damp were noted, it is not considered necessary to go to the expense of stripping the boardings at this stage, and the work appears functional. Hidden defects may exist. In any case, there did not appear to be sufficient ventilation in the roof void, which is necessary to prevent the possibility of damaging condensation occurring on the roof timbers or roof felt. We recommend ventilating the roof void. This could be achieved by using ventilating tiles on the roof slopes or new soffits with built-in ventilation grilles. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: IMPORTANT NOTE

standard_paragraphs.label: Injected DPCs – why they should be avoided
standard_paragraphs.text: Injected damp proof courses are marketed as a way of retroactively trying to solve rising damp. The technique works (in theory) by injecting silicone-based fluids into selected mortar joints under pressure. These fluids are intended to create a water-repellent line that stops moisture rising. In reality, this rarely works and is usually unnecessary. In some instances, this method leaves an irreversible scar on the building and may even worsen the problem. The damp-proofing fluid ( theoretical barrier ) is only really effective inside the bricks themselves. It doesn’t spread very far sideways through the mortar, probably only about 10 millimetres. When it’s first injected, it creates tiny channels (called capillaries) at the bottom of the wall, which can allow moisture in rather than keeping it out. The idea behind injected damp-proofing is that the fluid will spread through the wall and block rising moisture. But in reality, it mostly stays inside the bricks and doesn’t move much through the joints (mortar). The drilling process also creates small gaps that can actually let water in, especially if the system isn’t properly installed or maintained. Holes are usually drilled at regular intervals, and directly plugged with cement, making a perfect pathway for rainwater to travel into the wall and the already plugged internal finish. The effectiveness of the treatment is only guaranteed if combined with a waterproof render or tanking plaster on the inside face of the wall; this traps moisture and makes the wall damp, cold and therefore thermally inefficient. Low-level dampness in solid-walled, breathing structures can usually be resolved by addressing the cause of the damp, allowing the wall to dry out and then repairing it with vapour-permeable, capillary-open, lime-based mortars and plasters.

The weather conditions, internal and external temperatures, and especially Relative Humidity, can vary on a day-by-day basis. These factors will influence what we are able to see and also how the building reacts to moisture. Our initial observations are inconclusive. We advise you to obtain a further dedicated inspection and that you should specifically request it is compliant with the JPS 2022 – Joint Position Statement 2022, Investigation of moisture and its effects on traditional buildings. standard_paragraphs.label: Taken from Damp report
standard_paragraphs.text: Impervious horizontal barriers called Damp Proof Courses (DPC’s) which are intended to prevent moisture originating in the ground rising into a wall by a process known as capillarity have been mandatory in walls of buildings in London since about 1877 as a result of model bye-laws which in this instance is likely to be slate to the original walls which is usually located about 175 mm beneath the floorboards and at about the height of a solid floor although this isn’t always the case. There is evidence of remedial damp-proofing works as determined by chemical damp-coursing holes when viewed externally not that this means that a chemical DPC was actually necessary. The original Damp Proof Course should not be bridged externally or internally and the external ground levels kept to at least 150mm below it to prevent rain from splashing over it. Items should not be stored against the outside walls that might trap rain behind or that might direct it over the Damp Proof Course.

standard_paragraphs.label: VERY NEW LONG PARA (AMEND AS APPROPRIATE)
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted indications of damp at ground floor level, in various locations at the front and rear of the property. We recorded high damp readings surrounding the rear patio door in the rear living room at ground floor level, and also to the left side of the front left living room. Some dampness was also present surrounding the front entrance door. This is not an exhaustive list. The original floors at the property would have been suspended timber floors. However, based on a heel drop test, it appeared that the ground floor in the rear section of the rear living room and also in the entire kitchen area had been replaced at some point in the past with a solid floor, as it appeared very solid and firm and did not sound hollow when we undertook a “heel drop” test. However, without intrusive investigations, it is not possible to confirm the exact type of flooring. Based on a heel drop test, the floors in other areas, such as the front left living room, appear to be of suspended timber construction. There is an air vent/air brick on the side of the kitchen. However, as the floors at the rear appear to have been replaced with solid flooring, it is likely that this air vent is no longer in use and should therefore be blocked. Traditional construction absorbs moisture but allows it to evaporate when conditions become drier. This contrasts with modern construction, which relies on impermeable barriers to prevent moisture entering the fabric. Any moisture rising as a result of capillary action would have evaporated through the walls and floors, through mortar and air bricks/air vents, which provide ventilation for subfloors, allowing for a natural breathing cycle of the property. If the floors have been replaced with solid floor construction, an internal breach to the damp-proof course can occur via the solid floor or plaster. We advise that a section of the floor covering surrounding the patio door in the rear living room be lifted in order to establish the type of floor in the front living room. If the original suspended floor still exists, the condition of subfloor timbers should be checked for any potential rot. Similarly, the condition of subfloor timbers in the front left living room and surrounding the front entrance door should be checked to ensure that no rot has occurred as a result of higher moisture content. The original damp-proof course for a property of this age and type would have been situated below the floor level, and the original floors would have been of suspended timber construction. However, unfortunately, this can only be established via invasive inspections. Unlike timber suspended floors, where the damp-proof course will be situated below floor level, with solid constructed floors, the DPC should always be situated above the finished floor level and should be visible. Changing the floors can disturb the breathing cycle of an old house. The external ground level at the rear is approximately at the same level as the internal solid floor. Without opening up the structure and undertaking intrusive investigations, it is not possible to ascertain if an adequate Damp Proof Membrane has been provided for the solid floor. As mentioned before, a damp-proof course (DPC) is a waterproof layer built in or formed within the walls to prevent ground dampness from rising. It is considered likely that a damp-proof course (DPC) would have been incorporated within the structure, but the type of DPC could not be ascertained as it is concealed by internal and external wall finishes. Any DPC should be continuous with the Damp Proof Membrane to avoid the risk of water penetration and flooding. The surveyor’s view is that addressing the dampness is a staged process that involves eliminating all potential causes. External ground levels must be lowered, and the defective areas of the external wall render must be renewed. All cracks in the external walls and all joints surrounding the rear patio door require repair to ensure they remain fully watertight (see Sections D4 & D6). The external wall render should be neatly cut back to a horizontal line 150 mm above ground level, and a bellmouth profile should be formed. Ideally, this should be finished off with a stainless steel trim designed for the purpose to provide a neat appearance. Any defective brickwork revealed during this work should be repaired as necessary. In addition, there is currently inadequate provision of drainage to the external grounds, which may cause water to pool during heavy rain, increasing the risk of penetrating dampness. A small trench should be dug around the external walls of the property. This trench need only be approximately 150 mm wide and should be infilled with stones, ideally with a French drain (perforated pipe) beneath it to channel water away to a suitable outlet. The previous recommendation for infilling with Pea Shingle has now been superseded, as it has been found that this finer material holds moisture. At the same time, further investigations by a reputable contractor are needed to open up the floors and check the condition of the timber floors in areas adjacent to the damp-affected sections. It is also important to confirm whether the floor in the rear section of the living room, surrounding the rear patio door, is of solid construction, which can be established by removing a sample of the floorboards. If this is the case, it will be necessary to ensure that an adequate damp-proof membrane is in place and continuous with the damp-proof course. Intrusive investigations will be required to confirm this. Additionally, the affected internal plaster should be removed to at least 300 mm beyond the last visible sign of damp and replaced by a competent contractor familiar with working on old buildings. It is important to note that when external wall render and internal plaster are partly removed, this should ideally be done in summer, allowing the surfaces to remain unfinished for one to two months, depending on weather conditions. Making good should be postponed until all repairs are completed, and it is ensured that both the external walls and the interior are free from dampness and have had sufficient time to dry out completely. This issue may become an ongoing problem that could affect the future saleability of the property if not addressed effectively at an early stage. Some high street lenders may not lend on the property or could impose conditions related to damp, often requiring warranties for remedial works. Therefore, if the dampness issue persists after the aforementioned repairs, you should instruct a damp-proof specialist company to carry out a full survey. We recommend appointing a firm that is a member of the Property Care Association. You should ensure that a valid guarantee is issued by the company following the completion of the works, so you can pass this guarantee on to prospective buyers when reselling the property in the future. It is essential that any company employed provides a report detailing the dampness found, the proposed remedial works, and a floor plan indicating the areas where treatment will be undertaken, followed by a final guarantee certificate confirming that the works have been completed to a satisfactory standard under a meaningful guarantee. Condition Rating 3. NOTE: The original house was constructed entirely with breathable (gas-permeable) building materials. The walls and ceilings would have been treated with breathable materials. Over the last century, different owners have likely reduced the ‘breathability’ of the house by introducing modern, non-porous materials during improvements, including the installation of double-glazed windows. These changes inevitably reduce the ‘breathability’ of the house, slowing the rate at which moisture is naturally expelled through the building, leading to a build-up of moisture (interstitial condensation), particularly on relatively cold surfaces closer to the ground. In houses of this age, conventional commercial damp-proofing methods are unlikely to be effective. The most effective means of preventing damp from becoming a problem, and leading to rot, is to use only ‘breathable’ materials in repair and maintenance, and to avoid non-permeable manufactured materials such as acrylic-based paints and gypsum plaster. This, combined with maintaining a relatively constant interior temperature and providing adequate natural and mechanical ventilation, particularly in ‘wet rooms’, should ensure that damp does not increase to levels where it could damage the structure.

This remedial work has not been effective, as we recorded high damp readings in various locations at ground floor level, as explained below. Marketed as a solution for damp issues in buildings, the system claims to evaporate water from walls through the use of bricks, tubes, or pots inserted into drilled holes. Despite these claims, the system has come under scrutiny for its lack of proven effectiveness. Surveyors often recommend avoiding the Holland damp-proofing system in favour of more proven techniques. The surrounding cement render often traps moisture, exacerbating damp problems rather than resolving them. Any defective brickwork revealed by this work should be repaired as found to be necessary. In addition, there is no adequate provision of drainage to external grounds and in heavy rains this may cause water ponding which increases the risk of penetrating dampness. A small trench should be dug around the external walls of the property. This need only be approximately 150 mm width from the wall and infilled with stones, ideally with a French Drain (perforated pipe) beneath this, channelling the water away to a suitable outlet. The previous recommendations for infilling with Pea Shingle have now been superseded as it has been found that this finer material in fact holds moisture. At the same time, further investigations by a reputable contractor is required to open up the floors to check for the condition of timber floors in areas adjacent to front elevation. Also, the affected internal plaster should be removed to at least 300 mm beyond the last sign of damp and replaced by a competent contractor familiar with working on old buildings. It is important to note that when external wall render and internal plaster are partly removed, this should ideally be done in summer, allowing the surfaces to remain unfinished for a period of one to two months, depending on weather conditions. Making good should be postponed until all repairs are completed and it is ensured that both the external walls and the interior are free from dampness and have had sufficient time to dry out completely. NOTE: The original house was constructed entirely with breathable (gas-permeable) building materials. The walls and ceilings would have been treated with breathable materials. Over the last century, different owners have likely reduced the ‘breathability’ of the house by introducing modern, non-porous materials during improvements, including the installation of double-glazed windows. These changes inevitably reduce the ‘breathability’ of the house, slowing the rate at which moisture is naturally expelled through the building, leading to a build-up of moisture (interstitial condensation), particularly on relatively cold surfaces closer to the ground. In houses of this age, conventional commercial damp-proofing methods are unlikely to be effective. The most effective means of preventing damp from becoming a problem, and leading to rot, is to use only ‘breathable’ materials in repair and maintenance, and to avoid non-permeable manufactured materials such as acrylic-based paints and gypsum plaster. This, combined with maintaining a relatively constant interior temperature and providing adequate natural and mechanical ventilation, particularly in ‘wet rooms’, should ensure that damp does not increase to levels where it could damage the structure. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Damp found, refer to a Specialist
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted indications of damp at a number of points within the property. Further investigations will be required. This issue may become an ongoing problem which could affect the future saleability of the property if not dealt with effectively at an early stage. Therefore, you should instruct a damp proof specialist company to carry out a full survey and follow their recommendations. We suggest the firm who are appointed are a member of the Property Care Association. It is important the company employed should be asked to fully inspect the property and thereafter provide a report detailing evidence of dampness found, together with their recommendations for treatment and the likely cost involved. You should ensure that a valid guarantee is issued by the company following completion of the works, in order to ensure that you are able to pass such guarantee on to your buyer when you resell the property in future. We recommend a copy of the specialist's report be provided to us at which time we can give it consideration and make such further recommendations or provide such further advice as we consider appropriate. In addition, all the dvice given in section D4 of the report must be followed.( See also sections D4, E4, and F6). Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Short Para: Floor replaced with soild NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: A heel drop test suggests that the floor at the rear of the property at ground floor level is of solid construction. However, it is likely that the original floor in this area would have been of suspended timber construction. Without opening up the structure and conducting intrusive investigations, which is outside the scope of this survey, we cannot confirm if adequate waterproofing measures and a damp-proof membrane have been provided. Any damp-proof membrane should be continuous with the external damp-proof course (DPC), although this cannot be confirmed. For solid floors, unlike suspended timber floors where the DPC is sited below floor level, the DPC should always be positioned above the finished floor level and be visible. Changing the floors can disturb the natural breathing cycle of an older property.

standard_paragraphs.label: Damp under window, external repairs required (AMEND)
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted evidence of damp staining under the window in the first-floor rear bedroom. We tested this area with a damp meter, and it recorded high damp readings. The staining may be a result of a lack of adequate drip route for the window sills or that the joints and sealants surrounding the window may not be fully watertight.The surveyor’s view is that dealing with this dampness is a staged process and this issue has to be resolved through elimination of all potential causes. Further investigations by a competent contractor are required to provide adequate detailing for the window upstand, drip cap, and drip channel to allow for the runoff of the rainwater on the ground below. There is no adequate drip throat (groove) beneath the window sub-sill to the window. This is required to avoid the risk of water ingress internally. The drip throats beneath the window sub-sills should be kept clear of obstruction to prevent possible water ingress below and should be recut if necessary, which can usually be achieved by carefully running a grinder along a batten that has first been securely clamped to the underside. The dropped sub-sills should be recast or resurfaced to direct rain away from the property. The cracked sub-sills that haven’t dropped should be repaired/filled. Additionally, a general closer inspection of the external walls, window surrounds, joints, and sealants will also be required to ensure these areas are fully watertight. Once the cause of dampness has been established, internally, the affected internal plaster should be removed to at least 300 mm beyond the last sign of damp and replaced by a competent contractor who is conversant with old buildings. Any permanent repairs should be postponed until it has been established that the dampness is not recurring – or likely to appear again as soon as there is a spell of wet weather. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Condensation mould New build
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted the presence of mould on ||LOCATION||. Mould often occurs because of condensation. Mould appears as pinpoint black spots, usually on the side surfaces of external walls, in corners and in poorly ventilated spaces, such as behind cupboards and wardrobes. Exposure to mould can cause health effects in some people. Mould spores are always found in the air we breathe, but extensive mould contamination may cause health problems. Breathing mould can cause allergic and respiratory symptoms. Any mould should be removed by a mould removal professional. Utilising the home; washing clothes, cooking etc all contribute to a build-up of condensation and mould can occur where there is no sufficient ventilation. However, many properties are affected to some degree by condensation and in order to minimise the problem it is necessary to achieve a balance between ventilation and heating. Upon occupation of the property, it is likely that condensation levels will increase and black mould may reappear. Mould removal may be an ongoing maintenance issue so you are therefore recommended to seek advice from a mould removal professional on how to manage the issue going forward. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Condensation mould suggested remedy (Old properties)
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted the presence of mould on ||LOCATION||. Mould often occurs because of condensation. Alterations to the property, such as the installation of double-glazed windows, the use of non-breathable paint materials and external wall render which disrupts the natural breathing cycle, utilising the home; washing clothes, cooking etc all contribute to a build-up of condensation and mould can occur where there is no sufficient ventilation. However, many properties are affected to some degree by condensation and in order to minimise the problem it is necessary to achieve a balance between ventilation and heating. The installation of air bricks in the external walls combined with the constant use of adequate dehumidifiers and bathroom ventilation fans, particularly in cooler temperatures can help tackle condensation (see also Section E8). Upon occupation of the property, it is likely that condensation levels will increase and black mould may reappear. Mould removal may be an ongoing maintenance issue so you are therefore recommended to seek advice from a mould removal professional on how to manage the issue going forward. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Timber panels under windows

standard_paragraphs.label: Drylined may hide dampness
standard_paragraphs.text: The internal faces of the outside walls are drylined in various locations. Walls are sometimes dry lined in order to hide dampness. This usually takes the form of timber boarding fixed to timber battens on the walls or plasterboard attached to the walls with plaster. If supporting timbers are not adequately protected or the intervening space not ventilated, serious forms of decay and mould can develop. There is a risk these linings may conceal dampness or defects which would otherwise be identified.

standard_paragraphs.label: Drylined walls (A)
standard_paragraphs.text: The walls have been lined with plasterboard. This, often referred to as'dry lining' is a popular method of finishing off the internal surfaces of walls as it saves on costs and reduces the drying out period. Dry lining is where plasterboard sheets are fixed to either timber battens or dabs of plaster and then decorated over. This means there is a gap between the plasterboard and the walls. Because of this gap, it is difficult to screw directly into the walls, although a range of proprietary fixing products can be found in DIY stores. Accordingly, it is not recommended that heavy units be fixed directly to the walls,e.g. bookshelves. Rather, it is recommended heavy items be placed on freestanding units such as bookcases and fixings to the wall be made only to prevent overturning.

standard_paragraphs.label: Refer to engineer and potential Helifix
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted cracks to the internal walls in various locations, which were particularly evident to the rear left bedroom at first floor level, on the left party wall, and to the right bedroom, underneath the window. Expansion and contraction of materials in the building can result in cracking, known as expansion cracks. Regarding the repair of the cracks that may be subject to further minor movement, it is standard practice to recommend that the cracks are strengthened with the installation of ‘Helifix’ bars & resin injection repairs. This consists of 6 mm diameter stainless steel bars inserted into the bed joints at approx. 500 mm each side of the crack. The bars are inserted every 2-3 courses of brick. However, nevertheless you should obtain further advice from a Chartered Structural Engineer, who should undertake a more detailed investigation on your behalf to provide a remedy and cost estimate of repairs for the movement noted. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Expamet New Para (Flats)
standard_paragraphs.text: Cracks were noted in the wall surfaces in various locations. Minor cracks are typically found in properties of this age and design. Expansion and contraction of materials in the building can result in cracking, known as expansion cracks. From this single inspection, the cracking noted appeared to be longstanding. Such cracks can be filled when redecorating. As this property is located on a subsoil with clay geology, this may become a regular maintenance issue in the future and minor cracks may reappear again after repairs are undertaken. Should the cracking reappear in the short term, you may need to consider more invasive repair work. Regarding repair of the cracks, that may be subject to further minor movement, it is standard practice to recommend localised repairs be undertaken by re-bonding/re-toothing the masonry joints or reinforcing with a bed-joint reinforcement. Internally, the plaster should be removed, the brickwork should be cleared. It is recommended that the deep cracks are strengthened with the installation of ‘Helifix’ bars & resin injection repairs. This consists of 6 mm diameter stainless steel bars inserted into the bed joints at approx. 500 mm each side of the crack. The bars are inserted every 2-3 course of brick. The repaired area should be reinstated with Expamet 265 diamond lath to be plugged and screwed into the brickwork, and then the wall should be plastered with Thistle One coat plaster. You should obtain full cost estimates before a legal commitment to purchase is made. You may require consent from the building management before undertaking repairs and your solicitor should provide further advice. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Parquet Flooring Potential Asbestos NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: The ground floor hallway is covered with parquet flooring. In a property of this age, it is possible that the underlays beneath the parquet may contain asbestos. However, we are not asbestos specialists, and confirmation of this would require specialist testing, which is beyond the scope of our expertise and this home survey. We are also not aware whether parquet flooring is present in other parts of the property, such as beneath laminated or carpeted floor coverings. This can only be confirmed by removing the floor coverings, which is intrusive and outside the scope of our inspection. Should you choose to replace the floors in the future, which may involve removing the parquet flooring, it is essential that you treat them as though they contain asbestos unless specialist testing confirms otherwise. In such circumstances, you must obtain an asbestos report to confirm the presence or absence of asbestos before carrying out any intrusive refurbishment works involving the removal of parquet flooring. Asbestos is classified as controlled waste, and by law, you are required to inform any contractor you employ of the potential presence of asbestos (see Section I3).

Evidence of settlement to the ground floor slabs is usually provided by gaps being visible around the perimeter of the rooms beneath the skirting boards. Floor edges were inspected where possible. standard_paragraphs.label: Old Solid Floors No DPM Advice
standard_paragraphs.text: Many older solid floors (usually before the 1940s) do not have a barrier against dampness from the ground (called a damp-proof membrane or DPM). These can be more vulnerable to dampness than floors that have a DPM.

standard_paragraphs.label: Tiles/Flags On Earth Advice
standard_paragraphs.text: Many older floors do not include a layer of concrete and consist of a layer of tiles/flagstones laid directly on the soil. These can be more vulnerable to dampness than floors that are laid on concrete.

standard_paragraphs.label: Solid Floor No DPM Do Not Cover Advice
standard_paragraphs.text: Floors of this type rely on moisture gradually passing through the floor and evaporating harmlessly in a well-ventilated property. In these cases, you should not use any impervious coverings (for example vinyl sheeting, ceramic floor tiles, foam backed carpets, etc.) because these will prevent this moisture movement creating a dampness problem in other parts. Properties of this type should be properly ventilated. Poorly ventilated property can become more prone to problems with condensation, dampness on external walls, etc.

standard_paragraphs.label: Sulphate Attack Solid Floors
standard_paragraphs.text: The floor is vulnerable to sulphate attack.Solid floors in properties of this age and type are vulnerable to a problem called 'sulphate attack' where the concrete swells upwards. In the worst cases, this can damage internal walls and doors and can only be solved by complete replacement of the floor (see section J1 Risks).

You should ask an appropriately qualified person to inspect the floor including the underfloor space.Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Dry rot (3)
standard_paragraphs.text: As indicated, there is evidence the property is affected by a serious form of rot attack, the full extent of which cannot be ascertained without opening up the structure. Rot develops in buildings where there is damp timber in conditions of poor ventilation and high humidity. The dry rot fungus produces strands which may radiate for many feet from the initial infestation and are capable of passing over and through walls, floors and ceiling masonry. These strands link the initial source with secondary outbreaks. Furthermore it favours darkness which often makes it more difficult to find, and because of its invasive nature, it is often difficult to eradicate it fully from the more inaccessible areas. For the above reasons we recommend a suitably qualified firm is employed to inspect the property and report upon the extent of such timber decay, and to provide an estimate for treatment of the work. This firm should be a member of the Property Care Association. standard_paragraphs.label: Sleeper walls are of solid brick
standard_paragraphs.text: Most houses at the end of the Victorian period (1900) were built with suspended ground floors. A typical suspended timber floor from about 1900 comprises a series of joists supported by external and internal loadbearing walls and covered with floorboards. Deep joists were expensive (they still are) and to reduce joist size there were usually intermediate supports known as sleeper walls. These are small walls in built directly on the ground or on small foundations. To ventilate the sub-floor void terra cotta or cast iron air bricks were built-in to the external walls. In practice ventilation was not always effective, partly because there were not enough vents and partly because these houses were terraced. This meant that there were only two external walls. In addition, the sleeper walls were not always honeycombed (i.e. with ventilation gaps); this impeded cross ventilation. It is essential to maintain adequate ventilation beneath the timber ground floors to avoid moisture conditions which could lead to underfloor rot attack. There are air bricks at the front and rear of the property. However, the ventilation is restricted as the sleeper walls are of solid brick construction and there are no honeycombed sleeper walls. The ventilation to the subfloors should be improved. This can be achieved by installing additional air bricks to the front and rear of the property and by provision of honeycombed sleeper walls allowing for through cross ventilation. Condition Rating 2.

Having a back boiler in an older house poses several risks that homeowners should be aware of. Back boilers, often located behind traditional fireplaces, were common in older homes but have become outdated due to safety concerns and inefficiency. standard_paragraphs.label: Dampness to chimney breast
standard_paragraphs.text: We recorded high damp readings surrounding both chimney breasts inside the living room at ground floor level. We are aware that this dampness is more present on the side of the neighbouring property to the right, however high damp readings were also recorded inside of the subject property and we noted signs of damp staining in some areas of the chimney breasts. It is not possible to ascertain the exact cause of this dampness in one single inspection. Dampness in chimney breasts can happen due to a variety of reasons, namely as a result of rainwater penetrating inside the chimney breast; a build-up of condensation forming from inside the chimney breasts due to a lack of ventilation; or the presence of hygroscopic salts drawing moisture into the walls of the chimney breasts. The surveyor’s view is that dealing with this dampness is a staged process and this issue has to be resolved through elimination of all potential causes. It is important that a competent roofing contractor check all areas of the chimney stack on both sides of the subject and neighbouring property, including flashings at the abutments of the chimney stack with the main roof, flaunchings, and all the joints to ensure the chimney stack is fully watertight. At the same time, a chimney repair contractor should inspect the chimney and flues to ensure adequate ventilation is provided for the chimneys. It is important that adequate ventilation is provided for the chimney breasts. When a chimney is sealed up, airflow becomes restricted, which can lead to condensation forming. Any disused flues must be ventilated and the lining of the chimney breasts must be checked by a specialist. If the chimneys are not lined and have not been in use for a very long time, hygroscopic salts can also attract moisture and cause dampness in the chimney breasts. If this is the case, removing the damp will involve more intrusive work, including removal of all the affected areas of plaster. The walls then will have to be left for a few months to dry out before applying a salt neutraliser and replastering. Once the source of the leak has been stopped, it may take a few months for the damp to dry out. Any redecorations must be postponed until the source of dampness has been identified and eliminated. Chimney liners would help improve the efficiency of the chimneys and will help reduce excessive condensation. Further protection can be achieved by applying a damp proof membrane. With terraced and semi-detached properties, chimney breasts are often built back-to-back and will have multiple chimney pots on top of the stack that will be shared by adjoining properties. As this issue has affected both the subject property and the neighbouring property to the right, any repairs must be undertaken to both properties. Further investigations will be required to eliminate the potential causes of the dampness. If this problem persists, you should instruct a damp proof specialist company to carry out necessary repairs. We suggest the firm who are appointed are a member of the Property Care Association. It is important the company employed should be asked to fully inspect the property and thereafter provide a report detailing evidence of dampness found, together with their recommendations for treatment and the likely cost involved. You should ensure that a valid guarantee is issued by the company following completion of the works, in order to ensure that you are able to pass such guarantee on to your buyer when you resell the property in future. The Party Wall Act 1996 governs shared structures, such as chimney stacks. It is our understanding that to undertake any potential repairs to the shared party wall or structure, you are required to serve a Party Wall Notice on the affected neighbour and your solicitor should provide further advice. standard_paragraphs.label: Old flues (A)
standard_paragraphs.text: Where open fires are used, flues must be regularly swept to remove soot and birds' nests. With older properties this can sometimes dislodge the brickwork between the flues which over the years may have perished due to the action of the acids deposited by flue gases.Old chimney flues are prone to gradual deterioration and it is possible for smoke and fumes to escape through gaps in the mortar joints,often at floor level or in roof spaces where the surfaces are unplastered. It has been known for smoke to permeate between adjoining dwellings. No tests have been made but if this problem occurs, it will need to be rectified. There are modern specialist techniques for restoring old flues by lining with concrete, which can be done without disturbing the structure, however such specialist work is expensive.

standard_paragraphs.label: Debris falling the chimney breasts
standard_paragraphs.text: We noted signs of debris and mortar which have fallen down the chimney breast in the front living room. This usually tends to be noticed more in the summer when chimneys suffer from something called “reverse stack effect”. This is when the air outside is warmer than the air inside the house, the complete opposite of what happens in winter. Air flows down the chimney from outside into the room rather than up the chimney and brings down soot and mortar. This can happen with any open old unlined chimney. Sweeping helps remove any loose deposits and prolong the life of the chimney. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Water softener
standard_paragraphs.text: There is a X water softener inside the cupboard under the staircase at ground floor level. We were informed by the vendor that this is connected to the entire property with the exception of the utility room. A water softener works by passing hard water through a cylinder containing ion exchange resin. The resin inside the softener is designed to absorb all the hard minerals, calcium, and magnesium, and replace them with sodium ions turning hard water into soft water. Because the resin can only attract a certain amount of these minerals the resin needs to be periodically regenerated to work effectively. We have not undertaken a test to this equipment. There are also suggestions that softened water is not suitable for drinking water purposes. Softened water may contain a very slight increased amount of sodium (this will increase with water hardness) and for that reason, it is not recommended for people who are on a low sodium diet or for the preparation of baby formula milk. standard_paragraphs.label: Dry rot reported by client
standard_paragraphs.text: We were informed by the client that there has been a history of dry rot treatment at the property. Any treatments are hidden from view as they are concealed by the internal and external decorations. We would not be able to comment on concealed areas and we can only hope that these works have been undertaken under adequate supervision and with a meaningful warranty. The extent of these works are unknown to us. Your solicitor should obtain necessary information including warranties for the remedial works undertaken. Dry rot can be very destructive. You must ensure that a valid guarantee is issued by the company that has completed the works, in order to ensure that you are able to pass such guarantee on to your buyer when you resell the property in the future. Fungal decay can take several forms. Dry rot is a fungus generally confined to buildings which develop damp timber, usually under conditions of poor ventilation and high humidity. The fungus produces strands which may extend for several metres over and through such materials as brick and plaster and may link the original infestation with secondary outbreaks. Immediate steps should be taken to remove the affected timbers and eradicate the cause of rot. If the timbers are not removed or the cause not properly corrected there is a risk of an outbreak of dry rot developing which can rapidly spread. One of the major difficulties in eradicating dry rot in a building is to ensure that the strands are completely killed off and to ensure proper and full treatment. It is important to establish the full extent of an outbreak which will involve fully exposing the likely affected areas. Often the fungus can be difficult to find and eradicate and proper treatment is expensive. This is the risk that you should be aware of, therefore it is very important that adequate warranties will be obtained in respect of any remedial works undertaken at the property regarding dry rot treatment.
