standard_paragraphs.label: Condensation Mould NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: We observed the presence of mould in various locations throughout the property, particularly on the window surrounds and to walls and ceilings. Mould often occurs because of condensation. Mould appears as pinpoint black spots in poorly ventilated areas. Exposure to mould can cause health effects in some people. Mould spores are always found in the air we breathe, but extensive mould contamination may cause health problems. Breathing mould can cause allergic and respiratory symptoms. Properties of this type often suffer from condensation issues. Alterations to the property, such as the installation of double-glazed windows, the use of non-breathable paint materials and external wall render which disrupts the natural breathing cycle, utilising the home; washing clothes, cooking etc all contribute to a build-up of condensation and mould can occur where there is no sufficient ventilation. However, many properties are affected to some degree by condensation and in order to minimise the problem it is necessary to achieve a balance between ventilation and heating. The installation of air bricks in the external walls combined with the constant use of adequate dehumidifiers and bathroom ventilation fans, particularly in cooler temperatures can help tackle condensation from occurring. Mould removal can present ongoing maintenance challenges because, unless all mould spores are effectively eliminated, they can resurface, especially in conditions conducive to growth, such as in poorly ventilated and humid conditions. Even after visible mould is cleaned, dormant spores can remain in the environment, waiting for the right conditions to activate. High humidity levels and inadequate ventilation can trigger regrowth, making it crucial to not only remove existing mould but also address underlying moisture issues. Preventive measures, such as those outlined above, are essential to minimise the risk of recurrence and maintain a healthy living environment. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: PIV Ventilation unit NEW
standard_paragraphs.text: There is a Positive Input Ventilation (PIV) unit installed in the loft space, with white ducting connected to a vent in the ceiling above the landing to distribute air throughout the property. PIV systems are commonly installed to improve air circulation, reduce condensation, and prevent dampness or mould buildup. They work by drawing fresh, filtered air from outside or the loft area and gently distributing it throughout the home. This helps to improve indoor air quality by displacing stale, humid air, reducing the risk of condensation and mould growth. Modern PIV units often come with smart controls, allowing variable speed settings and wireless control for greater flexibility. They are especially beneficial in homes prone to condensation and poor ventilation, as they maintain consistent airflow to minimise these issues. Additionally, PIV systems can be energy-efficient, helping to reduce heating costs by circulating warmer air from the loft. However, their effectiveness can be reduced in poorly insulated or draughty homes, where the system may struggle to control condensation or distribute air evenly. Since PIV units draw air from the loft, their performance may also vary depending on loft conditions and temperature, particularly in very cold weather, where pre-heating of the air may be necessary. We have not carried out any testing on this unit, as it falls outside the scope of a standard home survey. Your solicitor should obtain the relevant documentation regarding the installed system and confirm whether any remaining warranty is in place that can be transferred to you upon completion of the sale. However, as previously noted, we observed signs of condensation mould in various areas of the property.

However, we cannot verify the full functionality or adequacy of these fans for this specific property, as no specialist tests have been conducted. Given the presence of condensation and mould throughout the property, it appears that the existing ventilation may be insufficient. Therefore, we recommend upgrading the current fans, particularly in the bathroom, to more powerful models that provide a minimum of three air changes per hour, ensuring effective moisture removal. Additionally, the bathroom fan should ideally be set to run for an extended period after use, particularly in colder months when humidity levels tend to increase. This will help to clear excess moisture from the air, reducing the likelihood of condensation forming. In conjunction with enhanced ventilation, it would also be beneficial to use a dehumidifier near the bathroom area, particularly if ventilation alone does not address the moisture issues. Without adequate ventilation, excess moisture can linger, leading to condensation settling on surfaces and potentially causing mould to develop and spread. Regular use of a dehumidifier can assist in managing humidity levels, particularly in spaces prone to dampness. Condition Rating 2.

The presence of regular electrical sockets in a bathroom poses significant safety risks due to the increased likelihood of water contact, which can lead to electric shock or short circuits. It is important to understand the potential risks associated with lead water pipes. Lead pipes, commonly used in older properties, can pose a health hazard as lead may leach into the water supply, especially if the water is soft or slightly acidic. Prolonged exposure to lead in drinking water has been linked to various health issues, particularly in young children and pregnant women. If this is a concern for you, we recommend having a specialist assess the pipework to confirm its composition. If lead pipes are found, consider replacing them to ensure the safety of the water supply. Identifying lead pipes may require intrusive investigations, as it is not always straightforward. This could involve contacting your water supplier, as some may offer free lead testing and inspections. Local water authorities may also provide advice or assistance in testing and replacing lead pipes. Other methods include requesting a water test to check lead levels, as elevated levels could indicate the presence of lead pipes, or arranging a professional plumbing inspection. Typically, plumbers rely on visual inspections, though it may be possible to use CCTV or other methods to ascertain the presence of lead pipes, depending on the circumstances. Consultation with a competent plumber can help establish this. Please note that further comment on this matter is outside the scope of our expertise and the survey report. Whilst the flue arrangement may comply with current Building Regulations, such occurrences could potentially pose a nuisance or discomfort, particularly for individuals with respiratory sensitivities. standard_paragraphs.label: Leakage from Pressure Relief Valve (PRV)
standard_paragraphs.text: There is evidence of leakage from the boiler's Pressure Relief Valve (PRV). This valve is a safety feature designed to release water if the pressure within the boiler system becomes too high, preventing potential damage or explosion. The most common reason for leakage from the PRV is excessive pressure within the boiler system. This could be due to a malfunctioning pressure regulator, an overfilled expansion vessel, or a fault in the filling loop, which might be allowing too much water into the system. However, we are not Gas Safe engineers or heating specialists, and therefore further advice from a heating engineer would be prudent. By addressing this issue promptly, you can prevent potential damage to the boiler and ensure that your heating system operates safely and efficiently. Condition Rating 3.

Upon installation of a new modern heating system, the only positively safe and reliable way to proceed, when a back boiler is no longer needed and if you wish to continue using the fireplace, is to totally remove the back boiler installation by breaking up the chamber that used to carry the hot water system and by removing any pipe work. standard_paragraphs.label: NEW-Old system Should be replaced (AMEND)
standard_paragraphs.text: Inside the cupboard adjacent to the bathroom, there is a cold water tank and a separate hot water cylinder. Both components are very old and show significant signs of rust and deterioration. Upon inspecting the cold water tank, we observed water contamination, rust, sediment, and slit. These issues were evident in a photograph taken of the tank’s interior. It is important to note that water storage tanks can become breeding grounds for Legionella bacteria, which can cause Legionnaires’ disease, a form of pneumonia. Legionella bacteria are known to thrive in standing water at temperatures between 20°C and 45°C. For health and safety reasons, it is strongly recommended that the cold water tank be replaced prior to occupation, as its current condition poses a significant health hazard. We advise consulting a competent plumbing contractor to explore the replacement of these tanks with more modern systems, such as unvented hot water cylinders, if deemed suitable. Unvented hot water cylinders offer several advantages: 1. Improved Water Pressure: They are sealed and pressurised systems that supply hot water directly from the mains, providing better water pressure compared to traditional vented systems. 2. Space-Saving: They eliminate the need for a separate cold water storage tank. 3. Hygiene: Being sealed systems, they are more hygienic than vented cylinders as they do not rely on a separate, exposed tank. 4. Quieter Operation: They avoid the noise associated with refilling a cold water tank. 5. Versatile Heating Options: They can be heated directly using immersion heaters. However, unvented cylinders may not be compatible with certain modern power showers or mixers. Additionally, they require an expansion vessel to manage pressure changes as the water heats up. As highlighted in Section F3 of this report, the hot water pressure in the flat is currently very low. A plumbing contractor should confirm whether installing an unvented system will resolve this issue or if an additional water pump might also be necessary. They will also be able to provide guidance on upgrading to a system that offers improved water pressure and eliminates the outdated components. Please note, we are not heating specialists or plumbers. The information provided is general in nature and intended to assist you. Further advice from a qualified plumbing professional is essential. standard_paragraphs.label: Combi boiler
standard_paragraphs.text: Hot water is provided by the combination boiler (see Section F4). This type of system usually removes the need for cold and hot water storage, thus reducing energy consumption. Typically with combination boiler domestic hot water systems, the flow rates through the hot taps are not particularly good, especially when more than one tap is in use. When hot water is needed, it can only be supplied at the speed at which the boiler can heat the water. Accordingly, filling of baths can take a long time in comparison with a conventional system, where stored hot water can be drawn off from a hot water cylinder.

standard_paragraphs.text: The boiler supplies hot water to be stored in the pressurised hot water cylinder, located in the boiler cupboard. The cylinder is large and should be able to supply the hot water requirements of the property. This type of cylinder has a pressure relief valve, which can discharge water through an overflow pipe. The pipe contains a tundish, which is principally to provide a break in the pipe so that cross contamination cannot occur. The tundish is open, offering a visual window into the flow of water through the overflow pipe. During the survey it was noted that there was a constant flow of water through the overflow. You need to contact someone who is familiar with installing and servicing un-vented hot water cylinders and who can determine where the fault(s) are and carry out the appropriate repairs.

standard_paragraphs.label: Pitch fibre pipes
standard_paragraphs.text: The underground drainage in this property contains sections of pitch fibre pipes. These are pitch impregnated fibre conduits which were briefly popular in the 1960s and 70s, but are no longer used. Whilst many installations are still in serviceable condition, it has been found that when subjected to pressure, such as might occur when the pipes were set on bricks before back? filling the trenches, they tend to suffer deformation in shape and in severe cases the pipes have been known to become flattened, causing blockages. Drainage installations of this type are often found to be leaking and in poor condition. If this occurs, the defective drains have to be taken up and replaced. Above ground drainage

standard_paragraphs.label: French drain required
standard_paragraphs.text: As mentioned before in section D4, external ground levels are too high. A distance of 150mm (6 inches) should be maintained between external levels and the damp proof course and internal floor levels in order to prevent the risk of damp penetration. Also, there is no adequate provision of drainage to external grounds and in heavy rains this may cause water ponding which increases the risk of penetrating dampness. A small trench should be dug around the external walls of the property. This need only be approximately 150 mm width from the wall and infilled with stones, ideally with a French Drain (perforated pipe) beneath this, channeling the water away to a suitable outlet. The previous recommendations for infilling with Pea Shingle have now been superseded as it has been found that this finer material in fact holds moisture. Condition Rating 3.

standard_paragraphs.label: Bamboo in neighbouring proprty
standard_paragraphs.text: There are bamboo plants growing at the neighbouring property to the ||left/right/rear||. Bamboo rhizomes in the ground can quickly spread far and wide, popping up new shoots along the way. Small sections of the rhizome can produce new bamboo plants easily, so careful management of the plant itself and the soil it inhabits is essential. If bamboo gets out of control, it can cause major problems for homeowners and cause damage to the boundaries and pavings, and sometimes cause structural damage to retaining walls and steps. Further advice from an Invasive Weed Management company would be prudent. Your legal advisor should enquire from the vendor as to whether there are any current disputes which you should be aware of prior to purchase. If the owner of the Bamboo plants is not willing to prune the growth to a reasonable size, it could potentially give rise to legal disputes in the future. We would suggest that with the current Vendor's consent you approach the owner of the bamboo plants and enquire as to whether they are prepared to regularly manage the bamboo plants in the future before any legal commitment to purchase has been entered into. Your legal advisor should provide you with further advice. (See sections I2 & H3).

standard_paragraphs.text: There is a Cherry tree situated at the front of the property, positioned within the public pathway. Whilst this tree did not seem to have caused any direct damage to the building, it was evident that the tree had exerted some pressure on the street pathway and the front enclosure of the property. This included noticeable deflection in the pathway and front boundary wall, where we also observed signs of a crack in the brickwork, likely caused by the tree roots pushing the ground up. This issue may pose as a continuous maintenance concern in the future, as any repairs made to the boundary wall or grounds of the front enclosure may reoccur after subsequent repairs. Proper management of the tree, including regular pruning to prevent it from exceeding its current size, is strongly recommended at an early stage. Since the tree is situated in the public pathway adjacent to the property, it is presumed that the maintenance of this tree falls under the responsibility of the local council. standard_paragraphs.label: Water butt
standard_paragraphs.text: There is a Water Butt in the garden. We recommend that the water be emptied regularly in order to avoid risk of water overflowing. A note of warning that water butts can be a breeding ground for Legionella bacteria, which can lead to Legionnaire’s Disease, a kind of pneumonia. The L. pneumonophila bacteria is known to multiply in standing water between temperatures of 20°C to 45°C. To make sure your water butt is safe, the RHS ( Royal Horticultural Society recommend) emptying it and scrubbing it out once a year. It also suggests insulating them to “reduce temperatures increasing in warm weather or paint them with a light colour to reflect the heat”. H — Issues for your legal advisers H1 Regulation

standard_paragraphs.label: Extra Information
standard_paragraphs.text: Work to refit a kitchen or bathroom with new units and fittings does not generally require Building Regulation approval, although drainage or electrical work that forms part of the refit may require approval under the regulations. If a bathroom or kitchen is to be provided in a room where there wasn’t one before, Building Regulation approval is likely to be required to ensure that the room will have adequate ventilation and drainage and meet the requirements in respect of structural stability, electrical and fire safety. In general terms, where 25% or more of a thermal element is being renovated, Building Regulations would normally apply (thermal elements include roofs, walls, and ground floors). The thermal insulation of the element would have to meet the standards required by the Building Regulations. If regulations or requirements have been breached or work carried out without, or not in accordance with the necessary approvals and/or requirements, then extensive and costly alteration works may well be needed to ensure compliance. The building will not satisfy a variety of contemporary standards of construction and performance criteria set out in the current Building Regulations such as, for example, thermal insulation. This statement is true of the vast majority of buildings in the UK. The statute under which the Building Regulations are made in the UK is the Building Act 1984. Neither this Act, nor the Regulations themselves are applicable retrospectively. This avoids the need for constant improvement of properties to satisfy current standards. photovoltaic panel NEW AMEND:

standard_paragraphs.label: SOLAR PANELS
standard_paragraphs.text: The property has solar photovoltaic (PV) panels designed to produce electricity for the house. These have been fitted to the front roof slope. In this type of system, the panels absorb sunlight, which is then converted into electricity by an inverter. This electricity can typically be used straightaway to power household appliances, or stored in a battery for later use when sunlight is unavailable. In some cases, any excess electricity that is not utilised or stored can be fed back into the grid. However, the vendor mentioned they do not have this arrangement in place, although we cannot comment on the accuracy of this statement. It should be confirmed by your legal adviser whether the photovoltaic panels fitted to this property are wholly owned by the vendor or are leased. There are different types of leasing agreements available, and your legal adviser should provide details on the agreement and, if so, whether the lease is lender-approved; some leasing agreements may not be lender compliant and thus reduce the suitability of this property for mortgage security, potentially restricting its saleability. Having PV panels on a residential property, especially under a lender-approved leasing scheme, can have notable implications for secured lending purposes. When the panels are leased rather than owned outright, the leasing agreement typically involves a third-party company retaining ownership of the PV system. This can create complications for lenders when the property is used as security for a loan, as the lease may need to be transferred to a new buyer in the event of a sale, or the lender may require the lease to be terminated or re-negotiated. Lenders often assess the impact of the lease on the property’s value and marketability. Furthermore, the terms of the lease could restrict the lender’s rights to repossess or sell the property if the borrower defaults, as the third-party leasing company may have a legal interest in the panels. Your legal adviser should advise further on all matters regarding any lease, if applicable, and how this would affect you as the purchaser of the property, to ensure there are no issues with financing or legal transfer. Your legal adviser should also advise on the repair and maintenance liabilities of the photovoltaic panels. Some leasing agreements may require the homeowner to maintain the panels themselves. We have not inspected or tested the panels. We also have not undertaken any tests on any associated equipment or meters, and we cannot confirm the adequacy and functionality of the equipment. We are not specialists, and any such tests would, in any case, fall outside the scope of a Home Survey. The service records should be checked, and, if the system has not been serviced within the last 12 months, a service should be commissioned from a specialist. It would nevertheless be advisable for you to ask an appropriately qualified specialist to inspect and report on this installation if it is important to you. According to the Planning Portal, “The installation of solar panels and equipment on residential buildings and land may be ‘permitted development’, meaning there is no need to apply to the local authority for planning permission.” However, there are important limits and conditions that must be met to benefit from these permitted development rights. We are not legal advisers and are not familiar with the specific regulations set by the relevant local authority regarding the installation of solar panels on the front roof slope, which has altered the appearance of the property, particularly as none of the adjoining properties have solar panels installed. Therefore, your solicitor should make further enquiries and advise you on the implications of this. They should also consult with the local authority to determine whether all the relevant limits and conditions have been met. For instance, planning permission may be required if the property is subject to an Article 4 Direction, which restricts certain development rights. Your solicitor should investigate this and provide you with further advice. If there is any uncertainty about whether the installation meets the permitted development criteria, we recommend asking the current vendor to apply for a Lawful Development Certificate (LDC). Even if the works are believed to be lawful under permitted development rights, having written confirmation from the council that planning permission was not required can be valuable. An LDC is not the same as planning permission but serves as proof that the work complies with the law. Obtaining an LDC is particularly helpful when selling the property in the future, as it provides clarity for potential buyers and their legal representatives. The vendor can apply for an LDC through the local council using the Planning Portal’s secure online application service, although a fee will be required. If requesting an LDC from the vendor might delay the sale process, you could apply for it yourself after purchasing the property, though this carries some risk. Should the installation require planning permission, there is the potential for enforcement action. Your solicitor can advise you on this matter.

standard_paragraphs.label: Window replacement
standard_paragraphs.text: Should you decide to replace or repair the windows, you may require planning consent. Replacing windows in a conservation area often requires careful consideration due to stricter regulations aimed at preserving the character and appearance of such areas. Generally, if you are replacing windows on a "like-for-like" basis, meaning that the new windows are of the same style, materials, and appearance as the original ones, you might not need planning permission. However, some conservation areas have Article 4 Directions in place, which remove certain permitted development rights. If this is the case, you may need planning permission for like-for-like replacements. Additionally, different local authorities have varying regulations and standards for conservation areas. It is essential to check with your local planning authority to understand the specific requirements and whether planning permission is needed. To be certain, it is always best to contact your local planning authority for advice. Your solicitor should provide further advice and confirm the implications of this matter with you. There is an additional factor to consider in that you may require the permission of the building management. Your legal adviser should confirm the maintenance agreement of the windows, any stipulations set out by the management company in relation to the repair and replacement of windows, and any complications which could arise in the undertaking of repair or replacement works in the future.

If a certificate is not available, a CML Professional Consultant Certificate ( PCC) which will be suitable for most mortgagee’s lenders must be obtained. This advice is very important to follow as you will have no contractual rights against the construction contractors or professional advisers engaged by the current owner unless such rights were conferred during the course of the negotiations to purchase the property for example by having an assignment of the vendor’s right against the contractors and professional advisers. standard_paragraphs.text: NOTE: As mentioned before in section E1, as the roof space has been converted and all areas of the roof voids are concealed from view, without intrusive investigations and opening up the structure, which is outside the scope of a home survey, we cannot confirm whether adequate insulation or ventilation has been provided in the roof voids, nor can we confirm the adequacy of the structure. It is important to ensure that adequate consents have been obtained, including Building Regulations approval. This is particularly crucial, as in recent months, it has come to our attention that some high street lenders, during the process of secured lending valuation, have stated that the valuer has been unable to provide a valuation figure for the property due to fire safety risks. Before proceeding, they require more information to be provided, including either the original Building Regulations completion certificate for the works, a Regularisation Certificate, or a Chartered Building Surveyor’s report with specific comments on the structural integrity of the conversion, means of escape, and provision of an adequate pre-warning alarm system, including any necessary recommended works to improve the safety of the conversion, along with an estimated cost. Alternatively, if these cannot be obtained, the lender will require confirmation from the mortgage applicant, acknowledging that health and safety, and fire risk concerns mean the attic room can never be used as habitable accommodation. Where this option is chosen, the applicant must acknowledge that the valuer, completing an inspection on behalf of the mortgage lender, has identified shortcomings in the design, specification, and construction of the attic room/ loft conversion, with associated concerns regarding health and fire safety, neither a Building Regulation completion certificate nor a Regularisation Certificate is available, and hence, the loft room cannot be used for living or sleeping purposes and it should only be used for storage, and the valuation for mortgage purposes will reflect this situation. We are unable to specifically comment on the rationale of mortgage lenders and valuers or the suitability of their advice, as each lender has different policies regarding secured lending. From our experience, applying to different mortgage providers can lead to varying results or evaluations. In such cases, we cannot provide further commentary. If any potential future requests arise from your lender (if applicable) or from prospective purchasers of the property once you own it, this issue may come up, and lenders may require the criteria mentioned above to be met before approving a mortgage application. Since the conversion was presumably completed many years ago, it is likely that it does not meet current regulations unless improvements have been made, such as in insulation and ventilation. However, this cannot be confirmed without intrusive investigations, which are beyond the scope of a home survey. Older structures often fall short of modern building standards regarding structural soundness, ventilation, or insulation, and some upgrades are usually expected. Confirming these conditions would require intrusive investigations and opening up the structure, which, as mentioned, is outside the scope of our survey. It is important to note that finding a qualified professional to undertake such an inspection may be challenging, and it is not a service our company offers. Therefore, the best approach would be to obtain Building Regulations approval or a Regularisation Certificate, if possible. However, be mindful that this process may involve property inspections and potential delays due to necessary structural investigations. Unfortunately, commenting further on this matter is outside the scope of our survey engagement. In summary, obtaining Building Regulations approval or, if not available, a Regularisation Certificate would be the best documentation for you should you decide to sell your property in the future. If not, you may risk future buyers finding it difficult to obtain a mortgage unless the above requirements are met, which may not be easily achievable.

For all such works, it is strongly advised that your solicitor confirms the availability of a Building Warranty or a Professional Consultants’ Certificate (PCC) to provide cover for latent defects and the quality of workmanship. Whilst Building Regulations approval confirms that minimum safety standards have been met, it does not offer indemnity for workmanship or long-term reliability. This is particularly important in respect of more recent extensions and alterations. A PCC is issued by an architect or suitably qualified professional consultant who has supervised the construction. This certificate confirms that the structure has been constructed to a satisfactory standard and in general accordance with the approved Building Regulations drawings. It remains valid for six years from the date of issue and must be supported by an insurance policy providing sufficient indemnity to address any construction-related defects that may arise during that period. Your legal adviser should ensure that adequate warranty and insurance cover are in place, as without this, you will have no contractual rights against the contractors or professionals engaged by the current owner unless such rights have been formally assigned to you as part of the purchase. In many cases, such warranties or PCCs may not exist, which exposes you to the risk of hidden defects. If this is the case, you may need to either accept that risk or obtain the seller’s consent to inspect and expose hidden construction elements, which could be disruptive and costly. You should also budget for any potential remedial works. It should be noted that indemnity cover typically lasts only six to ten years. You and your legal adviser should therefore make formal enquiries with the seller to determine whether any guarantees are available for the property, and if so, ensure that they are valid and fully transferable to you as the purchaser.

standard_paragraphs.label: Leasehold properties MANDATORY
standard_paragraphs.text: You should ask your legal adviser to investigate and advise upon the following: Your legal adviser should make enquiries in relation to the management of the common areas of the building, your shared maintenance agreement, and confirm whether any major works are planned or anticipated within the next service charge years. We recommend that you request your legal adviser to investigate the existence of any covenants or encumbrances of an onerous or restrictive nature affecting the building or any rights of way in relation to the property, and also the existence of any current planning applications regarding adjoining properties or land. Your legal adviser should confirm that the usual easements and rights of way exist in respect of flats and make further enquiries regarding the existence of covenants and cross-covenants for maintenance and the repair of common parts. We have not studied the lease of the property. Your solicitor should check whether the lease has more than 85 years remaining and confirm that there are no onerous covenants or restrictions within it. We always advise that if the lease is close to 85 years, you should consider extending it as soon as possible. Extending the lease of a property with a short term remaining becomes increasingly expensive as the lease length decreases. This becomes particularly more expensive once the lease falls below 80 years, therefore any notice under Section 42 for a lease extension must be served before that deadline. Commenting further is outside the scope of our service and we require separate instruction should the client wish to extend the lease. You should confirm with your legal adviser that the ground rent is non-escalating. Given a typical lease that applies to leasehold properties, you are proposing to enter into a contract that is effectively a full repairing and insuring lease. In simple terms, this means there are certain costs within the four walls of your flat for which you are responsible, and common expenses—such as external walls, the roof, internal common parts, and in all probability the front area of the property—would be maintained by the landlord, with the cost of that maintenance shared on a pro-rata basis between the leaseholders of the property. Your solicitor should make enquiries regarding the management accounts for the past three years and any future envisaged maintenance on the property. Your solicitor should also make enquiries regarding the establishment of what is known as a sinking fund. This is a provision whereby the landlord recovers sums from the tenants, over and above normal annual expenditure. The purpose of this additional payment is to be set aside in a safe investment and used to fund the cost of extraordinary items. Given the existence of a sinking fund, our view is that the portion of the fund relating to the property in question should pass with the sale. It is assumed all maintenance costs and service charges will be reasonably apportioned between the flat owners within the building, as previously mentioned, although it would be advisable for your solicitor to investigate this. Your legal adviser should ascertain responsibilities regarding insurance and maintenance and ensure that the appropriate reciprocal repairing covenants are in place to allow for adequate external maintenance to be carried out. We are not aware of any other significant considerations affecting the property, however, it is possible that relevant matters may come to light as a result of the enquiries made by your legal adviser. standard_paragraphs.label: NEW LONG PARA (AMEND AS APPROPRIATE)
standard_paragraphs.text: We could not ascertain whether the building contains Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (RAAC). RAAC is a lightweight form of precast concrete that was widely used in the UK from the 1950s to the 1990s. RAAC was primarily used by municipal architects in offices, schools, hospitals, and commercial properties, but it has also been found in a wide range of other buildings, some of which are not in the public sector. RAAC differs from traditional concrete in that it contains air bubbles, making it lightweight and easier to handle. RAAC has been used particularly in roof panels, but it can also be found in flooring, cladding, and other structural components. This list is not exhaustive. We understand that the building was constructed in the 1920s as a factory. Since RAAC became popular in the 1950s, it is highly unlikely that a building constructed in the 1920s would contain RAAC, as the technology and methods to produce it were not available then. Buildings from the 1920s typically used more traditional materials like concrete, steel, brick, or wood. Therefore, it is unlikely that the original structure contains RAAC. However, given that the building underwent extensive structural alterations when it was converted into residential flats in the 1990s, we cannot rule out the possibility that RAAC was used as part of those modifications. Although this is a rather rare scenario, it is not possible to confirm or establish definitively. RAAC is less durable than traditional concrete, and research has shown that it has a lower structural loading capacity than other reinforced concrete products. Its condition can deteriorate further if water is present due to leaks from roofs, which can compromise the reinforcement bars within RAAC planks. Without proper maintenance, these materials can degrade over time, leading to structural issues that pose safety risks. The primary risks associated with RAAC include its susceptibility to cracking, delamination, and loss of strength due to factors like moisture infiltration, environmental stress, and natural aging. These risks can lead to unexpected structural failures, endangering the safety of building occupants and necessitating costly repairs or retrofits. RAAC is also sensitive to changes in temperature and humidity, which can accelerate deterioration and further compromise its structural integrity. Buildings with RAAC components require regular inspections to identify signs of degradation, such as sagging ceilings, visible cracks, or water leaks. Since the building has a concrete frame with concrete elements in various locations, there's a possibility that RAAC might be present. However, we are not specialists and have not conducted any intrusive investigations or specialized tests to confirm its presence. As your surveyor, it's our duty to highlight any potential risks associated with the property, and you should be aware of the worst-case scenario. Your solicitor should inquire with the building management to determine if RAAC has been detected or if there is any information in their records, including any action plans related to this matter. If RAAC has been or is identified, it could significantly impact the future saleability of the property and, more importantly, affect the health and safety of the building's occupants. Given that RAAC is a relatively new topic, it's possible that some high-street lenders might decide not to lend on properties containing this material in the future. While this is a worst-case scenario, these are risks you should be aware of before purchasing the property. Please consult your legal advisor about these risks and confirm with the building management whether there is any information on RAAC or if there is adequate building insurance to cover any future defects arising from its potential presence. Your legal adviser should make enquires in relation to the management of the common areas of the building, your shared maintenance agreement and confirm whether any major works are planned or anticipated within the next service charge years. We recommend you request your Legal Advisor to investigate the existence of any covenants or encumbrances of an onerous or restrictive nature affecting the building or any rights of way in relation to the property, and also as to the existence of any current planning applications with regard to adjoining properties or land.

standard_paragraphs.label: General Risk
standard_paragraphs.text: There are a number of trees within possible influencing distance of the property, on suspected shrinkable subsoil. Whilst these do not appear to have caused damage to the building, proper management including pruning if appropriate to prevent them exceeding their current size is recommended at an early stage (See section G3). Tree roots can exert physical pressure on foundations and cause direct movement. On a clay subsoil, in particular, movement can occur due to their ability to absorb large amounts of moisture, which results in severe expansion and contraction of the subsoil. Tree roots extract moisture, causing shrinkage in the subsoil on which the foundations are bearing, particularly during drought conditions when shrinkage of the subsoil can cause subsidence of the foundations. Conversely, when trees are removed swelling of the subsoil can occur causing 'heave' resulting in upward movement of foundations. Tree roots can also cause disturbance to underground drains and service pipes which again can result in movement. Arrangements should be made for the trees to be kept regularly pruned to prevent them from increasing in size. An Arboriculturist report should be undertaken into the trees to report on the management and future maintenance strategy. We are not aware if any of these trees are subject to tree preservation order (TPO). A TPO is an order made by a local planning authority in England to protect specific trees. An order prohibits cutting down, topping, lopping, uprooting, wildful damage and wildful destruction of trees without the local planning’s written consent. If ||the owner/the owners|| of the Bamboo plants ||is not/are not|| willing to prune the growth to a reasonable size, it could potentially give rise to legal disputes in the future. We would suggest that with the current Vendor's consent you approach ||the owner/the owners|| of the bamboo plants and enquire as to whether they are prepared to regularly manage the bamboo plants before any legal commitment to purchase has been entered into. Your legal advisor should provide you with further advice. (See section H3)

standard_paragraphs.label: Trees close to building

Whilst these do not appear to have caused damage to the building, proper management including pruning if appropriate to prevent them exceeding their current size is recommended at an early stage (See section G3). Tree roots can cause disturbance to underground drains and service pipes which again can result in movement. Tree roots also can cause disturbance and damages to the grounds, garden pavings, boundary walls and fences. Arrangements should be made for the trees to be kept regularly pruned to prevent them from increasing in size. An Arboriculturist report should be undertaken into the trees to report on the management and future maintenance strategy. We are not aware if any of these trees are subject to tree preservation order (TPO). A TPO is an order made by a local planning authority in England to protect specific trees. An order prohibits cutting down, topping, lopping, uprooting, wildful damage and wildful destruction of trees without the local planning’s written consent. Further advice from your legal advisor is required (See section H3). I3 Risks to people

standard_paragraphs.label: Substation (EMF's) (A)
standard_paragraphs.text: The property is in an area which could be affected by electromagnetic fields as it is located next to an electrical substation. The question of whether electric and magnetic fields are linked in any way to ill-health is a long standing one which still has no conclusive answer. The possible effects of electromagnetic fields have been the subject of media coverage but the Health Protection Agency (HPA), an independent body with responsibility for advising on electromagnetic fields, has concluded that 'there is no clear evidence of adverse health effects at the levels of electromagnetic fields to which people are normally exposed'. However, because research is continuing into this topic, this view could change in the future. Public perception of this problem can affect marketability and future values. More information can be obtained from the Health Protection Agency (HPA) at 7th Floor, Holborn Gate, 330 High Holborn, London WC1V 7PP or the local electricity company. If you want reassurance, you should ask an appropriately qualified person to inspect the property and provide you with a report. You are advised to contact UK Power Networks and arrange for a specialist engineer to visit the property to undertake a risk assessment and provide you with the result of the test. standard_paragraphs.label: NEW Asbestos report is recommended
standard_paragraphs.text: It is highly recommended that a licensed asbestos contractor conducts a comprehensive report to identify the presence of asbestos materials, outline the necessary remedial actions, and provide associated cost estimates. As mentioned earlier, there is a potential presence of asbestos in various locations. Obtaining this report is particularly important if you plan to undertake renovations or alterations to the property. Legally, you are required to inform any contractor working on your property about the potential presence of asbestos. Therefore, obtaining a thorough asbestos report is the best course of action, as it will provide you with a clear understanding of any asbestos-related risks. Ideally, the report should also include cost estimates for the removal of asbestos, allowing you to anticipate any future expenses associated with its removal if asbestos is found. Asbestos materials are often concealed within the fabric of buildings or sealed building voids, making it impossible to consider the findings of any survey as completely conclusive. There is always the possibility that additional Asbestos-Containing Materials (ACMs) may be discovered during refurbishment or demolition work. Therefore, if you plan to undertake extensive renovations or alterations involving partial demolition of building elements, we strongly recommend conducting a Pre-demolition/Pre-refurbishment Asbestos Survey in these areas before proceeding with any such works.

You must treat them as though they contain asbestos unless it could be confirmed through testing that they are safe. The presence of asbestos would not normally constitute a health hazard unless the material which contains the asbestos is disturbed, drilled, or substantially damaged. When maintenance work, building improvements of alterations are undertaken, you should be mindful of the possibility of asbestos. If found, a licensed contractor will need to be employed for its removal/disposal and this could be costly.

standard_paragraphs.label: Asbestos 1
standard_paragraphs.text: Although the manufacture of asbestos-based building materials has generally ceased, many products containing asbestos can still be found both on and within buildings. These can include textured coatings, surface coatings, ceiling tiles, roof edge verges, eaves soffits, among others. Asbestos waste has also been found in lofts and floors, sometimes installed by owners as insulation. It is important to note that this list is not exhaustive.

standard_paragraphs.label: Asbestos 2
standard_paragraphs.text: Asbestos is a hazardous material and removal is expensive. Safe removal of asbestos requires trained expertise and we recommend that such work should only be carried out by a licensed asbestos removal contractor. There are regulations controlling the removal and disposal of certain types of asbestos. If you require further information as to the register of licensed contractors you should consult the local Environmental Health Officer.

standard_paragraphs.label: Asbestos 3
standard_paragraphs.text: Depending on its condition, asbestos cement found on and within domestic property can, in many cases, be left alone without causing any undue risk to the occupants. This is strictly on the basis the material is left undisturbed and unbroken, thus avoiding release of fibres. It is also normally advisable to have the surfaces sealed and it would be sensible for them to be marked to indicate the presence of asbestos.

standard_paragraphs.label: Asbestos 4
standard_paragraphs.text: Problems arise when asbestos based materials need to be removed for reasons such as maintenance or repair, and when alterations are made to a building. Depending on the function of the material, certain notifications have to be given, followed by removal by registered operatives, to disposal sites allocated specifically for this type of contaminated waste. Asbestos removal is expensive due to the substantial safety precautions which have to be taken.

Fire risk assessment for flats

standard_paragraphs.label: Fire risk - block of flats
standard_paragraphs.text: Block managers should be able to confirm that a suitable and sufficient fire risk assessment has been carried out by a competent professional; that an assessment has been undertaken within the last 12 months, that the recommendations within the action plan of the last assessment have been completed, that there have been no material changes (to the building, the fire safety measures or the occupancy) that could potentially undermine the validity of the fire risk assessment, that the assessment is compliant with the requirements of the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 and Fire Safety Act 2021 to include structure, external walls and flat entrance doors within the assessment ( See section H1). On occupation of the property, the Block Management must provide you directly with details on the evacuation strategy for the building (e.g. stay put or simultaneous evacuation), instructions on how to report a fire (e.g. use of 999 or 112, the correct address to give to the fire and rescue service, etc.), and any other instruction that tells residents what they must do when a fire has occurred. The Block Management must also provide you directly, on occupation of the property, with relevant information about the doors within the common areas, particularly flat entrance doors, and that all communal fire doors should be shut when not in use, residents and guests should not tamper with self-closing devices on fire doors and that you should report any fault with, or damage to, fire doors immediately to the Responsible Person/ Managing agent. They should also provide you with their Personal Emergency Evacuation Plan strategy which is designed to assist less-abled occupiers in evacuating the building in the event of a fire ( See section H1).

standard_paragraphs.label: Fire risk - converted flats
standard_paragraphs.text: On occupation of the property, the management company, or responsible persons managing the internal common areas, must provide you directly with details on the evacuation strategy for the building (e.g. stay put or simultaneous evacuation), instructions on how to report a fire (e.g. use of 999 or 112, the correct address to give to the fire and rescue service, etc.), and any other instruction that tells residents what they must do when a fire has occurred. The managing agent or responsible persons, must also provide you directly, on occupation of the property, with relevant information about the doors within the common areas, particularly flat entrance doors, and that all communal fire doors should be shut when not in use, residents and guests should not tamper with self-closing devices on fire doors and that you should report any fault with, or damage to, fire doors immediately to the responsible person/ managing agent. They should also provide you with their Personal Emergency Evacuation Plan strategy which is designed to assist less-abled occupiers in evacuating the building in the event of a fire, if this is necessary. Foam fill cavity wall insulation Not ascertained NEW: We were unable to confirm the presence of any retrofitted cavity wall insulation in the main walls. It is important to note that cavity wall insulation installed in the past may contain urea formaldehyde (foam fill) insulation. This type of insulation was commonly used in the 1970s and early 1980s but is no longer in use due to the associated health risks. Urea formaldehyde has garnered negative attention due to the potential for uncured materials to emit irritant gases. Over time, the insulation can degrade, releasing toxic gases that carry a carcinogenic risk for those exposed. Given the potential concerns, your solicitor should make further enquiries to confirm whether any cavity wall insulation is present at the property, and if so, whether it includes urea formaldehyde. Additional advice on this matter may also be sought from the Environmental Health Department of the Local Authority. After 1980's Unlikely to contain Urea Formaldehyde: Cavity wall insulations may contain Urea Formaldehyde (foam fill) insulation. However, Urea Formaldehyde cavity wall insulation was common in 70s and early 80s. This type of insulation is no longer used due to the health risks it poses. If the insulation has been added in 2006, we consider it unlikely that the cavity insulation may have this material. Your solicitor should make further enquiries and confirm this. There has been some negative publicity about this type of insulation regarding irritant gas being given off where the materials are uncured. Overtime, Urea Formaldehyde breaks down, releasing a toxic gas that poses a carcinogenic risk to those exposed. Further advice may be obtained from the Environmental Health Department of the Local Authority.

Older types of cavity wall insulation could possibly be Urea Formaldehyde (foam fill). Urea formaldehyde cavity wall insulation was common in the 1970s and early 1980s. This type of insulation is no longer used due to the health risks it poses. There has been negative publicity regarding this insulation, particularly concerning irritant gas being released when the materials are uncured. Over time, urea formaldehyde breaks down, releasing a toxic gas that poses a carcinogenic risk to those exposed. Your solicitor should make further enquiries and confirm the date of the cavity wall insulation, if the information is available. Further advice may be obtained from the Environmental Health Department of the local authority. Your legal advisor should be asked to investigate whether cavity insulation has been installed, the type of insulation used, and whether any guarantees exist for the work. It is important to note that cavity foam insulation can adhere to mortar droppings on wall ties, potentially creating a bridge across the cavity and leading to localised damp spots on internal walls. We recommend obtaining any relevant guarantees related to this work and ensuring that the benefit of such guarantees is transferred upon completion of the sale (see sections D4 & H2). Glass

No insulation in the ceilings and walls of loft: No insulation is provided to the walls or ceilings of the roof rooms. Rigid insulation is required in these areas. It is important that gaps are maintained between the insulation and the underside of the roof coverings or underfelt, which can be achieved by sliding rigid foam insulation slabs between the rafters. Ideally, these slabs should be 100mm thick, but it is important to maintain a 50mm ventilation gap above the slabs, and their thickness is therefore restricted by the size of the rafters. In some circumstances, it may not be possible to achieve this and it may be necessary to strip off the roof coverings to properly insulate these areas. To avoid overheating and deterioration of cables, any electric wiring in such areas will need to be encased in conduit to prevent contact with the insulation material.

standard_paragraphs.label: Roof insulation
standard_paragraphs.text: The roof space has been insulated with ||describe|| mm fibreglass quilting.

standard_paragraphs.label: Roof insulation recommendations
standard_paragraphs.text: We recommend the installation of 270mm fibreglass insulation (100mm between the ceiling joists and 170mm at right angles across the joists) in the loft, to conform to current recommended standards. Care must be taken at the edges to ensure insulation is not touching the underfelt or blocking the eaves ventilation. This will help to avoid condensation problems.

standard_paragraphs.label: Insulating above sloping ceilings
standard_paragraphs.text: The space between the rafters above the sloping ceilings requires a different type of insulation. It is important that gaps are maintained between the insulation and the underside of the roof coverings or underfelt, which can be achieved by sliding rigid foam insulation slabs between the rafters. Ideally, these slabs should be 100mm thick, but it is important to maintain a 50mm ventilation gap above the slabs, and their thickness is therefore restricted by the size of the rafters. In some circumstances, it may not be possible to achieve this and it may be necessary to strip off the roof coverings to properly insulate these areas. To avoid overheating and deterioration of cables, any electric wiring in such areas will need to be encased in conduit to prevent contact with the insulation material.

standard_paragraphs.label: New build no Ventilation system
standard_paragraphs.text: The property is constructed with modern materials and has double glazed windows/doors. New build properties usually have a ventilation system which consists of ceiling extract valves in each room connected to a ventilation unit, where ducting supplies fresh filtered air to the habitable rooms and extracts stale polluted air. However, this is not the case in this property. There is no adequate ventilation at the property, and this may be problematic in cooler temperatures and may cause condensation. This is a design issue with the building. Utilising the home; washing clothes, cooking etc all contribute to a build-up of condensation and mould can occur where there is no sufficient ventilation. However, many properties are affected to some degree by condensation and in order to minimise the problem it is necessary to achieve a balance between ventilation and heating. The constant use of dehumidifiers in cold days can help tackle condensation. Upon occupation of the property, it is likely that condensation levels will increase and black mould may appear.

standard_paragraphs.label: Adequate ventilation to the property
standard_paragraphs.text: Ventilation within the property is considered to be adequate, ||except to the roof voids?||

The current arrangement, whereby the fan simply discharges into the loft, is unsatisfactory and could lead to condensation dampness, increasing the risk of rot damage to the roof timbers. Bathroom ventilation

standard_paragraphs.label: Ventilation not working
standard_paragraphs.text: The mechanical ventilation within the bathroom (extract fan) was tested on the day of inspection and appeared not to be working. If there is no adequate ventilation in the bathroom, excess moisture can linger and deposit on surfaces, eventually allowing mould to grow and spread. We therefore recommend installing new sufficient ventilation, ideally a system that provides a minimum of three air changes per hour. We could not ascertain the final point of discharge from the current mechanical ventilation. A competent contractor should ensure there that there is a ventilation duct system which directs the moisture outside the building. You should instruct a contractor to investigate this before the installing any new ventilation. Condition Rating 2.

standard_paragraphs.label: Working but stronger is needed (No windows)
standard_paragraphs.text: The mechanical ventilation within the bathroom (extract fan) was tested on the day of inspection and whilst it appeared to be functional, the bathroom still suffers from condensation and it is our recommendation to install a new sufficient ventilation fan, ideally a Vent Axia system that provides a minimum of three air changes per hour. The fan should be programmed to be continue to run for a good long while after using the bathroom in cooler months. It would also be prudent to use a dehumidifier in the property, near bathroom area, particularly in the absence of a window in the bathroom. If there is no adequate ventilation in the bathroom, excess moisture can linger and deposit on surfaces, eventually allowing mould to grow and spread. Condition Rating 2.
